questions.text: The nucleus is:
questions.explanation: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the CNS. A ganglion is the equivalent in the PNS. Nerve fibers form tracts or nerves, not nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus = cluster of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS
options: A group of cell bodies within peripheral nervous system.
A group of cell bodies within central nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within peripheral nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within central nervous system.
A collection of nerve fibers in brain stem.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve that carries the sensation for the lower eyelid is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the upper eyelid and forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from the lower eyelid
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Loss of sensation from lower eye lid indicates injury of:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits through the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. Loss of sensation indicates injury to this nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid skin
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The 2 frontal bellies:
questions.explanation: The two frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle originate from the skin of the eyebrows and interdigitate with the orbicularis oculi. They are not attached to the superior temporal line.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis originate from skin of eyebrows
options: Form the only muscle of face.
Are attached to superior temporal line.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Orbicularis oris originates from:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle originates from the modiolus (a fibromuscular condensation at the angle of the mouth) and inserts into the lips. It acts as the sphincter of the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris originates from the modiolus
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Facial artery:
questions.explanation: The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. It has a tortuous course to accommodate jaw movements and ends at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery has a tortuous course and anastomoses with ophthalmic branches at the medial eye angle
options: Is a branch of internal carotid artery.
Enters face at antero-inferior angle of Buccinator.
Ends by anastomosing with supraorbital artery.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The main sensory nerve of the lower lip is:
questions.explanation: The mental nerve, a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division, V3), exits through the mental foramen to supply the skin of the lower lip and chin.
questions.keyConcept: Mental nerve (V3) is the main sensory nerve of the lower lip
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards orbicularis oculi muscle, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi has bony attachments both medially (medial palpebral ligament) and laterally (lateral palpebral raphe). Therefore, the statement that it has no medial bony attachment is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi has bony attachments medially and laterally
options: Its lacrimal part helps drainage of tears.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its orbital part has no bony attachment medially.
Its palpebral part lies in the eyelids.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The Occipito-frontalis muscle:
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The frontalis portion inserts into the epicranial aponeurosis.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis elevates the eyebrows
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sphincter of the lips is the:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle of the lips. The buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris = sphincter of the lips
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the occipital bellies of occipito-frontalis, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The two occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis are separated by the median tendinous intersection and take origin from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital bellies originate from the highest nuchal line
options: They are separated by an extension of epicranial aponeurosis.
They take origin from epicranial aponeurosis.
They are inserted into lateral 2/3 of highest nuchal line.
They are supplied by temporal branch of facial nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In adults, the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically terminates at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). In neonates, it ends at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Adult spinal cord ends at L1; neonatal spinal cord ends at L3
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In adults the spinal cord usually terminates at the:
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically ends at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is important clinically to avoid spinal cord injury during lumbar puncture, which is performed below this level.
questions.keyConcept: Adult conus medullaris ends at lower border of L1
options: Upper border of the 12th thoracic vertebra.
Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 4th lumbar vertebra.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced:
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1–L2 in adults) to avoid cord injury. The needle is typically introduced at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5 to avoid conus medullaris
options: Below or above tip of 4th L spine.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: At birth, the conus medullaris ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: At birth, the conus medullaris is located at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). It ascends to L1–L2 by adulthood due to differential growth.
questions.keyConcept: Birth conus medullaris at L3; ascends to L1–L2 in adults
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is purely sensory?
questions.explanation: The dorsal root of the spinal nerve is purely sensory, containing afferent fibers from the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor/efferent. The mixed spinal nerve trunk and its rami contain both sensory and motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root = purely sensory
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the nuclei of the anterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nuclear group extends at all levels of the spinal cord and supplies the axial muscles. Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal fibers; gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal fibers. The medial group supplies axial muscles, while the lateral group supplies limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anteromedial nucleus extends at all cord levels and supplies axial muscles
options: Its alpha neurons supply intrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anteromedial nucleus extends in all levels of spinal cord.
Its medial nuclear group supply muscles of limbs.
Its gamma neurons supply extrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anterolateral nucleus supplies muscles of hands & feet.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The ability to recognize an unseen familiar object placed in the hand depends on the integrity of which tract?
questions.explanation: Recognizing a familiar object by touch (stereognosis) requires fine touch and proprioception, carried by the cuneate tract from the upper limb. The gracile tract carries these sensations from the lower body.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Gracile tract:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract conveys proprioceptive and fine touch sensations from the lower half of the body. It carries impulses from T7 spinal segment and below, with its fibers passing medially to the cuneate tract.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract carries proprioception from lower body
options: Its sacral fibers are most lateral.
Originates from neurons of lamina I.
Terminates in ventral posterior lateral nucleus of thalamus (VPMN).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cuneate tract:
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract begins at the C8 spinal segment and carries conscious proprioception and fine touch from the upper limb. It does not start at mid-thoracic region—that level marks the beginning of the gracile tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract starts at C8, carries upper limb proprioception
options: Its main 2nd neuron is the accessory cuneate nucleus.
Its 3rd neuron passes in the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Its 3rd neuron terminates in the precentral gyrus.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Conscious proprioception from right lower limb are carried by:
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception from the right lower limb is carried by the right gracile tract, which ascends ipsilaterally in the posterior column and decussates in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract is ipsilateral for lower limb proprioception
options: Tracts of left posterior white column.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The left spinal lemniscus carries sensations of:
questions.explanation: The left spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature from the right side of the body (after decussation). Fine touch and proprioception use the medial lemniscus, not the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus carries contralateral crude sensation
options: Pain from the left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from the left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of the body.
Crude touch from the right side of the body.
Fine touch from right side of body.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The medial most fibers of the gracile tract are:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract carries sensations from the lower body. Sacral fibers are most medial (closest to the midline), while cervical fibers are most lateral in this tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers are most medial in gracile tract
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion in the right gracile tract leads to loss of:
questions.explanation: A lesion in the right gracile tract affects proprioception and fine touch from the right lower limb. Vibration sense testing of the right tibia would be diminished because this tract carries vibration sense.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion affects ipsilateral lower limb vibration
options: Sense of position of left big toe.
Sense of movement of right elbow joint.
Feeling of a pencil put in the right hand.
Site of touch on the right iliac fossa.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient suffered UMNL paralysis in the left lower limb with loss of vibration sense in the same limb and loss of pain sensation in the right lower limb; the most-likely lesion is:
questions.explanation: Right hemisection (Brown-Sequard): ipsilateral UMNL paralysis, ipsilateral loss of vibration/position sense, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature starting one level below. The description matches right hemisection.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss
options: Complete transaction of the spinal cord below TI.
Left hemisection of the spinal cord.
Right hemisection of the spinal cord.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For each statement in the left column, choose the appropriate artery in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests blood supply: radicular arteries form the main supply to lumbar segments; anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horn and lateral horn.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior horn

pairs.premise: 1) Form most blood supply to lumbar segments of spinal cord.
2) Supply lateral horn of spinal cord.
3) May arise from posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
4) Descend in the form of 4 longitudinal arteries.
5) Form the main supply of the cervical part of the spinal cord.

questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe shape of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly, extending from foramen magnum to the lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements (cervical at C5-T1 and lumbar at L2-S3) and shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus). It tapers inferiorly to form the conus medullaris. This shape is clinically important for lumbar puncture and understanding segmental anatomy.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord cylindrical shape, flattening, extensions, and conus medullaris
questions.modelAnswer: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly. It extends from foramen magnum to lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements: cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3). It shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus) and gradual tapering at its lower end (conus medullaris).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe nuclei of lateral horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lateral horn exists at two levels with different functions: T1-L2 contains the intermediolateral nucleus (cell column) for preganglionic sympathetic neurons (sympathetic outflow); S2-S4 contains the sacral parasympathetic nucleus for preganglionic parasympathetic neurons (rest and digest function). The lateral horn is absent at other levels.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: sympathetic (T1-L2 via intermediolateral nucleus) and parasympathetic (S2-S4 via sacral parasympathetic nucleus)
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of lateral horn: (1) Lateral horn is present from C8-L2 (sympathetic outflow) and S2-S4 (parasympathetic outflow). (2) Sympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Intermediolateral nucleus (cell column of T1-L2) - preganglionic sympathetic neurons; (3) Parasympathetic lateral horn nuclei: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2-S4) - preganglionic parasympathetic neurons.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Injury to the right paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The right paracentral lobule controls the left leg. Since motor pathways cross (decussate), injury to the right paracentral lobule causes paralysis of the contralateral (left) lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Right paracentral lobule controls left leg
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Frontal eye field.
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) controls voluntary conjugate eye movements. Lesions cause inability to look toward the opposite side (loss of conjugate eye deviation).
questions.keyConcept: Frontal eye field controls voluntary eye movement
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Superior parietal lobule.
questions.explanation: The superior parietal lobule is involved in spatial awareness and stereognosis (ability to recognize objects by touch). Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and hemispatial neglect.
questions.keyConcept: Superior parietal lobule mediates stereognosis
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: One of the following is not a content of the interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a space between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the oculomotor nerve, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, posterior perforated substance, and cerebral peduncles. The anterior perforated substance is lateral to the optic tract, not in the interpeduncular fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior perforated substance not in interpeduncular fossa
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column (GVA & SVA)?
questions.explanation: Special visceral afferent nuclei receive taste sensation. The nucleus solitarius (particularly its gustatory part) receives taste fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral afferent - taste fibers
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Somatic efferent column of nuclei includes:
questions.explanation: The nucleus that receives taste fibers is the nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus), particularly its rostral/gustatory part. It receives SVA fibers from CN VII (via chorda tympani), IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste sensation
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the somatic efferent column?
questions.explanation: This matching tests nuclei: facial nucleus - facial muscles; nucleus ambiguus - pharyngeal muscles; dorsal motor nucleus of X - visceral organs. All are branchiomotor or visceral motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe ligaments of temporomandibular joint.
questions.explanation: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is supported by several ligaments that provide stability and limit excessive range of motion. These ligaments prevent posterior and inferior displacement of the condyle and protect neurovascular structures.
questions.keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral, sphenomandibular, stylomandibular. Lateral ligament strengthens joint capsule; sphenomandibular is accessory ligament; stylomandibular limits protrusion.
questions.modelAnswer: Ligaments of the temporomandibular joint: (1) Lateral ligament—runs from the tubercle of zygomatic arch to the lateral aspect of the mandibular neck, strengthens the lateral side of the joint capsule and prevents posterior displacement of the condyle. (2) Sphenomandibular ligament—runs from the sphenoid spine to the lingula of mandible, an accessory ligament derived from Meckel's cartilage that suspends the mandible. (3) Stylomandibular ligament—runs from the styloid process to the angle of mandible, limits excessive protrusion of the mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe branches of inferior alveolar nerve.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve is the largest branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It enters the mandibular foramen and runs within the mandibular canal, giving off dental branches to all lower teeth and terminating as the mental nerve which provides sensation to the chin and lower lip.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior alveolar nerve supplies all lower teeth via dental branches and ends as mental nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the inferior alveolar nerve include: (1) Mylohyoid nerve—a motor branch given off before entering the mandibular foramen, supplying the mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric. (2) Dental branches—supplying the pulp of all lower teeth (incisors, canines, premolars, and molars). (3) Interdental branches—supplying the interdental gingiva and periodontal ligaments. (4) Mental nerve—terminal branch emerging through the mental foramen to supply the skin and mucous membrane of the chin and lower lip. (5) Incisive branch—continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve anteriorly to supply lower incisors and canines.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The tensor tympani muscle is attached to the malleus and is derived from the mesoderm of the:
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle is derived from mesoderm of the first branchial arch, specifically the first arch mesoderm. It is innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3) and attaches to the malleus to dampen sound vibrations. The pre-otic and occipital somites give axial muscles, not branchial arch muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor tympani derived from 1st arch mesoderm; innervated by CN V3; attaches to malleus.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Each of the following cells is derived from the neuroepithelial cells EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS and are derived from MONOCYTES (mesodermal origin), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. Neuroepithelial cells give rise to ependymal cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (all neuroglia), and motor neurons. Microglia are unique among CNS cells in being mesodermal in origin.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocytes), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. All other glial cells and neurons come from neuroepithelial cells.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The spinal cord in newly born infant reaches the level of:
questions.explanation: In the newborn infant, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris (end of spinal cord) reaches L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar punctures—needle insertion below L3 avoids spinal cord injury in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord in newborn reaches L3 vertebra; in adults it ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe the derivatives & nerve supply of 3rd pharyngeal arch.
questions.explanation: The third pharyngeal arch has the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) as its nerve. Skeletal derivatives include the greater horn of the hyoid and lower part of the body. The only muscular derivative is the stylopharyngeus muscle. The common carotid artery and internal carotid artery also arise from the third arch.
questions.keyConcept: 3rd arch: nerve CN IX; skeletal = greater cornu/lower hyoid body; muscle = stylopharyngeus; vessels = common and internal carotid.
questions.modelAnswer: Third pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Greater horn of hyoid bone and lower part of body of hyoid (from Reichert's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Stylopharyngeus muscle (the only muscle of the 3rd arch). (4) Vascular derivatives: Common carotid artery and proximal part of internal carotid artery. The stylopharyngeus is the only muscle innervated by CN IX.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament is called:
questions.explanation: The membrana tectoria is the upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament that covers the dens and cruciate ligaments of the atlas. It extends from the body of the axis to the basiocciput, covering the odontoid process. The alar ligaments connect the dens to the occipital condyles; the apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
questions.keyConcept: Membrana tectoria = upward extension of posterior longitudinal ligament covering dens and cruciate ligaments; covers C1-C2 joint.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The structure attached to the side of the odontoid process of the axis vertebra is the:
questions.explanation: The alar ligaments are a pair of strong ligaments attached to the sides of the odontoid process (dens) of the axis vertebra. They connect the dens to the occipital condyles and limit rotation of the head. The apical ligament connects the tip of the dens to the anterior rim of the foramen magnum; the transverse ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas.
questions.keyConcept: Alar ligaments attach to SIDES of odontoid process and connect to occipital condyles; limit head rotation.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The type of the atlanto-occipital joint is:
questions.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint is a CONDYLAR (ellipsoid) joint that allows nodding (flexion and extension) and lateral bending. It does NOT allow rotation—this movement occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. The atlanto-occipital joints are synovial joints with articular capsules reinforced by anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is CONDYLAR (ellipsoid); allows flexion/extension and lateral bending, NOT rotation.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The median atlanto-axial joint:
questions.explanation: The median atlanto-axial joint is a PIVOT (trochoid) joint that allows rotation of the head (turning the head from side to side). This is the key movement tested in the question. The lateral atlanto-axial joints are also pivot joints. The atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid and allows nodding. The apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
questions.keyConcept: Median atlanto-axial joint is PIVOT type; allows head rotation. Atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid; allows nodding.
options: Has the apical ligament connecting dens to atlas.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: During a normal child delivery, the attending physician noticed a swelling at the back of a newly born infant, giving a suspicious look for a birth defect. An urgent MRI was requested to assess the structure of the spinal cord. Where should u expect the spinal cord to end in this infant
questions.explanation: In a newborn, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because the vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris ends at L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar puncture, epidural anesthesia, and avoiding spinal cord injury. This infant's spinal cord would end at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord ends at L3 in newborns; by adulthood it ends at L1-L2. Vertebral column grows faster than spinal cord.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List adverse effects of spinal anesthesia
questions.explanation: Spinal anesthesia adverse effects include hypotension (due to sympathetic blockade), post-dural puncture headache, transient neurological symptoms, and rarely infection or neurological injury. Bradycardia can occur from high block.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal anesthesia complications include hypotension, headache, and rare neurological injury.
questions.modelAnswer:
Adverse effects of spinal anesthesia:

**Cardiovascular:**
- Hypotension (most common)
- Bradycardia (high blocks)
- Cardiac arrest (rare)

**Neurological:**
- Post-dural puncture headache (most common complication)
- Transient neurological symptoms (TNS)
- Cauda equina syndrome (rare)
- Spinal headache (worse when upright)

**Infection:**
- Spinal/epidural abscess
- Meningitis

**Chemical:**
- Chemical contamination
- Adhesive arachnoiditis

**Other:**
- Urinary retention
- Nausea and vomiting (hypotension-related)
- Backache at injection site
- Failed block or inadequate anesthesia
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List adverse effects of halothane
questions.explanation: Halothane adverse effects include hepatotoxicity (halothane hepatitis), malignant hyperthermia, cardiovascular depression (bradycardia, hypotension), arrhythmias, and increased cerebral blood flow (increased ICP).
questions.keyConcept: Halothane causes hepatotoxicity, cardiovascular depression, malignant hyperthermia, and increases cerebral blood flow.
questions.modelAnswer:
Adverse effects of halothane:

**Hepatotoxicity:**
- Halothane hepatitis (immune-mediated)
- Risk increases with repeated exposure
- Can be fatal

**Malignant Hyperthermia:**
- Life-threatening hyperthermia
- Triggered by halogenated anesthetics and succinylcholine
- Requires dantrolene treatment

**Cardiovascular:**
- Bradycardia
- Hypotension (myocardial depression)
- Sensitizes myocardium to catecholamines
- Arrhythmias

**Respiratory:**
- Respiratory depression
- Bronchodilation (can be beneficial)

**CNS:**
- Increased cerebral blood flow
- Increased ICP
- Cerebrovascular dilation

**Other:**
- uterine relaxation
- Skeletal muscle relaxation
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List adverse effects of nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide adverse effects include bone marrow suppression (megaloblastic anemia with chronic use due to B12 inactivation), neurological symptoms, and contraindications in air-filled cavities (diffuses in, causing expansion).
questions.keyConcept: Chronic N2O exposure causes B12 inactivation leading to megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage.
questions.modelAnswer:
Adverse effects of nitrous oxide:

**Hematological:**
- Megaloblastic anemia (chronic use)
- Inactivates vitamin B12
- Affects DNA synthesis
- Neurological symptoms possible

**Neurological:**
- Peripheral neuropathy (with prolonged exposure)
- Myeloneuropathy
- Subacute combined degeneration

**Middle Ear:**
- Pressure effects
- Barotitis media
- Diffuses into closed spaces

**Gastrointestinal:**
- Nausea and vomiting

**Other:**
- Abuse potential
- Diffuses into pneumothorax, bowel loops
- Contraindicated in air embolism risk

**Advantages (relative safety):**
- Minimal hepatic toxicity
- Minimal respiratory depression
- Rapidly eliminated
- No carcinogenicity

questions.text: Explain why dose of thiopental should not be repeated or taken by IV infusion unlike propofol?
questions.explanation: Thiopental should not be repeated because it has a long terminal half-life due to redistribution rather than metabolism. Re-administration leads to accumulation. Propofol is suitable for infusion because it undergoes rapid hepatic metabolism, allowing steady state levels with continuous infusion.
questions.keyConcept: Thiopental accumulates due to redistribution; propofol's rapid metabolism allows continuous infusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Thiopental should not be repeated or given by IV infusion because:

**1. Redistribution kinetics:**
- Thiopental redistributes from brain to muscle and fat
- Initial half-life is short (3-8 minutes)
- Terminal half-life is very long (5-17 hours)

**2. Accumulation:**
- Repeated doses lead to accumulation in fat
- Slowly released, causing prolonged sedation
- Delayed recovery hours after stopping

**3. Metabolism:**
- Slow hepatic metabolism
- Not suitable for infusion

**Propofol advantages for infusion:**

1. **Rapid metabolism:**
   - Hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism
   - Short context-sensitive half-time
   - Suitable for TIVA and infusion

2. **Clear recovery:**
   - Even after prolonged infusion
   - No accumulation

3. **Controllable:**
   - Easy titration
   - Predictable recovery time

**Clinical practice:**
- Thiopental: Single induction dose only
- Propofol: Infusion for maintenance

questions.text: Which part of the intestine can protrude through a wound just above the umbilicus and to the left?

The jejunum begins at the duodenojejunal flexure (at L2 level, left of the midline) and occupies the left upper abdomen. The transverse colon is more centrally located at the umbilical level, sigmoid colon is in the lower left pelvis, and ileum is predominantly in the right lower abdomen and pelvis. Jejunal hernias through abdominal wall defects are clinically recognized due to the fixed mesenteric attachment at the duodenojejunal junction.

questions.text: Which type of transmission (inheritance) is common in FTLD?
questions.explanation: Model Answer: Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD) commonly shows autosomal dominant inheritance with family history in 40-50% of cases. The most common inherited pattern is autosomal dominant, particularly associated with MAPT (tau) mutations on chromosome 17.
questions.keyConcept: FTLD frequently shows autosomal dominant inheritance with MAPT mutations being the most common cause of familial forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) most commonly shows autosomal dominant inheritance. The most frequent genetic cause is mutations in the MAPT (microtubule-associated protein tau) gene on chromosome 17, which encodes the tau protein. Other autosomal dominant causes include mutations in GRN (progranulin) and C9orf72 (hexanucleotide repeat expansion). Approximately 30-40% of FTLD cases have a family history, and genetic testing often reveals pathogenic variants in these three genes.

questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fast pain (first pain) is transmitted to the CNS by which fibres?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers (myelinated, fast-conducting) transmit first/quick pain, while C fibers (unmyelinated) transmit slow, throbbing second pain.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain fibers
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which combination of drugs should be avoided because both can cause agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine and carbamazepine both cause agranulocytosis; their combination dramatically increases this risk and is contraindicated.
questions.keyConcept: Agranulocytosis drug interaction
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The only medically justified long‑term use of phenobarbital is for:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital is justified long-term only for certain epilepsies (generalized tonic-clonic, partial seizures) due to its side effect profile.
questions.keyConcept: Phenobarbital use
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The main benefit of adding carbidopa to levodopa in Sinemet is that carbidopa:
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, preventing peripheral levodopa conversion and increasing CNS availability.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa mechanism
options: Inhibits peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The potency of inhaled anaesthetics is quantitatively defined as the:
questions.explanation: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) defines potency as the alveolar concentration that prevents movement in 50% of patients to a surgical stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Inhalational anesthetic MAC
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: An important virulence factor of *Cryptococcus neoformans* is the production of:
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans produces melanin via phenol oxidase, which protects against oxidative stress and is a major virulence factor.
questions.keyConcept: Cryptococcus virulence
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which characteristic is true of *Listeria monocytogenes*?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
questions.keyConcept: Listeria cold tolerance
options: It is strictly a human pathogen.
It can grow at refrigerator temperature (4°C).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In the urea cycle, which two compounds are end products (released from the cycle)?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle products
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which enzyme is stimulated by cortisol to increase epinephrine synthesis?
questions.explanation: PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by cortisol in the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT epinephrine synthesis
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cofactor is required for the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; BH4 deficiency causes PKU.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylation
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The inborn error of branched‑chain amino acid metabolism that causes a burnt‑sugar odour in urine is:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine with characteristic sweet odor.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD biochemistry
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a coenzyme for the oxidative decarboxylation of:
questions.explanation: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids including pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain ketoacids.
questions.keyConcept: TPP coenzyme function
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death) is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, classically presenting with the 4 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra deficiency
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which vitamin is directly involved in one‑carbon transfer reactions (e.g., purine and thymidylate synthesis)?
questions.explanation: Folate (as N5, N10-methylene-THF) donates one-carbon units in purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Folate one-carbon transfer
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Methyl‑THF donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form:
questions.explanation: Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
questions.keyConcept: Methyl-THF function
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following releases free ammonia in the body?
questions.explanation: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia production
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP are allosteric activators of glutamate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase regulation
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is activated by:
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate) is the essential allosteric activator of CPS I, the first urea cycle enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I activation
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which compound links the urea cycle with the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: Fumarate links the urea and citric acid cycles; it is produced from argininosuccinate in the urea cycle and enters the CAC.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle CAC link
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Serotonin is synthesised from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis precursor
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The central nervous system is soft because it:
questions.explanation: The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: CNS softness cause
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the 3 ligaments supporting the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments supporting the spinal cord are the filum terminale (coccygeal ligament), ligamentum denticulatum, and subarachnoid septum.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord support
questions.modelAnswer: Filum terminale, ligamentum denticulatum, subarachnoid septum.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of areas 5 & 7 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of areas 5 and 7 (superior parietal lobule) causes sensory neglect of contralateral side, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 5-7 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory neglect, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of area 8 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 8 (frontal eye field) causes conjugate deviation of eyes toward the side of the lesion (inability to look away).
questions.keyConcept: Area 8 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Conjugate eye deviation toward the lesion.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of SMA causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of SMA causes loss of spontaneous movement, speech initiation, and bilateral motor planning without paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: SMA lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Loss of spontaneous movement and speech initiation.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Hemisection:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection) causes ipsilateral motor loss and all sensory loss at the lesion level, ipsilateral proprioceptive loss below the lesion, and contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain loss below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: At lesion: ipsilateral loss of all sensations, ipsilateral LMNL; Below lesion ipsilateral: loss of proprioception, UMNL; Below lesion contralateral: loss of pain and temperature.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa contains the tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance (allowing blood vessels to penetrate), and the oculomotor nerve emerging between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Fossa contents: tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, oculomotor nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: SVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent (SVE) nuclei include the motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V), motor nucleus of facial (CN VII), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI) supplying branchial arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: SVE column nuclei: motor nuclei of CN 5, 7, and nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).
questions.modelAnswer: Motor nucleus of 5, Motor nucleus of 7, Nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: GVE column nuclei:
questions.explanation: General visceral efferent (GVE) nuclei include the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III for pupil constriction), superior salivatory (CN VII), inferior salivatory (CN IX), and dorsal vagal nuclei (CN X).
questions.keyConcept: GVE column nuclei: Edinger-Westphal, superior/inferior salivatory, dorsal vagal.
questions.modelAnswer: Edinger‑Westphal (3), Superior salivatory (7), Inferior salivatory (9), Dorsal vagal (10).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebelli:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebelli attaches along its base to the tentorium cerebelli, at its apex to the foramen magnum margins, along its posterior border to the internal occipital crest, and is free anteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebelli: tentorium base, foramen magnum apex, occipital crest posteriorly, free anteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: tentorium; Apex: margins of foramen magnum; Posterior border: internal occipital crest; Anterior border: free.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve through optic canal:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (CN II) passes through the optic canal, carrying visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, making it functionally part of the CNS rather than a true peripheral nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve (CN II) traverses the optic canal.
questions.modelAnswer: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery. The central retinal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery that enters the optic nerve. The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery at the lateral aspect of the optic chiasma.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve in front of crossing of tentorium margins:
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges in the interpeduncular fossa, anterior to the crossing of the tentorium margins, before dividing into superior and inferior branches that enter the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: Oculomotor nerve emerges anterior to tentorium crossing.
questions.modelAnswer: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) runs in the interpeduncular fossa, in front of the tentorial edge (tentorium cerebelli crossing). It exits the brainstem between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, entering the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus just below the trochlear nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of inferior alveolar nerve:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off the mylohyoid branch before entering the mandibular foramen, then continues as the mental nerve (exiting mental foramen) and incisive nerve (supplying lower anterior teeth).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid, mental, incisive nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) gives off: (1) Mylohyoid nerve — motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric; (2) Dental branches — to mandibular teeth; (3) Incisive nerve — to mandibular premolars, canine, and incisors; (4) Mental nerve — exits mental foramen to chin and lower lip.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The pterion is a clinically important landmark because it overlies the:
questions.explanation: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, making it a critical landmark as fractures here can cause epidural hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
options: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion of the left optic tract causes:
questions.explanation: A left optic tract lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia because optic tract fibers carry information from the contralateral visual field, so damage affects the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Left optic tract lesion: right homonymous hemianopia.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the spinal cord at levels:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from T1 to L2 levels, representing the thoracolumbar outflow of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons: T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The motor branch to mylohyoid arises from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve as the:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives the (motor) nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Motor branch to mylohyoid arises from posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Inability to recognize familiar objects by touch indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) results from lesions in the superior parietal lobule, which integrates sensory information for object recognition.
questions.keyConcept: Astereognosis: superior parietal lobule lesion.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Myelination inside the CNS depends on:
questions.explanation: Myelination in the CNS is performed by oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelination: oligodendrocytes (PNS: Schwann cells).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Skin of the hairy area of the temple is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) supplies the hairy temple area, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular division.
questions.keyConcept: Hairy temple: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The common facial vein drains into the ……… vein.
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein after forming from the facial and anterior facial veins joining.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein: drains into internal jugular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: An active muscle during whistling is:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle compresses and purses the lips during whistling, while buccinator muscle keeps food between teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Whistling: orbicularis oris contracts to purse lips.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth denotes weakness of ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: Buccinator weakness causes food accumulation in the vestibule because this muscle normally keeps food between the teeth during mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Food in vestibule: buccinator weakness.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following are tributaries of external jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The subclavian artery is divided into 3 parts by ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Tight scalene muscles can compress:
questions.explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle DOESN'T share in boundaries of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A nerve seen in the floor of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from upper canine teeth is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The upper canine teeth are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of infraorbital nerve, V2), which also supplies the upper incisors.
questions.keyConcept: Upper canine: anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the subclavian vein:
questions.explanation: The subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to the anterior scalene muscle (not posterior), making it vulnerable to compression during clavicle fractures.
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to anterior scalene.
options: It is the continuation of the axillary vein.
It is separated from subclavian artery by anterior scalene muscle.
It grooves the 1st rib posterior to scalene tubercle.
It receives the external jugular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Rotation of the head to say "No" occurs at ……… joint.
questions.explanation: Saying 'No' involves rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2), where the dens of the axis articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.
questions.keyConcept: Saying no: rotation at atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle develops from the pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: second pharyngeal arch derivative.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: First neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication is:
questions.explanation: The posterior columns (gracile and cuneate nuclei) are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and vertebral arteries, NOT by the anterior spinal artery. The anterior spinal supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior columns not supplied by anterior spinal artery
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Special visceral efferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent nuclei include: trigeminal motor nucleus (V), facial motor nucleus (VII), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII).选项D正确. The answer is D. These innervate pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral efferent nuclei: CN V, VII, IX, X, XI motor nuclei - innervate pharyngeal arch muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cranial nerve is not found in the open medulla?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) emerges from the pre-olivary sulcus of the closed medulla, not the open medulla. Cranial nerves IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla at the post-olivary area.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII emerges from the closed medulla; CN IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cranial nerve nucleus is located most medially in the medulla?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is located most medially in the medulla, receiving visceral sensory input from vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves for taste and visceral reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus is the most medial medullary nucleus, involved in visceral sensory processing.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cranial nerve nucleus contains both general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA) fibers?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla contains both GVA (visceral sensation including baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input) and SVA (taste) fibers, making it unique in having both modalities.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus processes both visceral afferent and special visceral afferent (taste) information.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cranial nerve supplies fibers to the nucleus ambiguus?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides the parasympathetic and motor fibers to the nucleus ambiguus for innervation of the stylopharyngeus muscle. The nucleus ambiguus also receives contributions from CN X and XI.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus innervates pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles via CN IX, X, and XI.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) the lesion is in one of the following arteries:
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) results from PICA infarction, causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, and hoarseness.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The thalamic nucleus in which spinal & medial lemnisci terminate is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus is the thalamic relay for somatosensory information from the body. Both the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch and proprioception from the body) and the spinal lemniscus (carrying pain and temperature from the body) terminate in the VPL nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VPL nucleus is where spinal lemniscus (pain/temp from body) and medial lemniscus (touch/proprioception from body) terminate.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 10‑year‑old girl has a cystic cerebellar tumour. Microscopy shows spindle cells with hair‑like processes, microcysts, and Rosenthal fibres. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma in children shows characteristic hair-like processes (ROSE), microcysts, and Rosenthal fibers; often cystic with mural nodule.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The circle of Willis lies within the ……… subarachnoid cistern.
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis lies within the interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern, surrounding the interpeduncular fossa between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis: lies in interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Internal carotid blood is lost in injury of the:
questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via branches of the ophthalmic artery. Injury to the forehead region would lead to blood loss from the internal carotid system. The chin and cheek are supplied by external carotid branches.
questions.keyConcept: Forehead injury can lead to internal carotid blood loss
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Anterior spinal artery supplies all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
options: The part of medulla medial to hypoglossal nerve.
The nucleus that supplies muscles of tongue.
The fibers that carry fine touch of opposite side of body.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of basilar artery
questions.explanation: The basilar artery gives off pontine (paramedian) branches, labyrinthine artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), superior cerebellar artery (SCA), and its terminal branches the posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar artery branches and distribution
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine branches, labyrinthine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, posterior cerebellar
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the arteries that form the circle of Willis
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis is formed anteriorly by the anterior cerebral arteries and anterior communicating artery, laterally by the internal carotid arteries and posterior communicating arteries, and posteriorly by the posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis components
questions.modelAnswer: ACA, anterior communicating artery, ICA, PCA, posterior communicating
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: One of the following arteries does not share in formation of circle of Willis:
questions.explanation: Middle cerebral artery does NOT directly participate in the circle of Willis; it arises from the internal carotid as a branch outside the circle. The circle includes ACA, PCA, ICA, and posterior communicating arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis exclusion
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which artery is connected to the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) by the posterior communicating artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior communicating artery (PCoM) connects the internal carotid artery (ICA) with the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), forming part of the circle of Willis and providing collateral circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior communicating artery links ICA to PCA as part of the circle of Willis.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A branch from the internal carotid artery is:
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is a crucial branch of the internal carotid artery as it emerges from the cavernous part, supplying the eye and orbital structures.
questions.keyConcept: Internal carotid branch: ophthalmic artery.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List lines of management of Cirrhotic ascites
questions.explanation: Management of cirrhotic ascites includes sodium restriction, diuretics (spironolactone and furosemide), therapeutic paracentesis for large ascites, avoiding NSAIDs, and addressing underlying cause. Refractory cases may need TIPS or liver transplant.
questions.keyConcept: Cirrhotic ascites management combines salt restriction, diuretics, and paracentesis with underlying disease treatment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lines of management of cirrhotic ascites:

**First-line:**
1. **Sodium restriction:** 2g/day (88 mmol/day)
2. **Diuretic therapy:**
   - Start with spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist)
   - Add furosemide if inadequate response
   - Target weight loss: 0.5 kg/day (non-edematous) or 1 kg/day (edematous)

**Second-line:**
1. **Large volume paracentesis:** For tense ascites
   - With albumin replacement (6-8 g/L of ascites removed)
2. **Avoid NSAIDs:** Renal impairment risk
3. **Avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs:** Hypotension risk

**Refractory ascites options:**
1. **Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)**
2. **Peritoneovenous shunt**
3. **Liver transplantation**

**Complications to monitor:**
- Hepatic encephalopathy
- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)
- Hepatorenal syndrome

questions.text: Antipsychotic‑induced akathisia is best treated with:
questions.explanation: Propranolol (beta-blocker) is first-line treatment for antipsychotic-induced akathisia, likely by blocking beta-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus.
questions.keyConcept: Akathisia treatment
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System

questions.text: Which antiepileptic is used as migraine prophylaxis and can cause weight loss and renal stones?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is used for migraine prophylaxis and causes weight loss and renal calcium phosphate stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).
questions.keyConcept: Topiramate uses
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which antidepressant is approved for management of chronic neuropathic pain (e.g., diabetic neuropathy)?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine (SNRI) and duloxetine are antidepressants approved for diabetic neuropathy and other chronic pain conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Antidepressants for neuropathic pain
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which statement about ester local anesthetics is false?
questions.explanation: Ester local anesthetics are MORE liable to cause allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite, not less.
questions.keyConcept: Ester local anesthetic allergy
options: They are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases.
Procaine is a member of this group.
They are shorter acting than amides.
They are less liable to induce allergy.
They are less liable to systemic toxicity than amides.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which opioid antagonist is also used to reduce alcohol craving?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone (opioid antagonist) is used in alcohol dependence treatment by blocking opioid receptors involved in the rewarding effects of alcohol.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone alcohol use
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which is a cannabinoid drug used for management of hashish (cannabis) dependence?
questions.explanation: Dronabinol (synthetic THC) is used medically for cannabis dependence, providing agonist effects that reduce withdrawal and craving.
questions.keyConcept: Cannabinoid dependence treatment
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Extradural vs Subdural hemorrhage:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from middle meningeal artery rupture causing arterial bleeding with rapid accumulation and lucid interval, while subdural hemorrhage involves bridging veins causing slower venous accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Extradural: arterial (meningeal); Subdural: venous (bridging veins).
questions.modelAnswer: Extradural: arterial (middle meningeal); Subdural: venous.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Intermediolateral group of neurons is in:
questions.explanation: The intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) contains the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons and is located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord gray matter (T1–L2).
questions.keyConcept: Intermediolateral cell column = lateral horn = sympathetic preganglionic neurons
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the internal features of the medulla, choose for each structure in left column, its appropriate description in right column:
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers (special visceral afferent) from the facial, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves. It is the only nucleus dedicated to visceral afferent processing.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste fibers

questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following branches arises from the inferior vagal ganglion?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve has two ganglia: the superior (jugular) ganglion and the inferior (nodose) ganglion. The inferior vagal ganglion gives origin to the pharyngeal branches, superior laryngeal nerve, and cardiac branches. The auricular branch arises from the superior vagal ganglion, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve arises from the vagus trunk below the inferior ganglion. The meningeal branches mainly come from the superior ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pharyngeal branch arises from inferior vagal (nodose) ganglion.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior cervical sympathetic ganglion is the largest cervical sympathetic ganglion, located at the level of C2-C3. It gives communicating branches to the last four cranial nerves (IX, X, XI, XII), pharyngeal branches for the pharyngeal plexus, cardiac branches to the superficial cardiac plexus, superior laryngeal nerve fibers, and external and internal carotid plexuses. It does NOT give direct tracheal branches (these come from the middle and inferior ganglia).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion does NOT give tracheal branches.
options: Communicating branches with last 4 cranial nerves.
A cardiac branch to superficial cardiac plexus.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG).
questions.explanation: The superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG) is the largest cervical ganglion, located at the level of C1-C3 and the internal carotid artery. Its branches include: (1) gray rami communicantes to C1-C4 spinal nerves; (2) a branch to the internal carotid artery forming the internal carotid plexus (distributed to the eye and blood vessels of the head); (3) branches to the external carotid artery; (4) the pharyngeal branch contributing to the pharyngeal plexus; (5) superior laryngeal nerve; (6) cardiac branches to the superficial cardiac plexus; and (7) communicating branches to the last four cranial nerves (IX, X, XI, XII).
questions.keyConcept: SCSG branches: gray rami C1-C4, internal/external carotid plexuses, pharyngeal branch, superior laryngeal, cardiac.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of SCSG: (1) gray rami to C1-C4; (2) internal carotid plexus to eye and head vessels; (3) external carotid plexus; (4) pharyngeal plexus branch; (5) superior laryngeal nerve; (6) cardiac branches to superficial cardiac plexus; (7) communicating branches to last four cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), arising from the inferior (recurrent) laryngeal branch that loops under the aortic arch on the left and subclavian artery on the right.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve: branch of vagus nerve (CN X).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding vagus nerve; all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve, descends within the carotid sheath, has two ganglia (jugular and nodose), and injury causes tachycardia due to loss of parasympathetic tone. However, the vagus is NOT joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve. Only the cranial root of accessory joins the vagus; the spinal root forms the separate spinal accessory nerve supplying SCM and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus is joined by cranial root of accessory, NOT spinal root.
options: It is the longest cranial nerve.
It is joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve.
It descends within the carotid sheath.
Its injury leads to palpitation and tachycardia (increase in heart rate).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cranial part of the accessory nerve arises from
questions.explanation: The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, carrying fibers that eventually join the vagus nerve to innervate laryngeal muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory nerve nucleus ambiguus origin
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cranial nerve sends afferent fibers to the nucleus solitarius?
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal), and X (vagus) send afferent (taste and visceral) fibers to the nucleus solitarius. The vagus nerve carries the largest contribution of visceral information.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus receives visceral and taste afferents from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cranial nerves on ventral medulla:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves associated with the ventral medulla are CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), CN XI (accessory), and CN XII (hypoglossal), emerging in order from above downward.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: 9, 10, 11, 12.
questions.modelAnswer: Glossopharyngeal (9), Vagus (10), Accessory (11), Hypoglossal (12).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the contents of interpeduncular fossa?
questions.explanation: The contents of the interpeduncular fossa include the tuber cinereum (hypothalamic eminence), mammillary bodies (posterior), posterior perforated substance (vascular area), and the oculomotor nerve emerges from the medial side of the cerebral peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa contents: tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, CN III.
questions.modelAnswer: Tuber cinereum (hypothalamic eminence), mammillary bodies (part of Papez circuit), posterior perforated substance (contains central branches of posterior cerebral artery), and the oculomotor nerve (emerges between cerebral peduncles).
questions.chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
