questions.explanation: A-delta fibers transmit fast, sharp, well-localized pain (first pain) via the neospinothalamic tract. C fibers transmit slow, dull, poorly localized pain (second pain) via the paleospinothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers mediate fast, localized pain; C fibers mediate slow, diffuse pain.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Fast pain is characterized by which duration?
questions.explanation: Fast pain (A-delta fibers) has a brief duration (~0.1 seconds), occurring immediately after stimulus and enabling rapid localization of noxious stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is brief (~0.1s) and well-localized due to A-delta fiber conduction.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of form and texture) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway for fine touch and proprioception to reach the sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioception for object recognition.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: In syringomyelia, sensory loss typically follows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia cord lesion pattern
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text:
The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory A 1:
A. Crude Touch.
B. Fast pain.
C. Vibration sense.
D. Proprioceptive sensation.
E. Stereognosis.
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by the anterior spinothalamic tract, not by somatosensory area 1 which processes fine/discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 does not process crude touch (anterior spinothalamic does).
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Brown-Sequard syndrome is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of vibration sense on the same side below lesion. Option A is correct. Hemisection causes ipsilateral dorsal column loss (vibration, proprioception) and corticospinal loss (motor) below; contralateral spinothalamic loss (pain, temperature). Options B, C, D are incorrect (motor loss is ipsilateral, reflex loss at lesion level is LMN, pain loss is contralateral).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard hemisection produces ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
options: Loss of vibration sense on the same side below level of the lesion
Loss of voluntary movements on the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of reflex movements on the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of pain sensation on the same side below the level of the lesion
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: 43 year old woman is evaluated in the hospital and is found to have multiple neurologic abnormalities from the level T 12 down. She has loss of vibration and proprioception on the left but these senses are present on the right side. She has absent pain and temperature sensation in the right side from T12 down. Motor power was lost in the left leg but normal motor strength in her right leg. What is the most likely cause of her neurologic symptoms?
questions.explanation: Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord. Option C is correct. Left hemisection explains: left vibration/proprioception loss (dorsal columns), right pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), left leg paralysis (corticospinal). Complete transection would affect both sides. Right hemisection would cause opposite findings.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral dorsal column and motor loss with contralateral spinothalamic loss indicates spinal cord hemisection on the side of motor/dorsal column deficits.
options: Complete spinal cord transection at upper thoracic segments.
Complete spinal cord transection at lower thoracic segments.
Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord
Hemisection on the right part of spinal cord
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: List and explain the effects of syringomyelia cavity involving the cervical and the thoracic segments of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord. At cervical levels, it typically affects the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation ('cape-like' or 'suspended' sensory loss) while preserving dorsal column functions (proprioception, vibration sense). Motor manifestations include lower motor neuron weakness and atrophy in the intrinsic hand muscles, with possible extension to affect corticospinal tracts causing UMN signs in the lower limbs. At thoracic levels, similar sensory findings occur at the trunk level, plus possible sympathetic disruption. The cavity expands over time, damaging crossing fibers first, then anterior horn cells (causing LMN signs), then corticospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia causes 'cape-like' pain/temperature loss by destroying crossing spinothalamic fibers while preserving proprioception.
questions.modelAnswer:
 Syringomyelia: widening of the central canal due to abnormal overgrowth of glial tissue of more
common in female which causes damage of pain and temperature fibers crossing in front of the
central canal. -  later fibers of crude touch and pressure are affected
 Effects of syringomyelia:
1. Loss of pain, touch and temperature at both sides of the body at the level of the affected segment
causing  “Jacket distribution anesthesia”
2. Dorsal column sensations “fine touch & proprioception” are intact this leads to dissociated
sensory loss
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
questions.explanation: According to Müller's law of specific nerve energies, each receptor is specific to its adequate stimulus. Receptors have LOW threshold for their specific stimulus. Receptor potential is directly proportional to stimulus intensity, not inversely.
questions.keyConcept: Law of specific nerve energies: each receptor responds only to its adequate stimulus at low threshold.
options: Receptors are non-specific to stimuli according to Muller’s law
Stimulation of certain receptors can produces different modalities of sensations
Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold
Receptor potential is inversely related to the intensity of stimulus according to Weber Fechner law
The same receptor may be stimulated by different stimuli to produce different sensations
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: A reflex arc includes:
questions.explanation: A reflex arc requires at minimum a sensory receptor, a sensory neuron, at least one synapse in the CNS, and an efferent motor neuron. This means at least two sets of sequential neurons (afferent and efferent).
questions.keyConcept: Reflex arc components: receptor → afferent neuron → CNS integration → efferent neuron → effector.
options: At least two sets of sequential neurons
At least two sequential sets of central synapses
At least two types of sensory receptors
At least two types of efferent neurons
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Regarding adaptation, Touch receptors are rapidly adapting receptors while pain receptors are slowly adapting receptors
questions.explanation: Touch receptors (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles) are rapidly adapting phasic receptors, while pain receptors (free nerve endings) are slowly adapting tonic receptors, reflecting their functional roles in sensory processing.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor adaptation rates and functional significance
questions.modelAnswer: Touch receptors (e.g., Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner corpuscles) are rapidly adapting receptors that respond to changes in stimulus intensity but stop firing during sustained stimulation, allowing the CNS to detect new stimuli. Pain receptors (nociceptors, e.g., free nerve endings) are slowly adapting receptors that continue firing as long as the damaging stimulus is present, ensuring the body is continuously warned of tissue injury.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Compare between crude touch sensation & thermal sensation regarding ( Def. receptors & afferent neuron type)
questions.explanation: Crude touch uses free nerve endings and type A-delta fibers (discriminative touch uses Meissner's corpuscles with A-beta fibers); thermal sensation uses thermal receptors with A-delta (cold) and C fibers (warm).
questions.keyConcept: Touch and thermal sensation receptor differences
questions.modelAnswer: Crude touch sensation is carried by the anterior spinothalamic tract, uses mechanical receptors (tactile discs, Ruffini endings), and transmitted by A-beta and A-delta fibers. Thermal sensation (heat/cold) is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, uses thermoreceptors (free nerve endings), and transmitted by A-delta and C fibers. Crude touch receptors have larger receptive fields and lower spatial resolution compared to thermal receptors.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which of the following does not contain channels that are activated by mechanical distortion?
questions.explanation: Hair end organs (Ruffini endings) are slowly adapting receptors for skin stretch, not activated by mechanical distortion. Muscle spindles, Pacinian corpuscles, and cochlear hair cells all use mechanically-gated ion channels.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanically-gated channels are found in sensory receptors for touch, pressure, and hearing; Ruffini endings detect static skin stretch rather than vibration.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which type of sensory receptors in the skin respond quickly at the onset of a stimulus but stop firing if the stimulus is constant?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors that respond quickly at the onset and offset of a stimulus but cease firing during sustained stimulation due to their large, encapsulated structure.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors detecting vibration and rapid changes.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which sensory receptor adapts rapidly to sustained skin stimulation?
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that adapt quickly to sustained skin stimulation, making them ideal for detecting motion and texture.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting tactile receptors in glabrous skin for motion detection.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) respond to noxious stimuli including intense mechanical distortion, heat (>45C), and chemical irritants (bradykinin, substance P, prostaglandins).
questions.keyConcept: Nociceptors are polymodal free nerve endings responding to mechanical, thermal, and chemical noxious stimuli.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: In secondary hyperalgesia, which describes the affected area?
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperalgesia occurs in the surrounding undamaged tissue adjacent to the primary injury site, where nociceptors become sensitized by inflammatory mediators released from damaged cells.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary hyperalgesia extends beyond the injury site due to central sensitization of dorsal horn neurons.
options: Inflamed tissue directly exposed to noxious stimuli
All dermatomes sharing the same dorsal root ganglion
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which explains pain relief when you rub the skin near an injury?
questions.explanation: Rubbing the skin activates A-beta mechanoreceptors that inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn through gating mechanisms in the substantia gelatinosa (gate control theory).
questions.keyConcept: Gate control theory: tactile stimulation inhibits nociceptive transmission via A-beta fiber activation of inhibitory interneurons in dorsal horn.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: A woman wore a dress on the beach. Later, wearing a jacket over the same area caused pain. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Wearing a jacket over tanned skin causes referred pain from sunburned skin, demonstrating referred pain where visceral or deep somatic injury is perceived as cutaneous pain.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain from deep tissue injury can be perceived as cutaneous pain due to convergence of somatic and visceral afferents on dorsal horn neurons.
options: Increase receptor sensitivity by tissue products
Activity-dependent increase in excitability of dorsal horn neurons
Increased threshold of peripheral nociceptors due to inflammatory mediators
Decreased inhibitory interneuron function in the spinal cord
Impaired saltatory conduction in primary afferent neurons
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which receptors inhibit pain sensation in the CNS?
questions.explanation: Endogenous opioid peptides (endorphins and enkephalins) released from periaqueductal gray and nucleus raphe magnus inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
questions.keyConcept: Endogenous opioid peptides from brainstem nuclei inhibit nociceptive transmission in the spinal cord dorsal horn.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which statement is true regarding deep pressure sensation?
questions.explanation: Deep pressure sensation is transmitted by A-beta fibers via dorsal column pathways and by A-delta fibers via spinothalamic tracts. It has a high threshold compared to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pressure uses A-beta fibers in dorsal columns and A-delta fibers in spinothalamic tracts.
options: It is mediated by slowly adapting receptors
It is transmitted only by free nerve endings
It adapts rapidly to sustained stimulus
It is carried exclusively by Aδ fibers
It is not associated with vibration
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which pair correctly matches a reflex with its sensory receptor?
questions.explanation: The inverse stretch reflex (autogenic inhibition) uses Golgi tendon organs as receptors that inhibit alpha motor neurons when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organs mediate inverse stretch reflex to prevent muscle damage from excessive tension.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which accurately describes the pattern of dissociative sensory loss in syringomyelia?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss with loss of pain and temperature but preserved touch and proprioception due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central canal.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia selectively damages crossing spinothalamic fibers, causing cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function.
options: Loss of pain and touch with preservation of temperature
Loss of touch and temperature with preservation of pain
Loss of pain with preservation of touch and temperature
Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch
Loss of temperature with preservation of touch and pain
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT true regarding the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar ataxia is sensory ataxia - it worsens with eye closure (positive Romberg). Option B is INCORRECT as stated. Actually, cerebellar ataxia is NOT sensory (sensory ataxia is dorsal column dysfunction). The correct answer is B because cerebellar ataxia is motor ataxia, characterized by clumsiness that is visible with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which hides behind visual compensation. Wait - re-reading: cerebellar ataxia is a motor (not sensory) ataxia that DOES NOT require visual compensation to demonstrate.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is a motor coordination deficit visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which requires eye closure to manifest.
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls movements of the ipsilateral muscles.
Cerebellar ataxia is a sensory ataxia.
Cerebellar lesions cause pendular knee jerks.
The intention tremor associated with cerebellar disease is worsened by movement.
The neocerebellar syndrome gait is zig-zag like.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text:
In Thermal sensations, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

A) Cold receptors are more numerous than Hot receptors, but Hot receptors adapt more rapidly than cold receptors.
B) Are transmitted through lateral division of anterolateral system.
C) Temperature higher than 45°C produces hot pain and temperature lower than 10°C produces cold pain.
D) The maximal discharge of hot receptors occurs at 45°C and of cold receptors occurs at 25°C.
E) They are carried by Aβ fibers.
questions.explanation: Thermal sensations are carried by Aδ fibers (cold) and C fibers (hot), not Aβ fibers. Aβ fibers carry touch, pressure, and vibration. Cold receptors adapt slower than hot receptors, and maximal discharge occurs at 25°C (cold) and 45°C (hot).
questions.keyConcept: Temperature sensation: Aδ (cold, 10-40°C), C fibers (heat, 30-45°C); transmitted via spinothalamic tract.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text:
Regarding somatosensory area 1 all are correct, Except:
A. Lies anterior to central gyrus.
B. Size of representation depends on number of receptors.
C. Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation.
D. Contralateral representation.
E. Share in pyramidal tract origin.
questions.explanation: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to the central gyrus (postcentral gyrus), not anterior; it receives contralateral input, has columns specialized for single sensation types, and its representation size reflects receptor density.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to central gyrus (postcentral gyrus).
options: Size of representation depends on number of receptors
Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which is correctly matched regarding the pain analgesic system?
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter is the origin of descending pain inhibitory pathways that project to nucleus raphe magnus and release opioids to inhibit dorsal horn pain transmission.
questions.keyConcept: PAG is the key origin of descending analgesic pathways utilizing endogenous opioids.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: The stretch reflex:
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is the fastest body reflex. Option B is correct. It is a monosynaptic reflex with minimal central delay (0.5-0.8 ms). Options A, C, D, E are incorrect: it is monosynaptic (not polysynaptic), receptor is muscle spindle (not Pacinian), has short (not long) central delay, results in contraction (not relaxation).
questions.keyConcept: The monosynaptic stretch reflex has the fastest conduction due to its simple, direct excitatory circuit.
options: Results in relaxation of the stretched muscle.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Which of the following could NOT be an exteroceptor?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are proprioceptors located within muscles that detect stretch and length changes. Exteroceptors receive stimuli from the external environment (thermoreceptors, nociceptors, Pacinian corpuscles, rods/cones).
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors like muscle spindles are interoceptors, not exteroceptors which sense external stimuli.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Lesion of the spinocerebellar tract typically produces:
questions.explanation: Spinocerebellar tract lesion causes ipsilateral ataxia and loss of proprioception from the limb, as these tracts carry uncrossed sensory information from muscle spindles and tendon organs.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellar tract damage produces ipsilateral limb ataxia and impaired proprioception.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text:
Which of the following maneuvers will weakens the stretch reflex in skeletal muscle?
A. Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
B. Disruption of the spinocerebellar tract
C. Disruption of the corticospinal tract
D. Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
E. Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
questions.explanation: Sectioning the dorsal root eliminates the afferent limb of the stretch reflex (Ia fibers from muscle spindles), causing immediate weakening or loss of the reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root sectioning: weakens stretch reflex by cutting afferent limb.
options: Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: physiology

questions.text: Urea cycle is a pathway that
questions.explanation: The urea cycle occurs exclusively in the liver (hepatocytes) and is the body's mechanism for converting toxic ammonia (NH3) into urea for excretion. It does not produce ammonia from urea; that would be the reverse reaction which does not occur physiologically.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle location in liver and its role in ammonia detoxification
options: takes place mainly in the liver cells.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: biochem

questions.text: What is diffuse axonal injury? And what is its common locations?
questions.explanation: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) results from acceleration-deceleration forces causing shearing of axons in white matter. Classic locations: corpus callosum (most common), periventricular white matter, and hippocampus. This is a severe form of traumatic brain injury. Option C 'Both A and B' is correct. DAI is often associated with severe disability and coma. The answer is C. MRI better detects DAI lesions than CT.
questions.keyConcept: Diffuse axonal injury occurs in white matter at corpus callosum and periventricular regions due to acceleration-deceleration.
options: Injury to white matter with axonal swelling due to acceleration and deceleration
Commonly occurring in the corpus callosum, periventricular white matter, and hippocampus
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: Where do approximately 70% of brain tumors occur in adults?
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of brain tumors in adults occur supratentorially (within the cerebral hemispheres or their coverings). This includes gliomas, meningiomas, and metastatic tumors. Infratentorial (posterior fossa) tumors (B) are more common in children. The answer is A. The supratentorial location in adults reflects the higher incidence of gliomas and metastatic disease in the cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: Adult brain tumors are predominantly supratentorial (70%) - cerebral hemispheres are the most common location.
options: Supratentorially (within the cerebral hemispheres or coverings)
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: What is the location and symptoms of a subdural hematoma?
questions.explanation: Subdural hematoma is located between dura and arachnoid (A). Symptoms include slow venous bleeding with delayed onset of headache, confusion, and altered consciousness (B). This differs from arterial epidural hematoma which presents acutely. Option C 'Both A and B' is correct. Acute subdural hematoma presents within 72 hours; chronic subdural may present weeks after injury. The answer is C. Subdural hematoma crosses suture lines unlike epidural.
questions.keyConcept: Subdural hematoma is venous bleeding between dura and arachnoid with delayed, progressive symptoms.
options: Symptoms include slow venous bleeding with delayed onset of headache and confusion.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: What is the key genetic finding in oligodendrogliomas?
questions.explanation: The key genetic finding in oligodendrogliomas is codeletion of chromosomes 1p and 19q. This occurs through unbalanced translocation t(1;19)(q10;p10). This codeletion is associated with better prognosis and excellent response to PCV chemotherapy (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine). Option B is CORRECT. EGFR overexpression (A) is seen in glioblastoma. IDH1 mutation (C) is found in many gliomas but not specific. MDM2 amplification (D) is in some glioblastomas. The answer is B.
questions.keyConcept: 1p/19q codeletion is the hallmark genetic abnormality of oligodendroglioma, predicting better prognosis.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: Where are pilocytic astrocytomas most commonly located?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas are most commonly located in the CEREBELLUM (posterior fossa). They also occur in optic pathways, brainstem, and spinal cord. The cerebellar location is classic, especially in children. The answer is B. This is the most common pediatric brain tumor and has excellent prognosis when completely resected.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma occurs most commonly in the cerebellum in children - excellent prognosis with resection.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: Addition of the following drugs to L dopa produce all the following except
questions.explanation: Entacapone DECREASES L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Entacapone inhibits COMT, which DECREASES L-dopa metabolism, thereby INCREASING its bioavailability and duration of action. Domperidone decreases nausea (A is correct). Benztropine decreases absorption (B is correct). Apomorphine decreases off time (C is correct).
questions.keyConcept: COMT inhibitors like entacapone prolong L-dopa action by preventing its peripheral breakdown.
options: Domperidone / decreases l dopa induced nausea & vomiting
Apomorphine / decreases off time of on-off phenomena
Entacapone / Decrease L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Conscious sedation may be induced by
questions.explanation: Fentanyl with Midazolam induces conscious sedation. Option A is correct. This combination (opioid + benzodiazepine) provides analgesia and amnesia for conscious sedation in minor procedures. Droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia (B). Domperidone is antiemetic (C).
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation combines fentanyl (analgesia) with midazolam (anxiolysis/amnesia) for procedural sedation.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Mention mechanism and adverse effects of sumatriptan.
questions.explanation: Sumatriptan's mechanism involves 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism causing cranial vessel constriction and inhibition of trigeminal pain pathways. Adverse effects include chest tightness, flushing, and paresthesia; contraindicated in ischemic heart disease.
questions.keyConcept: Sumatriptan treats migraine via cranial vasoconstriction and trigeminal pain pathway inhibition.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Mechanism of Sumatriptan:**
- Selective agonist at 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors
- Causes cranial vasoconstriction
- Inhibits trigeminal nerve firing
- Blocks neuropeptide release
- Reduces neurogenic inflammation
- Alleviates migraine pain

**Adverse Effects:**

1. **Cardiovascular:**
   - Chest pressure/tightness
   - Palpitations
   - Hypertension
   - Coronary vasospasm

2. **CNS:**
   - Dizziness
   - Paresthesia
   - Drowsiness

3. **Other:**
   - Flushing
   - Warmth
   - Neck pain

**Contraindications:**
- Ischemic heart disease
- Uncontrolled hypertension
- Peripheral vascular disease
- Basilar or hemiplegic migraine
- Concurrent MAOI use (serotonin syndrome)

**Drug Interactions:**
- SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome risk)
- Ergotamines (prolonged vasoconstriction)
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: The following is not common between pethidine & Buprenorphine:
questions.explanation: Both pethidine and buprenorphine are opioids with similar side effects including analgesia, respiratory depression, nausea/vomiting, and constipation. However, buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression - increasing dose beyond a certain point does not proportionally increase respiratory depression. Pethidine does NOT have this ceiling effect - its respiratory depression increases linearly with dose. This makes buprenorphine safer in overdose. Option B is the correct answer because respiratory depression IS NOT increased proportionally with dose in buprenorphine due to its partial agonist activity at mu receptors, unlike pethidine which shows dose-dependent respiratory depression.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine's ceiling effect on respiratory depression distinguishes it from pethidine's linear dose-dependent depression.
options: Respiratory depression is increased by increasing dose
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Conscious sedation may be induced by:
questions.explanation: Conscious sedation is achieved by combining a benzodiazepine (for anxiolysis, amnesia, sedation) with an opioid (for analgesia). Fentanyl (opioid) + Midazolam (benzodiazepine) is the classic combination. Fentanyl provides analgesia while midazolam provides anxiolysis and sedation. Option B (Midazolam/Droperidol) - droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia, not conscious sedation. Option C (Fentanyl/Domperidone) - domperidone is an antiemetic, not a sedative. Option D is incorrect. The combination allows reduced doses of each drug while achieving adequate sedation and analgesia for procedures like dental work.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation uses fentanyl (analgesic) + midazolam (benzodiazepine) for safe procedural sedation.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Constipation associated with the use of morphine may be relieved by
questions.explanation: Morphine-induced constipation is relieved by stool softeners (docusate), stimulant laxatives, and peripherally-acting opioid antagonists (methylnaltrexone) that don't reverse analgesia.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid-induced constipation treatment
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Neuropathic pain may be managed by
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain management includes tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, gabapentin), and atypical opioids (tramadol), all acting on different pain pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Neuropathic pain multimodal management
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Concerning sensory receptors, all the followings are true, Except:
questions.explanation: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily (unlike many other excitable tissues); they maintain responsiveness during sustained stimulation, though they may adapt at different rates.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: All the following receptors are phasic receptors Except:
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are tonic (slowly adapting) receptors that continue firing during sustained stimulation, unlike phasic receptors like Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, hair end organs, and Merkel's discs which adapt rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings are tonic receptors; others listed are phasic.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Pain sensation can be inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal grey to the dorsal horn, blocking pain signal transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid receptor stimulation inhibits pain sensation.
options: Increasing the pain threshold by kinin.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: One of the following anesthetic protocols is NOT correctly matched:
questions.explanation: Neuroleptanalgesia uses droperidol plus fentanyl, NOT propofol - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Neuroleptanalgesia = droperidol (neuroleptic) + fentanyl (opioid). Propofol is used for deep sedation/anesthesia. Options A, B, C are correctly matched.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroleptanalgesia combines droperidol with fentanyl for sedation and analgesia; propofol is a separate anesthetic agent.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following possesses a weak analgesic effect?
questions.explanation: Halothane has weak analgesic effect. Option B is correct. Volatile anesthetics vary in analgesia: halothane provides minimal analgesia, while ketamine (C) and nitrous oxide (A) provide significant analgesia. Fentanyl (D) is a potent opioid analgesic.
questions.keyConcept: Halothane lacks significant analgesic properties, distinguishing it from ketamine and nitrous oxide.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: One of the following anesthetics protocols is not correctly matched:
questions.explanation: Neuroleptanalgesia is the combination of a neuroleptic (droperidol) with an opioid (fentanyl), producing a state of calmness and analgesia without complete unconsciousness. Propofol plus fentanyl is actually IV anesthesia/conscious sedation, not neuroleptanalgesia. The correct combinations: A) Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia - CORRECT; B) Midazolam + Fentanyl produces conscious sedation - CORRECT; C) Propofol produces deep sedation/anesthesia - CORRECT; D) Propofol + Fentanyl = IV anesthesia, NOT neuroleptanalgesia (which requires droperidol). The answer is D because neuroleptanalgesia specifically refers to droperidol + fentanyl combination.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroleptanalgesia specifically refers to droperidol + fentanyl, producing calmness and analgesia.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following possesses a weak analgesic effect:
questions.explanation: Analgesic potency comparison: Fentanyl > Ketamine > Halothane > Nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide has WEAK analgesic effect. While N2O provides some analgesia (used in labor, dentistry), its potency is low. Ketamine provides moderate analgesia through NMDA antagonism. Halothane provides minimal analgesia. Fentanyl is a potent opioid with strong analgesic effects. N2O's weak analgesic effect means it's often combined with other agents for surgical procedures. The correct answer is A - nitrous oxide possesses weak analgesic effect compared to the other options.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide has weak analgesic potency compared to opioids (fentanyl) and ketamine.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Name some strong pure agonists opioids.
questions.explanation: Strong pure agonist opioids include: morphine, heroin, fentanyl, methadone, meperidine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone.选项D正确. The answer is D. These have full agonist activity at mu opioid receptors, providing maximum analgesia but also respiratory depression, sedation, and dependence potential.
questions.keyConcept: Morphine, fentanyl, methadone are strong pure mu opioid agonists - maximum analgesia with respiratory depression risk.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: What are the partial agonists opioids?
questions.explanation: Partial agonist opioids include buprenorphine (partial mu agonist) and pentazocine (partial kappa agonist, mixed agonist-antagonist).选项A正确. Buprenorphine is used for opioid dependence (Suboxone) and analgesia. Its ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it safer. The answer is A. Pentazocine can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine is a partial mu agonist with ceiling effect on respiratory depression - used in opioid dependence treatment.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: The following concerning zolpidem is not true
questions.explanation: Zolpidem is LESS liable to induce rebound insomnia than benzodiazepines - this is NOT true. Option C is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has more rebound insomnia potential compared to benzodiazepines because of its short half-life and selective BZ1 receptor action. Options A, B, D are true: zolpidem is short-acting with less hangover, acts on BZ1 receptor, and has less tolerance/dependence than BZDs.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has a short half-life and less hangover than benzodiazepines, but can cause rebound insomnia due to its short duration of action.
options: It is a short acting hypnotic causing less hang over than benzodiazepines
More liable to induce rebound insomnia & disturbance in REM sleep than benzodiazepines.
Its use is associated with less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines.

questions.text: The following drug is not matched with its mechanism of action
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5HT1A AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is a selective 5-HT1A partial agonist (not antagonist). Options A, B, C are correct: diazepam increases frequency of chloride channel opening, zolpidem binds BZ1 receptor, barbiturates increase duration of channel opening.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's anxiolytic effect comes from 5-HT1A receptor partial agonism, not antagonism.
options: Diazepam increases frequency of opening of chloride channels
Zolpidem binds with BZD1 subtype → increases GABA activity
Barbiturates increase duration of opening of chloride channels

questions.text: The following statement is Wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of Benzodiazepines
questions.explanation: Clinical duration of long-acting BZDs is longer than actual half-life - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Long-acting BZDs form active metabolites that prolong their effect beyond the parent compound's half-life. Options A, B, D are correct: IM absorption is slower (except lorazepam), lorazepam uses glucuronidation not oxidation, lorazepam has no active metabolites.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines have prolonged effects due to active metabolites, making actual duration longer than parent half-life.
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BDZs is shorter than the actual half life as they form active metabolites

questions.text: The following about thiopental is WRONG:
questions.explanation: Thiopental is NOT ultra-short acting due to rapid metabolism - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Thiopental is ultra-short acting due to RAPID DISTRIBUTION out of the brain, not rapid metabolism. It undergoes slow hepatic metabolism but rapid redistribution causes short duration. Options A, C, D are correct: rapid onset, enzyme inducer, no antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Thiopental's ultra-short duration is due to rapid redistribution from brain to other tissues, not rapid metabolism.
options: Has a rapid onset of action due to rapid crossing of BBB.
Ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Enzyme inducer and may precipitate porphyria.
May induce respiratory depression with no available antidote.
questions.chapterTitle: II. The Sensory System

questions.text: Compare between mechanism of action of barbiturates and benzodiazepines.
questions.explanation: Barbiturates and benzodiazepines both enhance GABA-A receptor function but through different mechanisms. Barbiturates increase the duration of chloride channel opening, while benzodiazepines increase the frequency of opening. Barbiturates are non-selective and work at multiple GABA-A subtypes, whereas benzodiazepines act more selectively at specific subunit-containing receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Both enhance GABAergic inhibition but differ in mechanism: barbiturates prolong channel opening duration while benzodiazepines increase opening frequency.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Comparison of Barbiturates and Benzodiazepines Mechanism of Action:**

**Barbiturates:**
- Bind to a distinct site on GABA-A receptor
- Increase duration of chloride channel opening
- Directly activate chloride channels even without GABA (unlike BZDs)
- Non-selective effect on all GABA-A receptor subtypes
- Have membrane-stabilizing effect at high doses

**Benzodiazepines:**
- Bind to benzodiazepine recognition site on GABA-A receptor
- Increase frequency of chloride channel opening
- Require presence of GABA for their effect (potentiate, not directly activate)
- Selective effect on specific GABA-A receptor subtypes (containing alpha 1, 2, 3, or 5 subunits)

**Key Difference:** Barbiturates directly activate chloride channels and prolong opening duration; benzodiazepines require GABA and increase opening frequency.

questions.text: Explain why clinical duration of action of diazepam does not correlate with their elimination half-life?
questions.explanation: Diazepam has a long clinical duration despite short half-life because it forms active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam) that accumulate and have long half-lives. The clinical effect persists until these metabolites are eventually cleared, which can take days.
questions.keyConcept: Diazepam's clinical duration exceeds its half-life due to active metabolite accumulation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Clinical duration of diazepam does not correlate with elimination half-life because:

**1. Active Metabolites:**
- Diazepam is metabolized to desmethyldiazepam (nordazepam)
- This metabolite is pharmacologically active and has a longer half-life (up to 200 hours)
- It accumulates with repeated dosing

**2. Tissue Storage:**
- Diazepam is highly lipophilic
- It accumulates in fat tissue
- Slowly released back into circulation

**3. Parent Drug vs. Effect:**
- Elimination half-life of diazepam: 20-50 hours
- Clinical effect persists much longer due to active metabolites
- Desmethyldiazepam half-life: 30-200 hours

**4. Clinical Implications:**
- Effects may persist for days after stopping
- Accumulation occurs with repeated dosing
- Withdrawal may be delayed

questions.text: Outline drug therapy of persistent anxiety.
questions.explanation: Persistent anxiety drug therapy involves SSRIs/SNRIs as first-line, with benzodiazepines for short-term bridge therapy, buspirone as alternative, and psychotherapy integration. Duration is typically 6-12 months after symptom control.

questions.modelAnswer:
Drug therapy for persistent anxiety:

**First-Line Agents:**
1. **SSRIs:** Fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram
2. **SNRIs:** Venlafaxine, duloxetine

**Second-Line/Bridge Therapy:**
1. **Benzodiazepines:** Lorazepam, clonazepam (short-term only, 2-4 weeks)
2. **Buspirone:** For generalized anxiety (delayed onset)

**Augmentation Strategies:**
- Add benzodiazepine for initial 2-4 weeks while waiting for SSRI effect
- Consider adding olanzapine or quetiapine for resistant cases

**Duration:**
- Continue treatment for 6-12 months after symptom remission
- Gradual tapering to avoid withdrawal

**Non-Drug Therapy:**
- Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
- Relaxation techniques
- Regular exercise

questions.text: List main differences between ester & amide local anesthetics with examples
questions.explanation: Ester local anesthetics (procaine, tetracaine) are metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, have higher allergy risk, shorter duration, and are less stable in solution. Amide local anesthetics (lidocaine, bupivacaine) are metabolized in liver, have longer duration, and lower allergy risk.
questions.keyConcept: Esters are metabolized in plasma by cholinesterase with higher allergy risk; amides are hepatic metabolized with longer duration.
questions.modelAnswer:
Main differences between ester and amide local anesthetics:

| Feature | Ester Local Anesthetics | Amide Local Anesthetics |
|---------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Metabolism** | Plasma cholinesterase | Hepatic CYP450 enzymes |
| **Allergy risk** | Higher (PABA metabolite) | Lower |
| **Duration** | Shorter | Longer |
| **Stability** | Less stable in solution | More stable |
| **Examples** | Procaine, Tetracaine, Benzocaine | Lidocaine, Bupivacaine, Ropivacaine |
| **Systemic toxicity** | Less (rapid plasma hydrolysis) | More (hepatic accumulation) |
| **Use** | Topical, short procedures | Infiltration, nerve blocks, regional |

**Note:** Ester anesthetics can cause severe allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite. Amides are preferred for most clinical applications due to longer duration and lower sensitization potential.

questions.text: Enumerate advantages and precautions that should be done during addition of vasoconstrictors to local anesthetics
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors in local anesthetics provide hemostasis, reduce systemic absorption, prolong duration, and decrease toxicity. Precautions include avoiding in end-arterial areas (digits, ears), cardiac patients (use felypressin instead), and with certain drug interactions.
questions.keyConcept: Vasoconstrictors enhance local anesthesia but require precautions in specific patient populations and anatomical sites.
questions.modelAnswer:
Advantages of adding vasoconstrictors to local anesthetics:

1. **Prolonged duration** of local anesthesia
2. **Reduced systemic absorption** of anesthetic
3. **Decreased systemic toxicity**
4. **Better hemostasis** during procedure
5. **Reduced bleeding** at surgical site

**Precautions:**

1. **Anatomical Contraindications:**
   - Do NOT use with epinephrine in digits, ears, nose, penis (end-arterial areas)
   - Risk of ischemic necrosis

2. **Cardiac Patients:**
   - Avoid epinephrine; use felypressin instead
   - Risk of arrhythmias with halogenated anesthetics

3. **Drug Interactions:**
   - Contraindicated with non-selective beta-blockers (unopposed alpha hypertension)
   - Caution with MAOIs and TCAs

4. **Technique:**
   - Aspirate before injection
   - Use lowest effective dose
   - Inject slowly

questions.text: List 4 factors affecting the local anesthetic activity
questions.explanation: Four factors affecting local anesthetic activity are: 1) pKa (determines onset - lower pKa = faster onset), 2) lipid solubility (determines potency - higher = more potent), 3) protein binding (determines duration - higher = longer duration), 4) vasodilator properties (determines duration - more vasodilation = shorter duration).
questions.keyConcept: Local anesthetic potency, onset, and duration are determined by pKa, lipid solubility, protein binding, and vasodilator effects.
questions.modelAnswer:
Four factors affecting local anesthetic activity:

**1. pKa (Ionization constant):**
- Determines onset of action
- Lower pKa = faster onset (more drug in un ionized form at physiological pH)
- Most local anesthetics have pKa of 8.0-9.0

**2. Lipid Solubility:**
- Determines potency
- Higher lipid solubility = more potent
- More drug crosses nerve membrane

**3. Protein Binding:**
- Determines duration of action
- Higher protein binding = longer duration
- Bupivacaine (95% bound) longer than lidocaine (64% bound)

**4. Vasodilator Properties:**
- Determines duration indirectly
- More vasodilation = faster absorption = shorter duration
- Addition of vasoconstrictors (epinephrine) counteracts this

The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane is a continuation of the anterior longitudinal ligament; the posterior membrane is similar to the ligamentum flavum.
questions.keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is synovial condylar; allows flexion/extension but NOT rotation. Anterior membrane = continuation of ALL; posterior membrane = like ligamentum flavum.
options: Its anterior membrane is a continuation of ant. longitudinal ligament.
Its posterior membrane is similar to the ligamentum flavum.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 5-day-old child has been treated in the intensive care unit since birth. A sample of cerebral spinal fluid is required. Where would be the safest place to perform a lumbar puncture?
questions.explanation: In a 5-day-old infant, the spinal cord ends at L3 (newborn level). Lumbar puncture below L3 (between L4 and L5) is safe because the spinal cord has already ended, avoiding risk of cord injury. In adults, the safe lumbar puncture level is L3-L4 or L4-L5. Needles below L3 in newborns avoid the terminated cord.
questions.keyConcept: In newborns, spinal cord ends at L3; safest lumbar puncture = below L3 (e.g., L4-L5) to avoid cord injury.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which tracts end on alpha and gamma neurons of extensor muscle?
questions.explanation: The vestibulospinal tracts (medial and lateral) end on both alpha and gamma motor neurons of extensor muscles, facilitating antigravity tone and postural stability. The medial vestibulospinal tract descends in the MLF to cervical levels; the lateral vestibulospinal tract descends throughout the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulospinal tracts: medial (MLF, cervical) and lateral (spinal cord) - facilitate extensor muscle tone for posture.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial and lateral vestibulospinal tracts. These tracts facilitate extensor muscle activity to maintain posture and balance against gravity.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the origin of radicular arteries?
questions.explanation: Radicular arteries arise from various sources: vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and the first lumbar artery. They enter the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina and reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and first lumbar artery. These segmental arteries enter through intervertebral foramina to supply the spinal cord.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Complete section of spinal cord above C5 results in
questions.explanation: Complete transection of the spinal cord above C5 results in quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs) due to interruption of all descending motor pathways at the cervical level, along with respiratory compromise.
questions.keyConcept: C5 cord transection quadriplegia
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arterial supply of anterior ends of caudate & lentiform nuclei is derived from:
questions.explanation: Anterior cerebral artery central branches supply anterior portions of caudate nucleus and lentiform nucleus, forming lenticulostriate arteries that also supply internal capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral central branches
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve group cell with same origin, function inside CNS:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers with the same origin, course, and termination within the CNS, such as the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: CNS tract definition
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Commissural Nuclei is between:
questions.explanation: Commissural nuclei connect sensory and motor nuclei on opposite sides of the spinal cord, facilitating crossed reflexes and coordinated movement.
questions.keyConcept: Commissural nuclei
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle continue in spinal cord through:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus continues in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal and sulcomarginal tracts, coordinating head-eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF continuation
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: External arcuate fibres carry impulses to:
questions.explanation: External arcuate fibers carry proprioceptive and vestibular information to the cerebellum via the peduncles, forming the mossy fiber input.
questions.keyConcept: External arcuate fibers
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: An injury to the posterior column of the lumbar spinal cord may be manifested as loss of:
questions.explanation: Posterior column lesion at lumbar level causes loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (tactile discrimination) in the ipsilateral lower limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior column lesion
options: fine touch at the upper limbs.
tactile discrimination at the lower limbs
crude touch at the upper limbs
pain & temperature at the lower limbs
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which lamina of the spinal cord corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa?
questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the posterior horn, specializing in pain and temperature modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa lamina
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient with a spinal cord lesion has loss of vibration and position sense in both legs but normal pain and temperature sensation. Which tract is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Bilateral loss of vibration and position sense with preserved pain/temperature indicates gracile tract lesion, as it carries proprioception and vibration from the legs.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following inhibits pain sensation?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibition pathways, reducing pain transmission at the spinal cord level.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid pain inhibition
options: Activation of the lateral spinothalamic tract
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the 2 enlargements present in the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3) enlargements for limb innervation, corresponding to brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord enlargements
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical enlargement and lumbar enlargement.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Compare between the spinal cord of the adult and the newborn:
questions.explanation: In adults the spinal cord extends from C1 to L1 vertebra, while in newborns it extends from C1 to L3 vertebra due to differential vertebral column growth.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord extent
questions.modelAnswer: Adult: C1 till L1; Newborn: C1 till L3.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of area 4 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes spastic paralysis of contralateral muscles with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski sign.
questions.keyConcept: Area 4 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign on contralateral side.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Origin of olivospinal tract:
questions.explanation: The olivospinal tract arises from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla and descends to the spinal cord to influence motor activity.
questions.keyConcept: Olivospinal tract origin
questions.modelAnswer: The olivospinal tract (olivary tract) originates from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla oblongata. These fibers descend in the spinal cord within the lateral funiculus and terminate on interneurons in the intermediate gray matter, primarily at cervical levels.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 arteries supplying spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three arteries supplying the spinal cord are the anterior spinal artery (ventral median spinal artery) and two posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord blood supply
questions.modelAnswer: One anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Artery supplying medial medulla and anterior 2/3 of spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla and anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the corticospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery
questions.modelAnswer: The anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplies the medial medulla and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. It arises from the vertebral arteries and descends through the anterior median fissure, supplying the pyramids, medial lemnisci, and corticospinal tracts.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Origin of radicular arteries:
questions.explanation: Radicular arteries arise segmentally from various aortic branches including vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, and first lumbar arteries, following nerve roots to supply the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries have segmental origins from aortic branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 6 veins draining spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord venous drainage follows a symmetrical pattern with anteromedian and posteromedian veins running vertically, plus four additional veins accompanying the ventral and dorsal nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord has six longitudinal veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, and four radicular veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteromedian, posteromedian, four veins along ventral and dorsal roots.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 lobes (functional):
questions.explanation: The cerebellum's functional lobes include archicerebellum (vestibular coordination), paleocerebellum (postural control), and neocerebellum (skilled movements).
questions.keyConcept: Three functional cerebellar lobes: archi-, paleo-, and neocerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Archicerebellum, paleocerebellum, neocerebellum.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arteries supplying medulla:
questions.explanation: The medulla receives blood from the anterior spinal artery, PICA (the largest branch), and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, with additional contribution from posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Medulla supplied by anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral branches, and posterior spinal arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal, PICA, medullary branches of vertebral, posterior spinal.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cervical sympathetic ganglia sites:
questions.explanation: The three paired cervical sympathetic ganglia are positioned at specific vertebral levels: superior ganglion at C2-3, middle ganglion at C6-7, and inferior ganglion (often fused with T1 as stellate ganglion) at C7 level.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical sympathetic ganglia: superior (C2-3), middle (C6-7), inferior (C7).
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: C2-3; Middle: C6-7; Inferior: C7.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In a complete spinal cord transection at the level of T6, which of the following would be expected?
questions.explanation: A complete transection at T6 would cause paraplegia (paralysis of both lower limbs) since this level is below the cervical region and does not affect upper limb innervation or respiratory muscles.
questions.keyConcept: T6 transection: paraplegia of both lower limbs.
options: Loss of pain sensation from the upper limbs
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb (elbow/wrist) is carried by the:
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from upper limb to cerebellum.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The axillary sheath is an extension from ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: UMNL of cranial nerves can result from cerebrovascular accident affecting ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies medial frontal and parietal regions including motor cortex areas controlling lower limbs; CVA here causes contralateral leg weakness and UMN signs.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: UMN lesion of cranial nerves (if affecting cortical areas).
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Medial medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia below the lesion, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, and ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia, proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue palsy.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia (flaccid), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, ipsilateral LMNL of tongue.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The neocerebellum is anatomically located in the following part of the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum (lateral parts of posterior lobe) is anatomically located in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum. It is concerned with planning and executing voluntary movements, particularly those requiring skilled precision.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum in posterior lobe
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the neocerebellum formed of?
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum consists of the lateral parts of the cerebellar hemispheres (the largest part in humans). It receives cortical input via the pontocerebellar pathway and is involved in planning and executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum: lateral cerebellar hemispheres. Receives cortical input, plans skilled movements.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral parts of the cerebellar hemisphere. This is the phylogenetically newest part (neocerebellum), connected to the cerebral cortex via the pontocerebellar pathway, and involved in planning and execution of skilled voluntary movements.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the arteries that supply the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum is supplied by three paired arteries: superior cerebellar artery (SCA - from basilar), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA - from basilar), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - usually from vertebral).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar arteries: SCA (superior), AICA (anterior inferior), PICA (posterior inferior).
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar artery (branch of basilar artery), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA - branch of basilar), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - usually from vertebral artery).
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which cerebellar structures are separated by fissura prima?
questions.explanation: The fissura prima separates the anterior and posterior lobes of the cerebellum. It divides the culmen (anterior lobe) from the declive, folium, and tuber (posterior lobe).
questions.keyConcept: Fissura prima divides the anterior and posterior cerebellar lobes, separating motor from non-motor regions.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which function is primarily controlled by the flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) primarily regulates balance and eye movements through connections with the vestibular nuclei. Lesions cause ataxia and nystagmus.
questions.keyConcept: Flocculonodular lobe controls vestibular function, balance, and eye movements via vestibular nuclei.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory can result in which of the following neurological deficits?
questions.explanation: PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum. PICA syndrome causes ipsilateral dysphagia, hoarseness, decreased gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus), and cerebellar signs, with contralateral pain/temperature loss.
questions.keyConcept: PICA syndrome presents with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits and contralateral sensory loss.
options: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arteries supplying cerebellum:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum receives blood from three paired arteries: superior cerebellar (SCA), anterior inferior cerebellar (AICA), and posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA) arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellum supplied by SCA, AICA, and PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar, anterior inferior cerebellar, posterior inferior cerebellar.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)?
questions.explanation: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) receives vestibular input and controls balance, posture, and eye movements, making it essential for spatial orientation.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulocerebellum: controls balance and eye movements.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lady 55 years old, developed right sided hemiplegia mainly in the upper limb due to cerebrovascular accident as proved by MRI. The lesion affects the frontal and parietal lobes.
questions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.

subQuestions.text: What is your diagnosis?
subQuestions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Cerebrovascular accident (ischemic stroke) in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA), affecting the lateral aspect of the frontal and parietal lobes.

subQuestions.text: Which vessel is most likely affected?
subQuestions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Left middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the lenticulostriate branches or the main trunk, supplying the lateral surface of the frontal and parietal lobes and the internal capsule.

questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which function is primarily controlled by the primary motor cortex (area 4)?
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) controls discrete, fine voluntary movements, especially of the distal limbs. It contains large pyramidal neurons (Betz cells) in layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex mediates fine, skilled voluntary movements via Betz cells and corticospinal output.
options: Gives you the idea to move
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is related to the anterior corticospinal tract?
questions.explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract arises from the medial precentral cortex, descends without decussating in the spinal cord, and terminates on interneurons controlling proximal muscles and axial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior corticospinal tract is uncrossed, controlling axial and proximal limb muscles.
options: Supplies the muscles of the trunk
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lamination of lateral corticospinal tract in spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract is laminated: cervical fibers are most lateral, sacral fibers most medial, controlling progressive distal-to-proximal muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal lamination
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical fibers most lateral, sacral most medial.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The spinal cord region that has the richest blood supply is:
questions.explanation: The cervical region of the spinal cord has the richest blood supply due to high metabolic demand and the watershed areas at C4-T1 levels, making it vulnerable to ischemic injury.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord has richest blood supply
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Give an account on blood supply (cervical part) of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries) supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns. Posterior spinal arteries (from PICA or vertebral) supply posterior 1/3 including posterior horn and posterior columns. Radicular arteries from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (anterior 2/3) and posterior spinal arteries (posterior 1/3)
questions.modelAnswer: Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → anterior spinal artery (formed at medulla) and two posterior spinal arteries; (2) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY supplies anterior 2/3 of cord (anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns); (3) POSTERIOR SPINAL ARTERIES supply posterior 1/3 (posterior horn, posterior columns); (4) RADICULAR ARTERIES from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the origin of anterior spinal artery & the parts supplied by it.
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery: ORIGIN formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; COURSE descends in the anterior median fissure; PARTS SUPPLIED: anterior 2/3 of spinal cord, anterior horn (motor), lateral horn (sympathetic), anterior and lateral white columns, and gray commissure with crossing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: vertebral artery origin, supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including motor and sympathetic regions
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery: (ORIGIN) Formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; (COURSE) Descends in anterior median fissure; (PARTS SUPPLIED) (1) Anterior 2/3 of spinal cord; (2) Anterior horn (motor); (3) Lateral horn (sympathetic); (4) Anterior and lateral white columns; (5) Gray commissure (with crossing fibers).
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Anterior spinal artery supplies the following structures Except:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord including the anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the origin of anterior spinal artery?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two arteries, each arising from a vertebral artery. The two branches join at the level of the foramen magnum to form a single median anterior spinal artery that descends in the anterior median fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: single median artery formed by union of two branches from vertebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a single median artery formed by the union of two anterior spinal arteries, each being a branch of the corresponding vertebral artery at the level of the medulla.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of vertebral artery
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery gives off meningeal, posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA), posterior spinal, anterior spinal, and medullary (paramedian) branches as it ascends through the foramen magnum.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebral artery branch types
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, Posterior inferior cerebellar, posterior spinal, anterior spinal, medullary branches
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Origin of anterior spinal artery:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two vessels, each arising from the corresponding vertebral artery, creating a single midline artery that descends along the anterior median fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery originates from the vertebral arteries as a common trunk.
questions.modelAnswer: Single artery formed by union of two anterior spinal arteries, each from vertebral artery.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Origin of posterior spinal artery:
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal artery typically arises from either the vertebral artery directly or from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), forming paired vessels that supply the posterior spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery may originate from vertebral artery or PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: The posterior spinal arteries (PSAs) arise from the vertebral arteries or the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA), usually as paired vessels. They descend along the dorsal roots, supplying the posterior columns and posterior horns of the spinal cord, receiving reinforcement from radicular arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Occlusion of right anterior cerebral artery may lead to:
questions.explanation: Right anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes left lower limb paralysis (contralateral) since it supplies the medial motor cortex controlling the leg.
