questions.text: Enumerate therapeutic uses of antipsychotics with examples
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics have diverse therapeutic uses beyond psychosis, including mood disorders, anxiety, and movement disorders.
questions.keyConcept: Antipsychotics are used for psychosis, bipolar disorder, major depression augmentation, and several non‑psychiatric conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Therapeutic uses of antipsychotics: (1) Psychotic disorders — schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder (typical: haloperidol, chlorpromazine; atypical: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine). (2) Bipolar disorder — acute mania and maintenance (olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole). (3) Major depressive disorder — augmentation (aripiprazole, quetiapine). (4) Severe anxiety (low‑dose haloperidol, risperidone). (5) Huntington's disease chorea (haloperidol). (6) Nausea/vomiting (prochlorperazine). (7) Intractable hiccups (chlorpromazine).

questions.text: Mention advantages of Atypical (New G.) over typical (Old G,) antipsychotics
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics have lower EPS rates, lower tardive dyskinesia risk, and treat both positive and negative symptoms compared to typical agents.
questions.keyConcept: Atypical antipsychotics offer superior tolerability with lower EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk while addressing both positive and negative symptoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Advantages of atypical over typical antipsychotics: (1) Lower incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia due to weaker D2 blockade and 5‑HT2A antagonism, which disinhibits dopamine release in nigrostriatal pathways. (2) Greater efficacy against negative symptoms of schizophrenia (e.g., flat affect, social withdrawal) — e.g., clozapine, risperidone. (3) Better cognitive outcomes. (4) Lower rates of hyperprolactinemia (except risperidone). (5) Broader receptor profiles (5‑HT2A, H1, alpha1, muscarinic) contributing to unique adverse effect profiles. (6) Reduced all‑cause mortality in schizophrenia patients compared to typicals.

questions.text: Outline advantages of typical antipsychotics
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics offer reliable efficacy, rapid onset of action, and lower cost compared to atypical agents.
questions.keyConcept: Typical antipsychotics provide reliable antipsychotic efficacy with rapid action and lower cost, despite higher EPS risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Advantages of typical (first‑generation) antipsychotics: (1) Proven efficacy for positive symptoms of schizophrenia — rapid and reliable reduction of hallucinations, delusions, and agitation. (2) Availability of depot formulations (haloperidol decanoate, fluphenazine decanoate) for non‑adherent patients. (3) Lower cost and wider availability. (4) Faster onset of action useful in acute agitation. (5) Long track record with well‑characterized adverse effect profiles. (6) Useful in patients who fail atypical antipsychotics (treatment‑resistant schizophrenia may respond to clozapine or high‑potency typicals).

questions.text: Advantages and disadvantages of adding benztropine with antipsychotics
questions.explanation: Adding benztropine to antipsychotics reduces EPS but risks anticholinergic toxicity, worsening of positive symptoms, and additive sedation.
questions.keyConcept: Benztropine co‑administration reduces EPS but carries anticholinergic risks and potential worsening of positive symptoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Advantages of adding benztropine with antipsychotics: (1) Reduces extrapyramidal symptoms (especially drug‑induced Parkinsonism and acute dystonia) by blocking muscarinic receptors in the basal ganglia, counteracting the dopamine‑acetylcholine imbalance caused by D2 blockade. (2) Allows maintenance of therapeutic antipsychotic dose without dose reduction. Disadvantages: (1) Anticholinergic adverse effects — dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion (especially in elderly), and worsening of narrow‑angle glaucoma. (2) Can worsen positive symptoms of psychosis (delusions, hallucinations) if dopamine blockade is reduced. (3) Risk of benztropine toxicity in elderly or dehydrated patients. (4) No benefit for tardive dyskinesia or akathisia in many cases.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions

questions.text: Outline autonomic adverse effects of antipsychotics
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics cause autonomic adverse effects including orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and blurred vision via alpha1, H1, and muscarinic receptor blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic effects of antipsychotics stem from receptor blockade causing orthostatic, cardiovascular, and anticholinergic manifestations.
questions.modelAnswer: Autonomic adverse effects of antipsychotics: (1) Alpha1‑adrenergic blockade — orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion. (2) Muscarinic (cholinergic) blockade — dry mouth (xerostomia), constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision (cycloplegia), tachycardia, worsening of narrow‑angle glaucoma. (3) Histamine H1 blockade — sedation, weight gain. (4) Cardiovascular — QTc prolongation (thioridazine, ziprasidone, iloperidone), tachycardia. These effects are more pronounced with low‑potency typical antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) and some atypicals (clozapine, quetiapine).

questions.text: List 2 antipsychotic drugs that may induce QT syndrome
questions.explanation: Thioridazine and ziprasidone are notable for QTc prolongation; thioridazine is a high‑potency typical antipsychotic with potent hERG channel blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Thioridazine and ziprasidone are antipsychotics with significant QT prolongation risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Two antipsychotic drugs that may induce QT syndrome: (1) Thioridazine — a low‑-ceiling, high‑potency typical antipsychotic that is one of the most significant QTc‑prolonging agents, primarily due to hERG potassium channel blockade. It carries a black box warning for sudden cardiac death. (2) Ziprasidone — an atypical antipsychotic with moderate QTc prolongation; though less than thioridazine, it still requires ECG monitoring in patients with cardiac risk factors or concurrent QT‑prolonging drugs.

questions.text: Outline drugs used in treatment of different periods of bipolar depression
questions.explanation: Bipolar depression treatment varies by phase: acute mania uses mood stabilizers + antipsychotics; bipolar depression uses quetiapine, lurasidone, or olanzapine‑fluoxetine combination; maintenance uses lithium or valproate.
questions.keyConcept: Bipolar disorder management is phase‑specific, with different drugs for manic, depressive, and maintenance phases.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs used in different periods of bipolar depression: (1) Acute manic phase — lithium carbonate + antipsychotic (e.g., haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone) for rapid control; valproate or carbamazepine as alternatives. (2) Acute bipolar depression — quetiapine (first‑line), lurasidone + lithium/valproate, olanzapine‑fluoxetine combination, or lurasidone alone. Lamotrigine is also used. (3) Maintenance phase — lithium (gold standard for suicide prevention), valproate, lamotrigine (particularly effective for depressive relapse prevention), aripiprazole, quetiapine. ECT for refractory cases.

questions.text: Explain why antipsychotic drugs are added to lithium in the beginning of therapy of manic phase of bipolar manic depression
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics are added to lithium in acute mania because lithium has a slow onset (1–2 weeks) while antipsychotics provide rapid control of agitation, hallucinations, and severe behavioral symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Antipsychotics are co‑prescribed with lithium in acute mania for their rapid symptomatic control while waiting for lithium's mood‑stabilizing effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Antipsychotics are added to lithium at the beginning of mania for the following reasons: (1) Lithium has a slow onset of action — therapeutic blood levels and mood stabilization take 1–2 weeks. (2) Antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone) provide rapid control of acute symptoms — agitation, hyperactivity, grandiosity, and psychotic features. (3) Combination therapy provides synergistic efficacy in severe mania. (4) Allows lower doses of both agents, reducing individual drug toxicity. Note: Lithium + antipsychotic combination requires monitoring for neurotoxicity (confusion, tremor, ataxia) even at therapeutic lithium levels.

questions.text: Mention 1st line treatment of bipolar depression

(2) Lurasidone (with lithium or valproate) — approved for bipolar depression. (3) Olanzapine‑fluoxetine combination — another evidence‑based option. (4) Lamotrigine — second‑line, primarily effective for prevention of bipolar depression relapse rather than acute treatment. (5) Electroconvulsive therapy — for treatment‑resistant or severe cases with psychotic features.

questions.text: Mention lines of management of lithium toxicity
questions.explanation: Lithium toxicity management includes stopping lithium, IV fluids, hemodialysis for severe cases, and correction of electrolyte imbalances.
questions.keyConcept: Lithium toxicity is managed with drug discontinuation, supportive care, and hemodialysis in severe cases.
questions.modelAnswer: Management of lithium toxicity: (1) Mild‑moderate toxicity (1.5–2.5 mEq/L) — immediate discontinuation of lithium, IV normal saline, monitoring of electrolytes and renal function. (2) Moderate‑severe toxicity (2.5–3.5 mEq/L) — same as above plus consider gastric lavage if within 1 hour of ingestion; consider whole bowel irrigation. (3) Severe toxicity (>3.5 mEq/L) or impaired renal function — hemodialysis is the treatment of choice as lithium is not protein‑bound and is amenable to dialysis removal. (4) Supportive care — control seizures with benzodiazepines (avoid phenytoin which lowers seizure threshold), manage fluid/electrolyte balance, treat arrhythmias. (5) Continuous cardiac monitoring. Note: Recovery from lithium toxicity may be prolonged (several days) due to redistribution from tissue compartments.

questions.text: Outline management of alcohol abuse
questions.explanation: Alcohol abuse management involves withdrawal treatment (benzodiazepines), long‑term support (naltrexone, acamprosate), and behavioral therapies.

questions.modelAnswer: Management of alcohol abuse: (1) Acute withdrawal — benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) as GABA‑A agonists to prevent seizures and delirium tremens; gabapentin or carbamazepine as alternatives. (2) Thiamine (B1) supplementation — to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome. (3) Relapse prevention — naltrexone (opioid antagonist reducing craving), acamprosate (GABA modulator reducing craving), disulfiram (aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor — causes unpleasant acetaldehyde reaction if alcohol consumed). (4) Psychosocial — cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational interviewing, 12‑step programs, family therapy. (5) Comorbid psychiatric conditions — treat co‑occurring depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder.

questions.text: Outline management of nicotine abuse
questions.explanation: Nicotine abuse management includes nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, bupropion, and behavioral counseling.

questions.modelAnswer: Management of nicotine abuse: (1) Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) — patches (long‑acting), gum, lozenges, nasal spray, inhaler (short‑acting); reduces withdrawal symptoms by providing controlled nicotine doses. (2) Varenicline — partial nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist, reduces craving and withdrawal. (3) Bupropion — atypical antidepressant (norepinephrine‑dopamine reuptake inhibitor) that reduces nicotine withdrawal and craving. (4) Combination therapy — NRT + varenicline or bupropion for higher success rates. (5) Behavioral therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational interviewing, and quitlines improve abstinence rates significantly. (6) Electronic cigarettes — controversial harm reduction tool. Success rates double when pharmacotherapy is combined with behavioral support.

questions.text: Mention mechanism of two drugs used in management of nicotine abuse (smoking)

questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism of two drugs used in nicotine abuse: (1) Varenicline — partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It prevents nicotine from binding (reducing reward from smoking) while providing moderate receptor activation (reducing withdrawal symptoms). Also acts at α3β4 and α7 receptors. (2) Bupropion — norepinephrine‑dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI); increases synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine in the mesolimbic reward pathway, reducing nicotine craving and withdrawal. It also antagonizes nicotinic receptors at higher concentrations.

questions.text: Discuss role of varenicline is management of nicotine abuse

questions.text: The following conditions decrease activity of local anesthetic EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Adding sodium bicarbonate INCREASES local anesthetic activity (not decreases). Bicarbonate raises pH, increasing the unionized (base) form of the anesthetic. The unionized form readily crosses nerve membranes; once inside (lower pH), it becomes ionized and blocks sodium channels. Therefore, option D (addition of sodium bicarbonate) actually INCREASES activity, making it the exception. Options A, B, C all DECREASE activity: repeated administration can cause tachyphylaxis; infection decreases activity (acidic environment traps drug extracellularly); decrease intracellular acidity (more ionized form extracellularly, less penetration). The correct answer is D because sodium bicarbonate enhances activity, contrary to what the question implies.

questions.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors were withdrawn (rofecoxib) or carry warnings due to increased cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke). They do have low GI ulceration risk and nephrotoxicity concerns. Celecoxib is contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors carry significant cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke) - FALSE statement
options: Are associated with low risk of gastric ulceration
Have a low risk of cardiotoxicity and stroke
Nephrotoxicity is a serious adverse effect
Celecoxib should not be given to patients with sulfonamide allergy
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is not an enzyme inducer?
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all enzyme inducers that increase metabolism of other drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer (unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital)
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement regarding antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Pregnant women with epilepsy should NOT discontinue antiepileptic drugs abruptly - the risk of seizures may outweigh the risks of the medication. Treatment should be continued with the lowest effective dose of the safest drug.
questions.keyConcept: Pregnant women should NOT discontinue AEDs abruptly (risky to mother and fetus) - FALSE
options: Females who get pregnant should discontinue the antiepileptic drug
They are contraindicated in neuropathic pain
Carbamazepine antagonizes the action of antidiuretic hormone
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is not acting through increase GABA activity?
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, not through GABA enhancement. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity (inhibitory neurotransmitter).
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine acts on NMDA receptors, not through GABA enhancement
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not an enzyme inducer:
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all potent enzyme inducers.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate NOT an enzyme inducer (inhibits CYP enzymes)
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which opioid is a long‑acting, pure agonist associated with milder withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Methadone is a long-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in opioid maintenance therapy, producing milder withdrawal due to its slow dissociation from receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Methadone pharmacology
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which opioid acts as a partial agonist at the μ receptor and is used in opioid dependence management?
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa antagonist, producing ceiling effects on respiratory depression and milder withdrawal.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine mechanism
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: An alcoholic patient shows dependence related to activation of opioid receptors. Which drug is used for treatment?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence by blocking opioid receptors involved in reward pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone for alcoholism
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which anti‑Parkinsonian drug commonly produces atropine‑like adverse effects (dry mouth, blurred vision)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine is an anticholinergic anti-Parkinsonian drug that produces peripheral atropine-like side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinergic Parkinson drugs
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue therapy to manage sudden episodes of motor deterioration in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is a rapid-acting dopamine agonist used subcutaneously as rescue therapy for sudden off episodes (akinesia) in advanced Parkinson's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine rescue therapy
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pharma

questions.text: Which of the following tumors is a WHO grade IV:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO grade IV tumor (most malignant). It arises in the cerebellum, more common in children. Diffuse astrocytoma (grade II-III) and oligodendroglioma (grade II-III) are slower-growing tumors. Ependymoma is grade II-III. WHO grading: Grade I (pilocytic astrocytoma - benign), Grade II (low-grade), Grade III (anaplastic), Grade IV (most aggressive - medulloblastoma, glioblastoma). Medulloblastoma is highly cellular, mitotically active, and has the worst prognosis among primary brain tumors in children, requiring aggressive treatment.
questions.keyConcept: WHO grade IV brain tumors (medulloblastoma) are the most malignant, distinguishing from grade II-III tumors.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a WHO grade I tumor (benign) with good prognosis. Characteristic features: occurs in children (most common pediatric brain tumor), commonly arises in cerebellum (though can occur elsewhere), often cystic with a mural nodule. Option D states 'bad prognosis' which is INCORRECT - pilocytic astrocytoma has excellent prognosis with complete surgical resection (5-year survival >90%). This is the EXCEPT question, so D is the answer. In contrast, diffuse astrocytoma (grade II) and anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III) have progressively worse prognoses.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign childhood cerebellar tumor with excellent prognosis after complete resection.
questions.chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions
questions.subject: pathology

questions.text: A chain of successive tracts in CNS having the same function is called:
questions.explanation: A pathway is a chain of successive tracts in the CNS serving the same function. A fasciculus is a smaller bundle within a tract. A lemniscus is a specific ascending brainstem pathway. A commissure connects two sides of the CNS, and a decussation is a midline crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Pathway = chain of successive tracts with identical function
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS having the same beginning, termination and function is called:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS sharing the same origin, termination, and function. A pathway is a chain of tracts. A lemniscus is an ascending brainstem bundle. A commissure connects hemispheres, and a decussation is a crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle with common origin, termination, and function
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The lowermost soft part of the auricle of ear is called:
questions.explanation: The lobule is the soft, fleshy lower part of the auricle (earlobe). The tragus is the small pointed projection anterior to the ear canal. The concha is the bowl-shaped depression.
questions.keyConcept: Lobule = soft lower part of the auricle (earlobe)
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Sensation from the angle of mandible is carried by:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the temple and anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve supplies skin over the angle of the mandible
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Tumor from central part of upper lip would likely spread to which group of lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The central part of the upper lip drains primarily to the submandibular lymph nodes. The upper lip also drains to the submental nodes via lymphatic crossing. The buccal and parotid nodes drain more lateral facial regions.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains to submandibular lymph nodes
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from ala of nose is carried by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) laterally and the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) at the tip.
questions.keyConcept: Ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and external nasal nerve (V1)
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The non-hairy region of the temple is supplied by which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplies the non-hairy skin of the temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp of the temple.
questions.keyConcept: Zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the non-hairy temple region
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which one of the following scalp nerves is derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It supplies the skin of the occipital region of the scalp. The auriculotemporal, great auricular, lesser occipital, and posterior auricular nerves are ventral ramus derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve = dorsal ramus of C2
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The artery that lies above parotid duct is a direct branch of:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery (external carotid), runs above the parotid duct. The facial artery enters the face at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse facial artery lies above the parotid duct
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection of lateral part of the upper eye lid leads to enlargement of which group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: The lateral part of the upper eyelid drains to the parotid (pre-auricular) lymph nodes. The medial part drains to the submandibular nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid lymph nodes
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve supplying the buccinator muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically via its buccal branches. Although it is in the region of the mandibular nerve, the motor supply is from the facial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is sensory to the scalp behind the auricle?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and the scalp behind the auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies scalp behind the auricle
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Retromandibular vein:
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the maxillary and superficial temporal veins. It begins inside the parotid gland, is deep to the facial nerve, and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein = maxillary + superficial temporal; lies deep to facial nerve in parotid
options: Is formed by union of maxillary & superficial temporal veins.
Is deep to facial nerve inside parotid gland.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of the orbicularis oculi is attached to the lacrimal sac and the posterior lacrimal crest. It helps drain tears by compression of the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches to lacrimal sac and aids tear drainage
options: Is attached to medial palpebral ligament.
Is attached to lateral palpebral raphe.
Is a part of orbicularis oris.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mandibular nerve is sensory to:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) carries sensation from the lower lip (via the mental nerve), chin, temporal region, and anterior ear. It does not supply the upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or tip of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory supply includes the lower lip and chin
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pulse felt at antero-inferior angle of masseter is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The facial artery can be palpated as it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery pulse is palpable at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from capsule of parotid gland is carried by:
questions.explanation: The parotid capsule is innervated by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), which carries pain fibers from the gland capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid capsule pain is carried by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3)
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Bleeding in which layer of scalp causes black eye?
questions.explanation: Bleeding into the loose areolar connective tissue layer of the scalp allows blood to spread freely and gravitate into the eyelids via the subaponeurotic space, causing a black eye.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue layer bleeding causes black eye via gravitational spread
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards scalp, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The scalp has numerous sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles. Its rich vascularity means wounds bleed profusely, and aponeurotic wounds gape due to muscle pull.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp has abundant sebaceous glands; wounds bleed profusely and gape if aponeurosis is cut
options: Its wounds gap if aponeurosis is cut.
Its veins communicate with intracranial venous sinuses.
It contains a muscle of facial expression.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The plane of movement of scalp is between:
questions.explanation: The scalp moves as a single unit because the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and epicranial aponeurosis are firmly attached. The plane of movement is between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp movement occurs between epicranial aponeurosis and pericranium
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The large blood vessels of scalp run in:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is richly vascularized and innervated.
questions.keyConcept: Blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve supply of the muscle of the sclap is:
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically the temporal and posterior auricular branches. The great auricular and great occipital nerves are purely sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The main sensory nerve of the upper lip is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division, V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip, lower eyelid, and cheek.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match the area of skin in left column with its corresponding nerve supply in the right column:
questions.explanation: Lateral upper eyelid → lacrimal nerve (V1). Tip of nose → external nasal nerve (V1). Lower lip → mental nerve (V3). Angle of mandible → great auricular nerve (C2–C3). Forehead → supraorbital nerve (V1).
questions.keyConcept: Specific facial skin areas have distinct sensory nerve supplies
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The pulse felt in front of tragus of ear against zygomatic arch is the pulse of:
questions.explanation: The superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, can be palpated in front of the tragus of the ear against the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse is palpable anterior to the tragus against the zygomatic arch
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Facial muscles:
questions.explanation: Facial muscles are sphincters and dilators of facial openings. They are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Facial muscles act as sphincters for facial orifices and are innervated by CN VII
options: Act as sphincters for facial openings.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The muscle that causes firm closure of eyelids is:
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi is responsible for firm (forced) closure of the eyelids. The palpebral part closes the eye gently.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi = forced eye closure; palpebral part = gentle closure
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards buccinator muscle, all the following is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) via its buccal branches. It is NOT innervated by the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the mandibular nerve
options: It is the muscle of the cheecks.
It arises from maxilla and mandible.
It is inserted in upper and lower lips.
It prevents accumulation of food in oral vestibule.
It is innervated by mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For each one of the layers of the scalp in left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: Skin = common site for sebaceous cysts. Epicranial aponeurosis = attached to superior temporal line. Loose connective tissue = dangerous layer. Pericranium = continuous with sutural ligaments. Dense connective tissue = wounds do not gape.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue is the dangerous layer of the scalp due to emissary veins

pairs.target: Is attached to superior temporal line.
Considered as dangerous layer of scalp

questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the subcutaneous connective tissue layer of scalp, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous connective tissue layer of the scalp is dense and fibrous. Infections here are localized because the tissue is dense. Wounds bleed profusely because fibrous septa prevent vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous connective tissue of scalp is dense; infection is localized and wounds bleed profusely
options: It contains arteries & nerves of scalp.
It connects skin of scalp with aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate the arteries of the scalp. Mention the origin of each artery.
questions.explanation: The arteries of the scalp include: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (from ophthalmic, internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (from external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (from external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (from external carotid).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp arteries: supraorbital/trochlear (internal carotid), superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital (external carotid)
questions.modelAnswer: The arteries of the scalp are: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of the external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (branch of the external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (branch of the external carotid). The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nerves of scalp in front of auricle.
questions.explanation: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (V3). (2) Temporal branch of facial nerve (CN VII, motor). (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp nerves anterior to auricle: auriculotemporal (V3), temporal branch of facial nerve, great auricular (C2–3), lesser occipital (C2)
questions.modelAnswer: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (branch of mandibular division V3), supplying the temporal region and anterior auricle. (2) Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), motor to the frontalis. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible and lower parotid region. (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2), supplying the upper lateral neck.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nerves of scalp behind of auricle.
questions.explanation: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2). (2) Lesser occipital nerve (C2, ventral ramus). (3) Greater auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Posterior auricular nerve (CN VII, motor).
questions.keyConcept: Scalp nerves posterior to auricle: greater occipital (C2 dorsal), lesser occipital (C2 ventral), great auricular (C2–3), posterior auricular (CN VII)
questions.modelAnswer: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2), supplying the occipital scalp. (2) Lesser occipital nerve (ventral ramus of C2), supplying the upper lateral neck and lower lateral scalp. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible. (4) Posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII), motor to the occipitalis and auricular muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe branches of Maxillary nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve, and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve (V2) branches: zygomatic, infraorbital, pterygopalatine ganglion branches
questions.modelAnswer: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (which divides into zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve (supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip), and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe branches of Mandibular nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek), auriculotemporal nerve (temple), lingual nerve (tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (mental nerve for lower lip and chin). It exits via the foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) branches: buccal, auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar (mental)
questions.modelAnswer: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek skin and mucosa), auriculotemporal nerve (temple and anterior auricle), lingual nerve (anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (which gives the mental nerve for the lower lip and chin). It exits the skull via the foramen ovale.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe parts of orbicularis oculi muscle.
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: outer thick portion, forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: thin portion in eyelids, gentle closure/blinking. (3) Lacrimal part: deep portion attached to lacrimal sac, aids tear drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi parts: orbital (forced closure), palpebral (gentle closure), lacrimal (tear drainage)
questions.modelAnswer: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: the outer thick portion attached to the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments; responsible for forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: the thin portion in the eyelids; responsible for gentle closure (blinking). (3) Lacrimal part: the deep portion attached to the lacrimal sac; aids tear drainage via the lacrimal canaliculi.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A D years old child fell off his bicycle & his head hit the pavement. A 2 cm long wound in his scalp was seen. Soon, he was sitting in a pool of blood.
questions.explanation: The scalp has a rich blood supply and dense connective tissue that prevents vessel constriction, leading to profuse bleeding. The dangerous layer is the loose areolar tissue because it contains valveless emissary veins.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp wounds bleed profusely due to rich vascularity and inability to constrict

subQuestions.text: Why does the scalp bleed profusely?
subQuestions.explanation: The dense fibrous septa in the scalp's subcutaneous layer tether the vessels open, preventing vasoconstriction and causing profuse bleeding.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Scalp dense fibrous tissue prevents vasoconstriction → profuse bleeding
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the fibrous tissue in the connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in this layer.

subQuestions.text: Name the arteries that supply the scalp.
subQuestions.explanation: The scalp is supplied by five paired arteries: supraorbital and supratrochlear (internal carotid), and superficial temporal, posterior auricular, and occipital (external carotid).
subQuestions.keyConcept: Five arteries supply the scalp: supraorbital, supratrochlear, superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Arteries supplying the scalp in front of the auricle: supraorbital artery, supratrochlear artery, and superficial temporal artery. Behind the auricle: posterior auricular artery and occipital artery.

subQuestions.text: Which is the dangerous layer of the scalp? Why is it dangerous?
subQuestions.explanation: The loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins that communicate with intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection to spread intracranially.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins → intracranial spread
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Loose areolar tissue layer because it contains the emissary veins that are valveless and can take infection to the inside of the skull.

questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Sacral fibers are the most medial fibers in the spinal cord during its ascend through:
questions.explanation: In the gracile tract, sacral fibers are located most medially (near the posterior median sulcus) while cervical fibers are most lateral. This somatotopic arrangement is maintained throughout the tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers most medial in gracile tract
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Injury of the right cortico-bulbar tract would affect muscles of:
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract controls lower facial muscles contralaterally. Lesion of the right corticobulbar tract causes paralysis of the left lower face (contralateral to the lesion).
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has contralateral control of lower face
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate the arteries that give radicular arteries to spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Arteries giving radicular arteries to spinal cord include: vertebral arteries, ascending cervical arteries (branch of inferior thyroid artery), deep cervical arteries (branch of costocervical trunk), intercostal arteries (for thoracic segments), lumbar arteries (for lumbar segments), and lateral sacral arteries (for sacral segments). These reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending/deep cervical, intercostal, lumbar, and sacral arteries
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries giving radicular arteries: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES; (2) ASCENDING CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of inferior thyroid); (3) DEEP CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of costocervical trunk); (4) INTERCOSTAL ARTERIES (for thoracic segments); (5) LUMBAR ARTERIES (for lumbar segments); (6) LATERAL SACRAL ARTERIES (for sacral segments).

questions.text: An old man developed UMNL paralysis of muscles of lower part of the face while muscles of upper part of face were preserved.
questions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
questions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Explain why the muscles of upper part are preserved?
subQuestions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
subQuestions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the upper part of the facial nucleus that controls the muscles of the upper 3 of the face receives fibers from the corticonuclear tract of both sides (bilaterally represented).

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] List the parasympathetic nuclei of the facial nerve?
subQuestions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
subQuestions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The parasympathetic nuclei of the facial nerve are: (1) Lacrimal nucleus (special lacrimatory nucleus) - supplies the lacrimal gland, mucous membranes of nose and palate via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion; (2) Superior salivatory nucleus - supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands via the chorda tympani.

subQuestions.text: [TYPE: essay] Enumerate the terminal branches of the facial nerve
