questions.text: Mention mechanism and uses of propofol
questions.explanation: Propofol acts by enhancing GABA-A receptor function. Uses include induction and maintenance of general anesthesia, sedation in ICU and procedures, and ambulatory surgery due to rapid recovery. Its main advantages are rapid onset and clear-headed recovery.
questions.keyConcept: Propofol provides rapid induction and recovery through GABAergic sedation, ideal for day surgery and ICU sedation.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Propofol Mechanism of Action:**
- Enhances GABA-A receptor activity
- Increases chloride conductance
- Potentiates inhibitory GABAergic transmission
- Acts on multiple GABA-A subunit compositions

**Uses:**

1. **Anesthesia:**
   - Induction of general anesthesia
   - Maintenance (total IV anesthesia)
   - Day-case surgery

2. **Sedation:**
   - ICU sedation
   - Procedural sedation
   - Sedation for diagnostic procedures

3. **Antiemetic:**
   - Antiemetic properties at subhypnotic doses

**Advantages:**
- Rapid onset (30-60 seconds)
- Rapid recovery (patients are alert within minutes)
- Clear-headed recovery
- Antiemetic effect
- Dose-dependent CNS depression

questions.text: The large blood vessels of the scalp run into:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels of the scalp run in the connective tissue layer (layer 2), between the skin and aponeurosis. They anastomose extensively.选项D正确. The answer is D. This layer is vascular and causes profuse bleeding when cut.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp blood vessels run in the subcutaneous connective tissue layer - profuse bleeding when injured.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Loss of sensation from the lower eyelid indicates injury of which nerve?
questions.explanation: Loss of sensation from lower eyelid indicates injury of infraorbital nerve (branch of V2 maxillary division of trigeminal).选项B正确. The answer is B. This nerve exits via infraorbital foramen.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid - injury causes sensory loss in that distribution.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following muscles can produce transverse wrinkles in the forehead?
questions.explanation: The frontalis muscle (assisted by procerus and corrugator supercilii) can produce transverse wrinkles in the forehead when contracting.选项A正确. The answer is A. Frontalis is innervated by temporal branches of facial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Frontalis muscle produces transverse forehead wrinkles - facial nerve (temporal branch) innervates it.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Bleeding beneath the pericranium of the scalp:
questions.explanation: Bleeding beneath the pericranium (subperiosteal hematoma) is LIMITED because pericranium is firmly attached to skull bones - it doesn't spread like the loose areolar layer.选项A正确. The answer is A. In contrast, bleeding in loose areolar layer is diffuse.
questions.keyConcept: Subperiosteal hematoma is localized - pericranium is firmly attached to bone unlike loose areolar layer.
options: Spreads underneath all of the scalp.
Makes a swelling that takes the shape of the underlying bone.
Reaches to the back of neck.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The motor nerve of the scalp behind the auricle is:
questions.explanation: The motor nerve of the scalp behind the auricle is the posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.选项B正确. The answer is B. It innervates posterior auricular and occipital muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricular branch of facial nerve supplies muscles behind the auricle - motor to that area.
options: Posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.
Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Buccinator:
questions.explanation: Buccinator muscle: forms the cheek, keeps food between teeth during chewing, is pierced by parotid duct (Stensen's duct), and is innervated by facial nerve (buccal branch).选项C正确. The answer is C. It acts to blow, whistle, and chew.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: cheek muscle pierced by parotid duct, facial nerve innervation, keeps food between teeth.
options: Is one of the muscles of mastication.
Is supplied by buccal branch of mandibular nerve.
Arises from both mandible and maxilla.
Is covered by investing layer of fascia.
Accumulates food in vestibule of mouth.

questions.text: The upper lip:
questions.explanation: The upper lip: receives sensory innervation from infraorbital nerve (V2), motor from facial nerve, and lymph drains to submandibular nodes.选项E正确. The answer is E. The philtrum is midline - upper lip sensation is infraorbital.
questions.keyConcept: Upper lip: infraorbital nerve (V2) sensation, facial nerve motor, submandibular lymph drainage.
options: Lies in the dangerous area of face.
Its philtrum is obliterated in infections.

questions.text: Which of the following contains parasympathetic postganglionic fibers?
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion contains parasympathetic postganglionic fibers (from greater petrosal nerve and nerve of pterygoid canal).选项A正确. The answer is A. It relays parasympathetic to lacrimal, nasal, palatine glands.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine ganglion: parasympathetic postganglionic fibers - lacrimal, nasal, palatine secretion.

questions.text: Lymph from central part of upper lip drains directly to:
questions.explanation: Lymph from central part of upper lip drains directly to submental lymph nodes (central group).选项B正确. The answer is B. Submental nodes drain the central lower face and lip.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains to submental nodes - important for lip cancer spread.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve supply of the muscle of the scalp is:
questions.explanation: The nerve supply of scalp muscles (including frontalis, occipitalis) is via facial nerve branches - temporal, posterior auricular, and other branches.选项D正确. The answer is D. Sensory innervation is via trigeminal branches.
questions.keyConcept: Motor to scalp muscles: facial nerve (temporal and posterior auricular branches) - sensory: trigeminal branches.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from upper lip is carried by.
questions.explanation: Pain from upper lip carried by infraorbital nerve (branch of V2 maxillary division of trigeminal).选项B正确. The answer is B. This nerve exits via infraorbital foramen.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from upper lip - exits at infraorbital foramen.

questions.text: Infection of lateral part of the upper eye lid leads to enlargement of this group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: Infection of lateral part of upper eyelid drains to parotid lymph nodes (superficial parotid nodes).选项C正确. The answer is C. The medial eyelid drains to submandibular nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid nodes; medial eyelid drains to submandibular nodes.

questions.text: All of the following regarding orbicularis oris muscle is correct Except:
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oris: surrounds mouth, has no bony attachment, has multiple muscle insertions including modiolus, and is innervated by facial nerve.选项C正确. The answer is C. It closes lips and helps speech.

options: It is a muscle of facial expression.
It is supplied by facial nerve.
Its fibers form complete circles around the mouth.
It can close the oral (labial) fissure.

questions.text: The following is a branch of the superficial temporal artery in the face:
questions.explanation: Superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of external carotid) gives off the transverse facial artery in the face.选项D正确. The answer is D. The transverse facial artery runs above parotid duct.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse facial artery is a branch of superficial temporal artery - runs above parotid duct in face.

questions.text: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi
questions.explanation: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi: is attached to medial palpebral ligament, closes eye gently (orbicularis has orbital and palpebral parts).选项A正确. The answer is A. The lacrimal part specifically compresses lacrimal sac.

questions.explanation: The buccal branch of mandibular nerve (V3) supplies: motor to lateral pterygoid, and sensory to cheek (buccal mucosa, skin over buccinator).选项B正确. The answer is B. This is sensory to cheek, NOT motor to buccinator.

questions.text: The lingual nerve:
questions.explanation: Lingual nerve (V3): carries general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue, runs lateral to hyoglossus muscle, carries chorda tympani (taste) fibers.选项E正确. The answer is E. It runs close to third molar roots.

questions.text: A lesion of mandibular nerve immediately after its exit from foramen oval may lead to:

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding chorda tympani; all are correct statements Except:
questions.explanation: Chorda tympani: carries taste from anterior 2/3 tongue (via lingual nerve), carries parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands, crosses middle ear, joins lingual nerve.选项C正确. The answer is C. It does NOT supply the tongue directly - runs with lingual nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Chorda tympani: taste + parasympathetic to submandibular/sublingual - runs with lingual nerve to tongue.
options: It is a branch of facial nerve.
It joins lingual nerve deep to lateral pterygoid.
It is related to medial side of lower third molar.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the DORSAL aspect of the closed medulla, forming the tubercles seen on the posterior surface. These nuclei receive proprioception and fine touch from the lower and upper body respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei: dorsal closed medulla; receive proprioception and fine touch.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lowermost level of medulla shows:
questions.explanation: The lowermost medulla (near spinomedullary junction) shows the DECUSSATION OF CORTICOSPINAL FIBERS (motor decussation). The pyramids are not yet formed. The inferior olivary nucleus appears at higher (open medulla) levels. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal decussation: lowermost medulla (motor decussation). Sensory decussation is higher. Olivary nucleus is higher still.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fibers derived from which nucleus run transversally to form the trapezoid body?
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL cochlear nucleus gives rise to fibers that cross transversely to form the trapezoid body in the pons. These are part of the auditory pathway to the superior olivary nucleus. The dorsal cochlear nucleus projects via the intermediate acoustic stria.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral cochlear nucleus → trapezoid body → superior olivary nucleus (auditory pathway).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the site of primary motor area?
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (area 4) is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and extends onto the anterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial surface (representing the lower limb).
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor area: precentral gyrus + anterior paracentral lobule (leg). Body representation is inverted.
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus of frontal lobe and anterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). Representation is upside-down and contralateral: face near lateral sulcus, upper limb above, trunk, lower limb on medial surface.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the 3 arteries that supply the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord is supplied by three arteries: one anterior spinal artery (running in the anterior median fissure) and two posterior spinal arteries (running near the dorsal roots). Segmental arteries (radicular arteries) reinforce these along the cord length.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (1), posterior spinal arteries (2), segmental (radicular) arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery (single, midline), two posterior spinal arteries (lateral), and segmental arteries (multiple, reinforce the longitudinal arteries along the cord length).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the 6 veins that drain the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord veins include: one anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), one posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and two each of anterolateral and posterolateral veins running with the nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, paired anterolateral and posterolateral veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and four lateral veins running along the ventral and dorsal nerve roots on each side.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerves are affected by the cerebellopontine angle tumor?
questions.explanation: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (typically acoustic/vestibular schwannoma) affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss and vertigo, and CN VII (facial) causing facial paralysis. These nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellopontine angle tumor: affects CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear).
questions.modelAnswer: Facial nerve (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). These cranial nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle and are commonly affected by acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the boundaries of the interpeduncular fossa?
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma, anterolaterally by the optic tract, posterolaterally by the cerebral peduncle, and posteriorly by the upper border of the pons. The floor is the posterior perforated substance.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa: anterior = optic chiasma; lateral = optic tract; posterolateral = cerebral peduncle; posterior = upper pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: optic chiasma. Anterolaterally: optic tract. Posterolaterally: cerebral peduncle. Posteriorly: upper border of pons. The floor is formed by the posterior perforated substance.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the arteries that supply the medulla.
questions.explanation: The medulla is supplied by: anterior spinal artery (medial medulla), posterior inferior cerebellar artery (lateral medulla), direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, and posterior spinal artery (posterior surface).
questions.keyConcept: Medulla blood supply: anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral artery branches, posterior spinal artery.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery (supplies medial medulla including pyramids and hypoglossal nucleus), posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - supplies lateral medulla including vestibular nuclei and cerebellum), medullary branches of vertebral artery, and posterior spinal artery (supplies posterior medulla).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve passes infront of the point of crossing of the free margin and the attached margin of tentorium cerebelli?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) passes ANTERIOR to the point where the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli meets its attached margin. The trochlear nerve passes AT this point. This anatomical landmark is important in herniation syndromes.
questions.keyConcept: CN III passes anterior to tentorial notch; CN IV crosses at the tentorial edge.
questions.modelAnswer: Oculomotor nerve (CN III). It passes anterior to the point where the free margin meets the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli. This is relevant to tentorial herniation where CN III can be compressed against the tentorial edge.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve passes at the point of crossing of the free margin and the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to pass through the tentorial notch - it crosses between the free and attached margins of the tentorium at the point of their crossing. It is the most dorsal cranial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve that crosses at the tentorial notch.
questions.modelAnswer: Trochlear nerve (CN IV). It is the only cranial nerve that passes at the point of crossing of the free and attached margins of the tentorium cerebelli. CN IV has the longest intracranial course and decussates before emerging from the dorsal midbrain.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the nerve supply of muscles of mastication.
questions.explanation: All muscles of mastication are supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3) except the medial pterygoid, which is supplied by the trunk of the mandibular nerve. The medial pterygoid also receives fibers from the nerve to tensor veli palatini.
questions.keyConcept: Mastication muscles: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk of V3).
questions.modelAnswer: All are supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3) except medial pterygoid, which is supplied by the trunk of the mandibular nerve directly. The anterior division supplies temporalis, masseter, and lateral pterygoid.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the actions of muscles of mastication.
questions.explanation: All muscles of mastication elevate the mandible (close the jaw) EXCEPT the lateral pterygoid, which depresses the mandible (opens the jaw). Temporalis retracts the mandible. Medial and lateral pterygoids perform side-to-side grinding movements.
questions.keyConcept: Mastication actions: elevation by all except lateral pterygoid (depression); retraction by temporalis; side-to-side by both pterygoids.
questions.modelAnswer: All protrude the mandible except Temporalis (which retracts). All elevate the mandible except Lateral pterygoid (which depresses). Medial and Lateral pterygoids perform side-to-side (grinding) movements. Masseter and temporalis are primarily elevators; medial pterygoid assists in elevation and protrusion.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the lateral relations of lateral pterygoid.
questions.explanation: The lateral relations of the lateral pterygoid include: ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid plexus of veins. These structures surround and limit the lateral pterygoid.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid laterally: mandible ramus, medial pterygoid superficial head, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: Ramus of mandible (lateral to lateral pterygoid), superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid plexus of veins.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of posterior division of mandibular nerve.
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives off: auriculotemporal nerve (sensory to temple and ear), lingual nerve (sensory to anterior 2/3 of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
questions.keyConcept: Posterior V3: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves. Anterior V3: muscles of mastication + buccal nerve.
questions.modelAnswer: Auriculotemporal nerve (sensory to temple and external ear), lingual nerve (sensory to anterior 2/3 of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (sensory to lower teeth, chin; motor to mylohyoid and anterior digastric).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention 4 branches of maxillary nerve.
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off: meningeal nerve (dura of middle cranial fossa), two ganglionic branches (to pterygopalatine ganglion), zygomatic nerve (to orbit and temple), and posterior superior alveolar nerves (to upper molars).
questions.keyConcept: V2 branches: meningeal, ganglionic (to pterygopalatine ganglion), zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal nerve (to dura of middle cranial fossa), two ganglionic branches (to pterygopalatine ganglion for parasympathetic), zygomatic nerve (to lateral orbit and temple), and posterior superior alveolar nerve (to upper molars and gums).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of third part of maxillary artery.
questions.explanation: The third (terminal) part of the maxillary artery gives off: posterior superior alveolar artery, infraorbital artery, greater and lesser palatine arteries, sphenopalatine artery (to nasal cavity), pharyngeal artery, and artery of pterygoid canal.
questions.keyConcept: 3rd maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine (greater/lesser), sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior superior alveolar artery (to upper molars), infraorbital artery (to infraorbital region), greater and lesser palatine arteries (to palate), sphenopalatine artery (to nasal cavity), pharyngeal artery (to nasopharynx), and artery of pterygoid canal.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the drainage of pterygoid plexus of veins.
questions.explanation: The pterygoid plexus of veins drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. The pterygoid plexus receives blood from muscles of mastication and surrounding structures.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein → retromandibular vein → external jugular vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Maxillary vein. The pterygoid plexus of veins drains into the maxillary vein, which unites with the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, which then drains into the external jugular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands (from its inferior wing) and the thymus (from its ventral wing), explaining the common origin of these structures.
questions.keyConcept: Third pharyngeal pouch derivatives
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior parathyroid gland and epithelium of thymus
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding tentorium cerebelli
questions.explanation: The tentorium cerebelli roofs over the posterior cranial fossa (not middle); its free border is attached to the anterior clinoid process (not post clinoid), and oculomotor/trochlear nerves pierce dura at this junction.
questions.keyConcept: Tentorium cerebelli attachments and relations
options: It roofs over middle cranial fossa
Its free border is attached to anterior clinoid process
Its attached border is attached to post clinoid process
It includes transverse venous sinus in its attached border
Oculomotor and trochlear nerves pierce dura at the point of crossing of its free & attached borders
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Vertebrobasilar system supplies the following Except:
questions.explanation: Vertebrobasilar system supplies cerebellum, inner ear (labyrinthine artery), occipital cortex (PCA), and pons; the temporal pole is supplied by MCA, not vertebrobasilar.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebrobasilar territories
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding the scalp the following statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels of the scalp run in the subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is the layer between the skin and epicranial aponeurosis. This layer contains fat and fibrous septae connecting skin to aponeurosis. Option B stating 'loose subaponeurotic space' is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp blood vessels located in subcutaneous connective tissue, not subaponeurotic space
options: Infection from scalp wounds can spread to superior sagittal sinus.
Its blood vessels run in the loose subaponeurotic space.
Its skin, superficial fascia and aponeurosis move as one layer.
Frontal bellies of occipito-frontalis can corrugate skin of forehead.
Occipital bellies are supplied by facial nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The large blood vessels of scalp run into
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels of the scalp run in the subcutaneous connective tissue layer (between skin and aponeurosis). This layer has numerous anastomoses and lacks valves, allowing free blood flow. Injury causes profuse bleeding from this highly vascularized layer.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp vessels in subcutaneous connective tissue layer with extensive anastomoses
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior a branch of the retromandibular vein to form external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The posterior auricular vein joins the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) to form the external jugular vein. The facial vein drains into the common facial vein, then internal jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricular vein unites with retromandibular vein to form external jugular
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Loss of sensation from the lower eye lid indicates injury of which nerve?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division V2) provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip via the infraorbital foramen. Injury causes loss of sensation in this distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies lower eyelid sensation
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pulse felt in front of tragus of ear against zygomatic arch is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The pulse palpable in front of the tragus against the zygomatic arch is from the superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of external carotid). This is a common site for checking pulse and temporal artery biopsy.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse palpable anterior to tragus
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which part of the brain controls motor function of the right leg?
questions.explanation: The leg area of the primary motor cortex is located on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, controlling the contralateral lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Motor control of the leg is represented medially in the paracentral lobule of the primary motor cortex.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cartilages of the larynx develop embryologically from which of the following pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) develop from pharyngeal arch 4 (and 6), with the exception of the epiglottis which develops from the ventral pharyngeal wall.
questions.keyConcept: Laryngeal cartilages originate from pharyngeal arches 4 and 6, except epiglottis from ventral pharyngeal wall.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Taste sensation behind the vallecula is carried by:
questions.explanation: Taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue (including behind the vallecula) is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the inferior ganglion and nucleus tractus solitarius.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX carries taste from the posterior third of tongue via the solitary nucleus.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers directly to the lacrimal gland for lacrimation?
questions.explanation: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion directly to the lacrimal gland, along with nasopalatine and orbital branches.
questions.keyConcept: Greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers from pterygopalatine ganglion to lacrimal gland.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fracture of the zygomatic arch is most likely to impair the function of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle is supplied by the masseteric branch of the mandibular nerve (V3), which passes through the mandibular foramen. The zygomatic arch provides attachment for masseter.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter muscle is innervated by V3 masseteric nerve, which passes through mandibular foramen.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which major vein does the common facial vein typically drain into?
questions.explanation: The common facial vein typically drains into the internal jugular vein (IJV) at the angle of the jaw. It is formed by the union of the anterior facial vein and submental vein.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein joins the internal jugular vein near the angle of the mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The angle of the mandible is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The angle of the mandible receives sensory innervation from the auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) and the inferior alveolar nerve (also V3). The buccal nerve also contributes.
questions.keyConcept: V3 branches (auriculotemporal, inferior alveolar) supply sensation to the mandibular angle.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve to the pterygoid canal is formed by the union of which nerves?
questions.explanation: The nerve to the pterygoid canal (Vidian's nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Vidian's nerve joins parasympathetic (greater petrosal) and sympathetic (deep petrosal) fibers to the pterygoid canal.
options: Auriculotemporal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve and lesser petrosal nerve
Deep petrosal nerve and chorda tympani
Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
Auricular branch of vagus and glossopharyngeal nerve
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The postganglionic fibers of the sphenopalatine (pterygopalatine) ganglion are derived from which nerve?
questions.explanation: Postganglionic fibers from the sphenopalatine ganglion travel via the zygomatic nerve and then the zygomaticotemporal nerve to reach the lacrimal gland, bypassing the need for separate parasympathetic innervation.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenopalatine ganglion fibers reach the lacrimal gland via zygomatic branches of V2.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The retromandibular vein divides within the parotid gland into anterior and posterior divisions. Each division then unites with which veins respectively?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein divides into anterior and posterior branches within the parotid gland. The anterior branch joins the facial vein, and the posterior branch joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein bifurcation in parotid gland forms anterior and posterior divisions for venous drainage.
options: Internal jugular vein and subclavian vein
Anterior facial vein and posterior auricular vein
External jugular vein and internal jugular vein
Posterior facial vein and external jugular vein
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which vein joins with the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein?
questions.explanation: The superficial temporal vein joins with the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein in the parotid gland region. The retromandibular vein then divides within the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein forms from union of superficial temporal and maxillary veins in the parotid region.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerves pass through the pterygoid canal?
questions.explanation: The greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus) join to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian's nerve), which passes through the pterygoid canal.
questions.keyConcept: Vidian's nerve carries parasympathetic (CN VII) and sympathetic fibers through the pterygoid canal.
options: Deep petrosal and greater superficial petrosal
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All characters of proprioception pathway of face, head except:
questions.explanation: Facial proprioception uses unipolar neurons (no ganglia) with the mesencephalic nucleus as first order neuron; it is multipolar with proprioceptive ganglia, not sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial proprioception pathway
options: mesencephalic nucleus is first order neuron
main sensory nucleus is second order neuron
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: First order neuron in touch from head face is .............. while second order neuron is ..........
questions.explanation: For facial touch, the first order neuron is in the trigeminal nucleus (mesencephalic for proprioception, principal sensory for touch) and the second order is the main sensory nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial touch neurons
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All characters of spino-olivary tract except:
questions.explanation: The spino-olivary tract ascends to the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to mediate cerebellar climbing fiber input for motor learning, not eye/head reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Spino-olivary tract
options: arise from nerve cell in posterior horn (IV,V)
ascend at all level of spinal on opposite side
drive reflex, movement of eye, head
ascend in inferior olivary nucleus in medulla
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The central nervous system is soft because:
questions.explanation: The CNS lacks connective tissue (except at surfaces), making it soft; this also explains its vulnerability to mechanical injury.
questions.keyConcept: CNS softness cause
options: It consists of neurons joined by connective tissue.
It is rich in blood vessels.
It does not contain connective tissue.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arcuate fibres carry:
questions.explanation: Arcuate fibers (both internal and external) carry proprioceptive impulses from the body to the cerebellum and brainstem nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate fiber function
options: Pain and temperature from the head.
Pain and temperature from the body.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The first order neurons for pain and temperature pathway from face and head are located in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons for pain and temperature from the face have cell bodies in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, with central processes entering the spinal nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial pain first neuron
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: One of the following is correct:
questions.explanation: Olfactory nerve filaments from the nasal mucosa synapse in the olfactory bulb, which then projects via the olfactory tract to cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory pathway
options: The anterior perforated substance lies on the medial side of the optic chiasma.
The olfactory nerve filaments end in the olfactory bulb.
The lateral olfactory root ends in the cuneus.
The infundibulum connects the tuber cinereum with the parotid gland.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 23‑year‑old man is found unconscious after a fall. CT shows a biconvex, lens‑shaped hyperdensity between the skull and the dura. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation: A biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdensity between skull and dura is an epidural hematoma, typically from traumatic middle meningeal artery rupture.
questions.keyConcept: Epidural hematoma
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A newborn boy has an underdeveloped mandible and zygomatic bone, low‑set slanting eyes, and facial asymmetry. Which pharyngeal arch is most likely defective?
questions.explanation: First pharyngeal arch derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and muscles of mastication; defect causes Treacher Collins-like features.
questions.keyConcept: First arch derivatives
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 56‑year‑old man with polycystic kidney disease develops sudden severe headache and nuchal rigidity. CT shows subarachnoid haemorrhage. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, associated with polycystic kidney disease and autosomal dominant inheritance, is the most common cause of spontaneous SAH.
questions.keyConcept: Subarachnoid hemorrhage cause
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A newborn has an underdeveloped mandible, zygomatic bone, and low‑set ears. Which pharyngeal arch is defective?
questions.explanation: First pharyngeal arch defect (Treacher Collins syndrome) causes underdeveloped mandible, zygomatic bones, and low-set ears.
questions.keyConcept: First arch defect
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Operant conditioning is a type of:
questions.explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is associative learning where behavior is modified by its consequences (reward or punishment).
questions.keyConcept: Operant conditioning
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Extent of the scalp:
questions.explanation: The scalp extends from the supraorbital margin anteriorly to the external occipital protuberance posteriorly, and to the superior temporal line laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp extent
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: supraorbital margin; Posteriorly: external occipital protuberance and highest nuchal line; Laterally: superior temporal line.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Compare frontal and occipital belly nerve supply:
questions.explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis is innervated by the temporal branch of facial nerve; the occipital belly is innervated by the posterior auricular branch.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis innervation
questions.modelAnswer: Frontal belly: temporal branch of facial nerve; Occipital belly: posterior auricular branch of facial nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Sensory nerve supply of scalp:
questions.explanation: Anterior to auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal nerves; posterior to auricle: great auricular, lesser/greater occipital, third occipital.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp sensory innervation
questions.modelAnswer: In front of auricle: supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal; Behind auricle: great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital, third occipital.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Boundaries of face:
questions.explanation: The face is bounded superiorly by the hairline, inferiorly by the lower mandibular border, and laterally by the auricles connecting both sides.
questions.keyConcept: Facial boundaries
questions.modelAnswer: Superior: hair line; Inferior: lower border of mandible; Sideways: from one auricle to the other.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Facial artery terminates by anastomosing with:
questions.explanation: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery, completing the arterial supply around the eye and nose.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery termination
questions.modelAnswer: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery), forming rich collateral anastomoses at the angle of the mouth and near the nose. It also anastomoses with the transverse facial artery and the labial arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 2 branches of facial artery in face:
questions.explanation: The two terminal branches of the facial artery within the face are the superior labial artery and inferior labial artery supplying the lips.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery face branches
questions.modelAnswer: Superior labial and Inferior labial.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of ophthalmic nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches in the face include supratrochlear, supraorbital (from frontal nerve), and infratrochlear nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Ophthalmic nerve facial branches
questions.modelAnswer: Supratrochlear, supraorbital, palpebral branch of lacrimal, infratrochlear.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off infraorbital, zygomatic, and greater palatine nerves in the face, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper teeth.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches
questions.modelAnswer: Infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, greater palatine nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 branches of infraorbital nerve:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of V2) gives inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, and anterior superior alveolar branches.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve branches
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, anterior superior alveolar.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of mandibular nerve in face:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) gives mental and auriculotemporal branches on the face; the motor branches (masseteric, temporal, buccal) supply muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve facial branches
questions.modelAnswer: Mental nerve (from inferior alveolar), auriculotemporal nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerves affected by cerebellopontine angle tumor:
questions.explanation: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (typically acoustic neuroma) first affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss and vertigo, then CN VII (facial) causing facial weakness.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumor affects cranial nerves 7 and 8.
questions.modelAnswer: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (commonly vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma) affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) causing hearing loss and tinnitus; CN V (trigeminal nerve) causing facial numbness; and CN VII (facial nerve) causing facial palsy. Brainstem compression may also occur.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 4 structures winding around cerebral peduncle:
questions.explanation: Four structures wind around the cerebral peduncle: optic tract (medial), trochlear nerve (lateral), posterior cerebral artery (superior), and basal vein (dorsal).
questions.keyConcept: Structures around cerebral peduncle: optic tract, trochlear nerve, PCA, basal vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Optic tract, Trochlear nerve, Posterior cerebral artery, Basal vein.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Boundaries of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma, anterolaterally by the optic tract, posterolaterally by the cerebral peduncle, and posteriorly by the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries: optic chiasma, optic tract, cerebral peduncle, upper pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: optic chiasma; Anterolateral: optic tract; Posterolateral: cerebral peduncle; Posterior: upper border of pons.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Attachments of falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri attaches superiorly to the crista galli and frontal crest, posteriorly to the tentorium's upper surface, along its upper border to the sagittal sulcus lips, and its free lower border encloses the inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri attachments: crista galli, tentorium, sagittal sulcus, inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Apex: crista galli and frontal crest; Base: upper surface of tentorium; Upper border: lips of sagittal sulcus; Lower free border: encloses inferior sagittal sinus.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve piercing cribriform plate:
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of special sensory fibers that pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb from the nasal mucosa, making it unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory nerve pierces cribriform plate to reach olfactory bulb.
questions.modelAnswer: The olfactory nerve (CN I) passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The filaments of CN I traverse the foramina in the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb. Fractures here can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve through hypoglossal canal:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, which lies above the foramen magnum, carrying motor fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve passes through hypoglossal canal above foramen magnum.
questions.modelAnswer: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal (anterior condylar canal) of the occipital bone. It exits the skull to supply the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, mediating tongue movements and shape changes for speech and swallowing.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve supply of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: All muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid) are innervated by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3), except the medial pterygoid which receives a branch from the trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Muscles of mastication: all by anterior division of V3 except medial pterygoid (trunk).
questions.modelAnswer: All by anterior division of mandibular nerve except medial pterygoid by trunk.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Actions of muscles of mastication:
questions.explanation: The muscles of mastication produce protrusion (lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, masseter) except temporalis which retracts; elevation is produced by all except lateral pterygoid which depresses; medial and lateral pterygoid together produce side-to-side grinding movements.
questions.keyConcept: Mastication actions: protrusion (except temporalis), elevation (except lateral pterygoid), side-to-side movement.
questions.modelAnswer: All protrude except temporalis retracts; All elevate except lateral pterygoid depresses; Medial & lateral pterygoid produce side‑to‑side movement.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid:
questions.explanation: Structures lateral to the lateral pterygoid include the ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, and pterygoid venous plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral relations of lateral pterygoid: mandible, medial pterygoid, temporalis tendon, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.
questions.modelAnswer: Ramus of mandible, superficial head of medial pterygoid, tendon of temporalis, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 ligaments of TMJ:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments associated with the TMJ are the lateral ligament (thickening of joint capsule), stylomandibular ligament (from styloid to mandible), and sphenomandibular ligament (from spine to lingula).
questions.keyConcept: TMJ ligaments: lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral, stylomandibular, sphenomandibular.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of posterior division of mandibular nerve:
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the mandibular nerve gives three branches: auriculotemporal (sensory to temple and ear), lingual (sensory to anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar (sensory to lower teeth and chin).
questions.keyConcept: Posterior V3 branches: auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 4 branches of maxillary nerve:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off a meningeal branch, two ganglionic branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion, the zygomatic nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve branches: meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, two ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of 3rd part of maxillary artery:
questions.explanation: The third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery gives posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater and lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal branches, and the artery of the pterygoid canal.
questions.keyConcept: Third maxillary artery: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, pterygoid canal.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater & lesser palatine, sphenopalatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Drainage of pterygoid plexus:
questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus drains into the maxillary vein, which then joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein, ultimately connecting to the external jugular system.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus drains to maxillary vein.
questions.modelAnswer: The pterygoid plexus drains into the retromandibular vein via the maxillary vein, which joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. It also communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein and drains into the cavernous sinus via emissary veins.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) coordinates movements between which structures?
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects the vestibular nuclei to the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, coordinating eye movements with head movements in the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.keyConcept: MLF coordinates eyes and head via vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The chief retractor of the mandible is the:
questions.explanation: Posterior temporalis fibers retract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis is the chief retractor of mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient shows ipsilateral tongue atrophy, contralateral loss of vibration, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature of the body. The lesion is in the:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII, medial lemniscus, pyramid).
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion with ipsilateral atrophy: hypoglossal nerve lesion.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The occipitofrontalis muscle accounts for the ……… layer of the scalp.
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle forms the third (musculoaponeurotic) layer of the scalp, connecting the galea aponeurotica to the orbital margins.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis: third layer of scalp.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Skin over occipital bone up to the vertex is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The posterior primary rami (dorsal rami) of C2 and C3 supply the skin over the occipital bone up to the vertex, including the greater and lesser occipital nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital area: supplied by dorsal rami of C2 and C3.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of ……… veins.
questions.explanation: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior facial vein: formed by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication and mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter: first pharyngeal arch derivative.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches behind the lacrimal sac (posterior to it), not in front, to compress and dilate the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi lacrimal part: attached behind lacrimal sac.
options: Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its lacrimal part is attached in front of the lacrimal sac.
It develops from the second pharyngeal arch.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from the lower eyelid is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) carries pain sensation from the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, exiting through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid pain: infraorbital nerve (V2).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Ethmoidal arteries supply the cranial dura via ……… arteries.
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) give off anterior meningeal arteries that supply the cranial dura in the anterior fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Ethmoidal arteries supply dura via anterior meningeal branches.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The retropharyngeal space lies:
questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering pharynx/esophagus) anteriorly and prevertebral fascia posteriorly, extending from skull base to T1.
questions.keyConcept: Retropharyngeal space: between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following lies superficial to temporalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve lies superficial to the temporalis fascia as it ascends toward the temple, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve: superficial to temporalis fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle acting as a powerful retractor of the mandible is:
questions.explanation: The temporalis muscle is a powerful retractor of the mandible, pulling the mandibular condyle backward to close the mouth after opening.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis: powerful retractor of mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The trunk of the mandibular nerve supplies ……… muscle(s).
questions.explanation: The trunk of the mandibular nerve gives off medial pterygoid nerve (supplying medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palati) before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.keyConcept: V3 trunk supplies: medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, tensor palati.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Bad extraction of lower 3rd molar tooth may cause loss of sensations from:
questions.explanation: Bad extraction of lower third molar can damage the inferior alveolar nerve (running in the mandibular canal), causing anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 3rd molar extraction: possible lingual nerve damage (anterior 2/3 tongue).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: To operate on the lower teeth, the ……… nerve is anaesthetized.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) is anesthetized for lower teeth operations, injected near the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the ramus.
questions.keyConcept: Lower teeth surgery: inferior alveolar nerve anesthetized.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A branch from the 3rd part of maxillary artery is:
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar artery is a branch of the third part of maxillary artery that supplies the upper molars and sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior superior alveolar artery: branch of maxillary artery part 3.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A nerve passing between the 2 heads of lateral pterygoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory fibers to the cheek.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve passes between two heads of lateral pterygoid.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The skin of the prominence of cheek is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin over the cheek prominence (zygomatic area), a branch of V2 via the zygomatic nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cheek prominence: zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve of pterygoid canal is formed by union of ……… nerves.
questions.explanation: The nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidians nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal: greater petrosal + deep petrosal nerves.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Deviation of the uvula to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The uvula deviates AWAY from the lesioned side due to weakness of the palatine muscles on the affected side. Deviation to the right indicates left vagus (CN X) injury.
questions.keyConcept: Uvula deviates AWAY from lesioned side (CN X motor).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The jugular foramen transmits all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, and the inferior petrosal sinus. The hypoglossal nerve passes through its own canal (hypoglossal canal) separately.
questions.keyConcept: Jugular foramen: CN 9,10,11, inferior petrosal sinus (not hypoglossal).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Difficulty in protruding the tongue with its deviation to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Tongue deviation toward the right side during protrusion indicates right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, as the unaffected genioglossus pulls the tongue toward the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviates TOWARD lesioned hypoglossal nerve side.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII carrying parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands).
questions.keyConcept: Submandibular ganglion parasympathetic root: chorda tympani (CN VII).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The ……… nerve suspends the pterygopalatine ganglion in its place.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended by the maxillary nerve (V2) which provides its sensory roots passing through without synapsing.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve suspends pterygopalatine ganglion.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The common carotid artery divides at the level of ……… vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 vertebral level).
questions.keyConcept: Common carotid bifurcates at upper border of thyroid cartilage (C4).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following drain into the internal jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein; other veins like inferior thyroid, middle thyroid, and vertebral vein also drain into the IJV.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains INTO internal jugular (so it doesn't drain external jugular).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: An abscess in the center of lower lip may cause enlargement of ……… lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: An abscess in the lower lip drains to the submandibular lymph nodes due to lymphatic drainage patterns of the anterior face.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip abscess: submandibular lymph nodes enlarge.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The lower lip is derived from:
questions.explanation: The lower lip is derived from the mandibular prominence (frontonasal process gives upper lip philtrum and maxilla), with lateral portions from the maxillary prominence.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip: derived from mandibular prominence.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from ……… prominence.
questions.explanation: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from the maxillary prominence (second pharyngeal arch), which also forms the upper lip lateral portions and secondary palate.
questions.keyConcept: Upper cheek: maxillary prominence.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Excessive fusion between maxillary and mandibular prominences causes:
questions.explanation: Fusion of maxillary and mandibular prominences in utero causes microstomia (small mouth) or aglossia (absent tongue) if severe.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary-mandibular fusion: microstomia or aglossia.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Abnormal early closure of coronal suture leads to:
questions.explanation: Early closure of the coronal suture causes brachycephaly (shortened anteroposterior skull diameter) due to compensatory growth in other directions.
questions.keyConcept: Coronal suture early closure: brachycephaly.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In facial nerve lesion (Bell's palsy), all the following could be manifested EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. It causes inability to close the eyelids and facial muscle weakness. Hearing is generally unaffected; in fact, sounds may seem louder (hyperacusis) due to stapedial nerve involvement.
questions.keyConcept: Bell's palsy does NOT cause weaker hearing; hyperacusis may occur due to stapedial nerve involvement
options: Falling of food out of mouth.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cranial nerve that has the most medial attachment to the pons:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) has the most medial attachment to the pons, emerging in the median line at the pontomedullary junction. The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach more laterally.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial pontine attachment
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cranial nerve nucleus that supplies muscles of the larynx is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius is the visceral afferent column (receiving taste and visceral sensation), not the GVE column. GVE nuclei include Edinger-Westphal (III), superior/inferior salivary nuclei (VII/IX), and dorsal motor nucleus of X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius is visceral afferent, not efferent
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following are nuclei of facial nerve EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord: anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The pharyngeal arch supplied by the only pontine cranial nerve that is NOT attached to the lower border of pons is:
questions.explanation: The medial zone of medulla containing the pyramid is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure. This zone includes the pyramid and medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies medial medulla
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Sensory innervation to the dura above the tentorium cerebelli is from which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery, which passes through the foramen spinosum and grooves the inner table of the skull at the pterion. This creates a lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes extradural hemorrhage
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from the palatine tonsil is carried on the following cranial nerve:
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil receives its general sensory innervation (pain, touch, temperature) from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), specifically through its tonsillar branch that innervates the mucosa over the tonsil. This explains why tonsillar pain may be referred to the ear via the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Pain from palatine tonsil is carried by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries special visceral afferent (taste) fibers from the posterior one-third of the tongue to the nucleus solitarius. It does NOT supply all pharyngeal muscles (only stylopharyngeus); the constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. It also does NOT pass superficial to hyoglossus (it passes between the superior and middle constrictors to reach the pharynx). Therefore, only statement B is correct.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX carries taste from posterior one-third of tongue; does NOT supply all pharyngeal muscles.
options: Carries taste sensation from posterior 1/3 of tongue.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the mucous membrane of the oropharynx, including the palatine tonsils and posterior one-third of the tongue. The nasopharynx is supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2) via the sphenopalatine ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal supplies oropharynx, not nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, or larynx.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It carries C1 spinal nerve fibers that branch off to supply the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. CN XII does NOT lie within the carotid sheath (it crosses superficially over it), is NOT joined by C2, is purely motor (NOT sensory), and emerges between the pyramid and the olive (not between the olive and ICP).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve carries C1 fibers and supplies thyrohyoid and geniohyoid; joined by branch from C1 not C2.
options: Emerges from medulla between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Leaves the skull through jugular foramen.
Lies within the upper part of carotid sheath.
Is joined by a branch from C2.
It sensory to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards branches of glossopharyngeal nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve has several branches: the tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) contributes to the lesser petrosal nerve for parotid secretion; the tonsillar and lingual branches carry sensation from the tonsil and posterior one-third of the tongue (including taste); the pharyngeal branch carries sensory and motor fibers to the pharyngeal plexus; and the muscular branch supplies the stylopharyngeus. However, taste from the anterior TWO-THIRDS of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (CN VII), not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior two-thirds tongue taste is CN VII (chorda tympani), NOT glossopharyngeal.
options: Its tympanic branch shares in providing nerve supply to parotid gland.
Its pharyngeal branch carries sensory fibers.
It gives a muscular branch to stylopharyngeus.
Its tonsillar branch supplies soft palate.
Its lingual branch carries special sensation from anterior 2/3 of tongue
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of hypoglossal nerve.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle, descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, and curves forward above the hyoid bone to reach the tongue. Its branches include: (1) meningeal branch to the dura of posterior cranial fossa; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers) contributing to the ansa cervicalis; (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1 fibers); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1 fibers); and (5) lingual branches to the muscles of the tongue (hyoglossus, genioglossus, styloglossus, and intrinsic tongue muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal branches: meningeal, C1 to ansa cervicalis, C1 to thyrohyoid/geniohyoid, lingual branches to tongue muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of hypoglossal nerve: (1) meningeal branch to posterior cranial fossa dura; (2) descending hypoglossi (C1 fibers to ansa cervicalis); (3) nerve to thyrohyoid (C1); (4) nerve to geniohyoid (C1); (5) lingual branches to all extrinsic and intrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, superior/inferior longitudinal, transverse, vertical).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The branchial arch supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle (the only muscle derived from the 3rd arch) and provides sensory innervation to the pharynx, middle ear, and posterior third of the tongue. CN V3 is 1st arch; CN VII is 2nd; CN X superior laryngeal is 4th.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the 3rd pharyngeal arch.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The pharyngeal arch supplied by the only pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to the lower border of the pons is the:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is the only cranial nerve attached to the lower border of the pons (all others attach at the upper border). It supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye, derived from the 6th pharyngeal arch. The 1st arch nerve is CN V (trigeminal), which attaches to the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: CN VI (abducent) is the only cranial nerve attached to the LOWER border of the pons; innervates lateral rectus (6th arch).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The only cranial nerve that decussate before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the ONLY cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) before emerging from the brainstem. It decussates in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves emerge without crossing.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV (trochlear): only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence; crosses in superior medullary velum.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy
