questions.text: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract provides only contralateral innervation to which of the following cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract provides bilateral innervation to muscles of the head and face, EXCEPT for the lower facial muscles (chin, lips) which receive only contralateral input. This bilateral pattern preserves function if one hemisphere is damaged.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar fibers to lower face are uniquely contralateral; all other cranial nerve motor nuclei receive bilateral input.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cranial nerves on ventral pons:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves associated with the ventral pons include CN V (trigeminal), CN VI (abducent), CN VII (facial), and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear), emerging at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine cranial nerves: 5, 6, 7, 8.
questions.modelAnswer: Trigeminal (5), Abducent (6), Facial (7), Vestibulocochlear (8).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Branches of glossopharyngeal nerve:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives six branches: tympanic (to middle ear), carotid (to carotid body/sinus), pharyngeal (to pharynx), muscular (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, and lingual branches.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.
questions.modelAnswer: Tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar, lingual.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure motor cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a pure motor nerve carrying general somatic efferent fibers to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, with no sensory component.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is pure motor to tongue muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Facial nerve DOESN'T give parasympathetic supply to ……… gland.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve provides parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal gland via the greater petrosal nerve and to submandibular and sublingual glands via chorda tympani; the parotid gland receives parasympathetic from CN IX.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve doesn't parasympathetically supply parotid gland (CN IX does).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The hypoglossal nerve pierces ……… muscle at the end of its course.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) pierces the genioglossus muscle near its insertion before distributing to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve pierces genioglossus muscle.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nerve attached to the lower border of pons above pyramid is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) is attached to the lower border of the pons, in the groove between the pons and pyramid of the medulla. It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve at lower pons above pyramid
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nerves lies close to the median plane in the transverse furrow between pons and medulla?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction, close to the median plane (between the pons and pyramid). It is the most medial of the cranial nerves at this junction.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve most medial at pontomedullary junction
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards pons, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo
options: Cerebello-pontine angle gives attachment to VI & VII cranial nerves.
Nervus intermedius is the medial root of the facial nerve.
VIII cranial nerve lies medial to VII cranial nerve.
Its ventral surface shows a sulcus for vertebral artery.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards back of pons, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial
options: Its apex is continuous with cerebral acqueduct.
Locus ceruleus lies at upper end of sulcus limitans.
Sulcus limitans lies lateral to medial eminence.
Vestibular area lies lateral to superior fovea.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Proprioceptive sensation from the big toe ascends to the brainstem through which fibers?
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower limb ascends via the gracile fasciculus in the posterior columns to the gracile nucleus in the medulla, then decussates as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile fasciculus carries lower limb proprioception to the medulla before decussation.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which artery and its branches are primarily responsible for supplying the pons?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery and its branches (paramedian and circumferential pontine arteries) supply the pons. The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the anteroinferior pons, while superior cerebellar artery supplies the upper pons.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar artery supplies pons through paramedian and circumferential branches.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome causes:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral face, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, Horner syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral loss of pain/temp from face, contralateral loss from body, ipsilateral paralysis of palate/pharynx/larynx, loss of taste, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for the sensory innervation of the lower eyelid?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of V2) provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, entering through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid sensory innervation: infraorbital nerve (V2).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery is responsible for the supply of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the motor and sensory areas for the contralateral lower limb due to its course along the medial cerebral hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: supplies contralateral lower limb motor/sensory areas.
options: Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral upper limb.
Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral lower limb.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Thrombosis of posterior inferior cerebellar artery affects:
questions.explanation: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, nystagmus), cerebellar ataxia, facial pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
questions.keyConcept: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Neocerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum, the largest and most recent functional region, is formed by the lateral parts of the cerebellar hemispheres and is responsible for planning and executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellum = lateral cerebellar hemisphere for skilled movements.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral parts of cerebellar hemisphere.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 4 cerebellar nuclei:
questions.explanation: The four deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial are: dentate (largest), emboliform, globose, and fastigial, each projecting to different thalamic and brainstem targets.
questions.keyConcept: Four cerebellar nuclei: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial.
questions.modelAnswer: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere is concerned with which of the following functions:
questions.explanation: The non-dominant hemisphere (usually right) is primarily responsible for control of behavior, emotional expression, and visuospatial functions. The dominant hemisphere handles speech and language.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant frontal lobe controls behavior/emotions
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the site of Broca’s area?
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It is the motor speech center, responsible for speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area: inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis + opercularis), dominant hemisphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). This is the motor speech area responsible for expressive language production.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the site of supplementary motor area?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (MII, area 6 on the medial surface) is located in the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the paracentral lobule. It is involved in speech planning and initiation.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area: medial frontal gyrus, medial surface of frontal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial frontal gyrus (medial surface of frontal lobe), anterior to the paracentral lobule. Also called MII or SMA, involved in planning and initiating complex movements including speech.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Where is the supplementary motor area located?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located in the medial surface of frontal lobe, anterior to the primary motor cortex (area 4), in Brodmann area 6.
questions.keyConcept: SMA is medial frontal cortex involved in motor planning, located anterior to primary motor cortex.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The area of reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movement lies in ……… lobe of the cerebral hemisphere.
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe contains the area for reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movements - the visual fixation center in the frontal eye field projects to superior colliculus for reflexive gaze.
questions.keyConcept: Reflex conjugate eye movement area: occipital lobe.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The corticospinal fibers are broken into bundles in:
questions.explanation: In the pons, the corticospinal fibers are broken into bundles by the transverse pontocerebellar fibers, creating the scattered appearance of the basis pontis.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal fibers scattered in basis pontis
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Internal carotid artery supplies:
questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal and supplies the forehead via the supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic artery. It does not supply the chin, cheek, or temple.
questions.keyConcept: Internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via ophthalmic branches
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion of the anterior cerebral artery would most likely result in paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including the motor cortex representing the lower limb (paracentral lobule). Occlusion causes contralateral paralysis primarily affecting the leg and foot. The MCA supplies the lateral hemisphere (face, arm); the PCA supplies the occipital and inferior temporal regions.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery supplies medial hemisphere; occlusion causes contralateral LEG paralysis (paracentral lobule).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the origin of posterior spinal artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal arteries may arise directly from the vertebral artery or from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). They descend as two channels on the posterior surface of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery: arises from vertebral artery or PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Either directly from the vertebral artery or as a branch of PICA.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the beginning and termination of vertebral artery.
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery begins as a branch of the first (proximal) part of the subclavian artery and terminates at the lower border of the pons by joining the contralateral vertebral artery to form the basilar artery.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebral artery origin and termination
questions.modelAnswer:
Begins as a branch of first part of subclavian artery
Ends at lower border of pons by joining the other vertebral artery to form basilary artery
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the beginning and termination of basilar artery.
questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed at the lower border of the pons by the union of the two vertebral arteries and terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar artery formation and termination
questions.modelAnswer:
It’s formed by union of right and left vertebral arteries at lower border of pons
Ends at upper border of pons by giving its two terminal branches “right and left posterior cerebral arteries”
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by anterior cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere (except occipital lobe), a one-inch strip of the superior lateral surface, and the medial part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery cortical territories
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial surface: All except occipital lobe
Lateral surface: One inch strip superiorly
Inferior surface: Medial part of orbital surface
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by middle cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral cerebral surface (excluding occipital pole and superior/inferior border strips), the lateral orbital surface, and the temporal pole.
questions.keyConcept: Middle cerebral artery cortical territories
questions.modelAnswer:
Lateral surface: large area except occipital lobe+ a strip along superior border+ a strip along inferior border
Inferior surface: lateral part of orbital surface+ temporal pole
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by posterior cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial and lateral occipital surfaces, the inferior temporal surface (except temporal pole), and contributes to the visual cortex via calcarine artery.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior cerebral artery cortical territories
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial surface: occipital lobe
Lateral surface: occipital lobe+ strip along lower border of hemisphere
Inferior surface: tentorial part except temporal pole
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In the dominant hemisphere cortical branches of middle cerebral artery supply the following areas Except.
questions.explanation: MCA supplies auditory area, Broca's area, and frontal eye field; the whole primary motor area (for face and hand) is supplied by MCA, not an exception; the leg area is ACA.
questions.keyConcept: MCA cortical supply areas
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cortical branches of middle cerebral artery supply:
questions.explanation: MCA cortical branches supply lateral part of orbital surface, lateral surface (most except occipital), and temporal pole; occipital lobe and paracentral lobule are supplied by PCA and ACA respectively.
questions.keyConcept: MCA cortical supply
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery supplies all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cerebral surface, orbital inferior surface, and genu of internal capsule, but the anterior limb is supplied by the middle cerebral artery via perforating branches.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery supplies medial surface and genu, not anterior limb of internal capsule.
options: Most of medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere.
Medial aspect of orbital part of inferior surface of the hemisphere.
All anterior limb of internal capsule.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The part of the internal carotid artery which DOESN'T give branches is:
questions.explanation: The cervical part of the internal carotid artery (from carotid bifurcation to skull base) does not give branches; branches arise from the petrous, cavernous, and cerebral portions.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical internal carotid: no branches.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Subperiosteal hematoma:
questions.explanation: Subperiosteal hematoma is localized and takes the shape of the underlying bone because the periosteum is firmly attached to the skull sutures, limiting spread.
questions.keyConcept: Subperiosteal hematoma takes the shape of the underlying bone due to periosteal attachment at sutures
options: Takes the shape of the bone.
Lies in loose areolar tissue layer.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Extradural hematoma occurs due to the rupture of the vessel that passes through:
questions.explanation: Extradural hematoma is caused by rupture of the middle meningeal artery, typically from trauma to the pterion. The artery passes through the foramen spinosum and grooves the greater wing of sphenoid, making it vulnerable to injury.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery through foramen spinosum causes extradural hematoma
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 2-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty sucking. His mother reports that he has been having trouble breastfeeding for the past few weeks. She also notices that he has difficulty closing his lips completely. Which of the following muscles is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oris is the muscle of the lips that allows pursing, tightening, and closure of the mouth (essential for breastfeeding and sucking). Weakness causes inability to close lips completely (milk dribbles out). The buccinator keeps food between teeth during chewing; the frontalis and occipitalis are muscles of facial expression in the scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris surrounds the mouth and is essential for lip closure and sucking; weakness causes dribbling of milk.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Extradural hemorrhage is caused by rupture of:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage caused by rupture of middle meningeal artery (usually from temporal bone fracture).选项C正确. The answer is C. This is a surgical emergency - lucid interval then rapid deterioration.
questions.keyConcept: Extradural hematoma: middle meningeal artery rupture - 'talk and die' syndrome, biconvex shape on CT.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which antiepileptic drug is associated with the highest risk of neonatal cleft lip and cleft palate?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome causing cleft lip/palate, digital hypoplasia, and growth retardation.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin teratogenicity
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Hemorrhage reaching the ……… layer of the scalp can cause black eye.
questions.explanation: Blood in the loose areolar tissue layer (subaponeurotic space) of the scalp can track around the orbit producing 'black eye' (periorbital ecchymosis).
questions.keyConcept: Black eye: hemorrhage in loose connective tissue layer of scalp.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate structures in basis pontis.
questions.explanation: Structures in the basis pontis include: (1) LONGITUDINAL FIBERS - corticopontine, corticospinal, corticobulbar fibers descending through the pons; (2) TRANSVERSE FIBERS - pontocerebellar fibers linking the pons with the cerebellum (these are interrupted by longitudinal fibers); (3) PONTINE NUCLEI - gray matter between fiber bundles receiving cortical input; (4) BASILAR ARTERY runs in the basilar sulcus. The basis pontis is separated from tegmentum by the trapezoid body.
questions.keyConcept: Basis pontis: longitudinal fibers (corticospinal), transverse fibers (pontocerebellar), pontine nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: LONGITUDINAL FIBERS: corticopontine, corticospinal, corticobulbar descending through pons. TRANSVERSE FIBERS: pontocerebellar linking pons with cerebellum. PONTINE NUCLEI: gray matter between fiber bundles receiving cortical input. BASILAR ARTERY runs in basilar sulcus. Basis pontis is separated from tegmentum by trapezoid body.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does lesion of Area 4 cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of Area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes contralateral hemiplegia, most affecting fine skilled movements of the distal limbs. The face and hand representations are most affected due to their large cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Area 4 lesion: contralateral hemiplegia, especially fine movements (face, hand). UMN signs below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia especially affecting fine skilled movements. The paralysis is most pronounced in the distal parts of the contralateral limbs (especially hand and foot), with spasticity and hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron signs).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the efferent fibers of the ICP.
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries efferent fibers: cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebelloreticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebelloolivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These complete feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: ICP efferents: cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebelloolivary fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebello reticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebello olivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These form feedback pathways from cerebellum to brainstem.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the afferent fiber of the MCP.
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) carries only afferent fibers - the corticopontocerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, pass through the basilar pons, and enter the cerebellum as the MCP. There are no efferent fibers in the MCP.
questions.keyConcept: MCP: afferent only. Corticopontocerebellar fibers from cerebral cortex through pons to cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Cortico ponto cerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, synapse in the pontine nuclei, cross to the contralateral side, and enter the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle is supplied only by contralateral corticobulbar fibers?
questions.explanation: The lower face (chin, lips below the mouth) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Upper face muscles (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receive bilateral innervation.
questions.keyConcept: Lower facial muscles are innervated only by the contralateral motor cortex, unlike upper face muscles.
options: Muscles of the upper part of the face
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which facial muscle receives only contralateral cortical innervation?
questions.explanation: The mentalis muscle (chin) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Other lower facial muscles receive partial bilateral innervation, which is why upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral only innervation of lower face muscles distinguishes UMN from LMN facial palsy.
options: Orbicularis oculi of the upper face
Orbicularis oris of the lower face
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following direct tract except:
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal and rubrospinal tracts are indirect (multineuronal) tracts, while olivespinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, and sulcomarginal are direct.
questions.keyConcept: Direct vs indirect tracts
options: ventral reticulo-spinal tract and sulco-marginal tract
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Afferent fiber of MCP:
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries corticopontocerebellar fibers, the largest afferent pathway to the cerebellum, originating from the pontine nuclei receiving cerebral cortex input.
questions.keyConcept: MCP afferent is corticopontocerebellar pathway from pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Corticopontocerebellar fibers.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 external features of ventral medulla:
questions.explanation: The ventral medulla's three external features are the pyramid (motor decussation), olive (olivary nucleus), and inferior cerebellar peduncle containing ascending sensory fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral medulla features: pyramid, olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: PYRAMID — longitudinal ridge containing corticospinal fibers; OLIVE — prominences formed by inferior olivary nuclei; INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE — on posterolateral surface containing ascending sensory fibers.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient has weakness of the right lower face, but can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Preserved forehead wrinkling indicates intact upper motor neuron (UMN) innervation to the facial nucleus's upper face region; weakness of only the lower face indicates a UMN lesion affecting the contralateral corticobulbar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Lower face weakness with spared forehead: contralateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesion.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Rootlets of glossopharyngeal nerve lie:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons and medulla.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of facial nerve at stylomastoid foramen leads to:
questions.explanation: A lesion at stylomastoid foramen causes lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting all muscles on that side, including the forehead (loss of frontalis and orbicularis oculi).
questions.keyConcept: Stylomastoid lesion: LMN facial paralysis (entire ipsilateral face).
options: Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Motor loss on the contralateral half of the face.
Motor loss on the ipsilateral half of face.
Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral half of soft palate.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present DORSAL to the cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), not ventral. It consists of pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia circuit. Its dopamine content gives it its dark color.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra: dorsal to crus cerebri, contains dopamine, connected to basal ganglia.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention 3 external feature of the ventral surface of the pons.
questions.explanation: The ventral surface of the pons shows: the basilar groove (lodging the basilar artery), the middle cerebellar peduncle (lateral), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. The pons has two parts: basilar (anterior) and tegmental (posterior).
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar groove (basilar artery), MCP laterally, transverse pontine fiber bundles.
questions.modelAnswer: Middle cerebellar peduncle (on each side), basilar artery sulcus (central groove), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. These features reflect the pontine structure with its basilar and tegmental portions.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon reflex
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 external features of ventral pons:
questions.explanation: The ventral pons displays three characteristic features: the middle cerebellar peduncle laterally, the basilar artery groove centrally, and transverse grooves indicating underlying fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons features: middle cerebellar peduncle, basilar groove, transverse fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: MCP, Basilar artery sulcus, transverse grooves.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the blood supply of basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus) are supplied by central branches of the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. The lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) are the primary supply.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: supplied by lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) and anterior cerebral artery branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, particularly the lenticulostriate arteries which penetrate the basal ganglia through the anterior perforated substance.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which structure is part of the neostriatum?
questions.explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen (also called the striatum). It receives cortical input and dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum comprises caudate and putamen, the major input structures of the basal ganglia.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the pyramidal tract, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The corticospinal fibers descend as scattered bundles in the basis pontis because they are interrupted by transverse pontine fibers. This is a normal anatomical feature of the pontine base.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal scattered in pons by pontine fibers
options: It arises from motor area 4 only.
It passes through anterior limb of internal capsule.
It descends within the medial 3/5 of basis pedunculi.
It descends as scattered bundles in basis pontis.
Its crossed fibers in medulla form anterior corticospinal tract.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe termination of pyramidal tract.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract terminates on anterior horn cells: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed, small) terminates similarly but only in upper cervical segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tract terminates on anterior horn motor neurons; corticobulbar terminates on brainstem motor nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: Termination of pyramidal tract: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed) terminates similarly but only in upper segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the lamination of pyramidal tract in the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract fibers are organized with fibers for facial muscles in the genu (knee), upper limb fibers most anterior in the posterior limb, and lower limb fibers most posterior in the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule pyramidal tract: genu = face, anterior posterior limb = upper limb, posterior posterior limb = lower limb.
questions.modelAnswer: Fibers for face muscles are in the genu; upper limb area lies most anterior and lower limb area lies most posterior in the posterior limb of internal capsule. This anterior-to-posterior arrangement in the posterior limb represents head-to-toe body map.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which descending motor pathway serves as an alternate route to the corticospinal tract?
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus, decussates immediately, and descends in the lateral funiculus. It serves as an accessory pathway for corticospinal function, particularly for flexor muscle control.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract is a crossed extrapyramidal pathway for motor control of distal limbs.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lamination of pyramidal tract in internal capsule:
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract is arranged: anterior limb (frontal connections), genu (face), posterior limb (arm, leg) from front to back.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal internal capsule
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior limb: frontal connections. Genu: face muscles. Posterior limb: arm representation anteriorly, leg representation posteriorly (somatotopic organization: head to toe from front to back).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which tract is the main alternative (indirect) pathway to the corticospinal tract for motor control?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus/rubrospinal tract is the principal alternative motor pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: main indirect pathway from cerebellum via red nucleus to spinal cord.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For each term in the left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: A ganglion is a collection of cell bodies outside the CNS. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A nucleus is a collection of cell bodies within the CNS. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibers outside the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion = peripheral cell bodies; nucleus = central cell bodies; tract/lemniscus = CNS fiber bundles

pairs.target: A collection of cell bodies outside CNS
A bundle of nerve fibers within CNS
A collection of cell bodies within CNS
A collection of ascending fibers within brain stem
A bundle of nerve fibers outside CNS

questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A pathway is a chain of successive tracts with the same function. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. Afferent means input toward a structure. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies outside the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle; pathway = chain of tracts; lemniscus = ascending brainstem fibers
options: Ganglion – a group of cell bodies within CNS.
Pathway – a chain of successive tracts having different functions.
Lemniscus – a collection of descending fibers within the brain stem.
Afferent – an output going away from a certain structure.
Tract – a bundle of nerve fibers within CNS.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Pain from upper lip is carried by:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve, a terminal branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), exits through the infraorbital foramen to supply skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the upper lip
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 45-years-old woman is suffering from numbness over the tip of her nose. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation: The tip of the nose is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (ophthalmic division, V1). Therefore, numbness suggests damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Tip of the nose sensation = ophthalmic division (V1) via external nasal branch
options: Anterior division of the mandibular nerve
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the scalp is the:
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, supplies the scalp in the temporal region and the skin over the anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp via the temporal region
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe branches of Ophthalmic nerve that share in nerve supply of face.
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches into the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve and anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches: lacrimal, frontal (supraorbital/supratrochlear), nasociliary
questions.modelAnswer: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) gives rise to the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve, anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves, and the long ciliary nerves.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The second order neuron in the pathway of pain from the face is:
questions.explanation: Pain from the face travels via the trigeminal nerve. The first order neuron cell bodies are in the trigeminal ganglion, second order neurons are in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of CN V carries face pain 2nd neuron
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The corticonuclear tract has unilateral connections with:
questions.explanation: The corticonuclear tract has bilateral connections with most cranial nerve nuclei, except the lower facial nucleus (which is only contralateral) and the trochlear/trigeminal motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 7 facial nucleus has unilateral corticonuclear input
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the motor Decussation, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Motor decussation (pyramidal decussation) occurs in the caudal part of the medulla, where about 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Motor decussation in caudal medulla
options: It occurs in caudal part of medulla.
It is formed by internal arcuate fibers.
It shows the crossing of 20% of the fibers.
All of the above is true.
None of the above is true.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards corticobulbar tract, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract ends on bilateral cranial nerve nuclei, not only contralateral. Some nuclei (like the lower facial) have predominantly contralateral input, but all have some bilateral contribution.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has bilateral cranial nerve connections
options: It ends on contralateral cranial nerve nuclei only.
The part of facial nucleus that controls right half of orbicularis oris muscle receives left corticonuclear tract.
The left genioglossus muscle is controlled by right corticonuclear tract.
It forms a part of upper motor neuron.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A nerve attached to the cerebello-pontine angle:
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is attached at the cerebellopontine angle, along with the facial nerve. This is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and olive where these nerves emerge.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following olivary nuclear complex is not contained in medulla?
questions.explanation: The medial accessory olive is part of the olivary nuclear complex within the medulla. The superior olivary nucleus is in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus not in medulla
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For each nucleus in left column, choose its appropriate description in right column:
questions.explanation: The muscles NOT supplied by nucleus ambiguus include the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, which are branchiomotor muscles of the trigeminal nerve (motor V).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus does not supply tensor muscles

pairs.target: e. Its fibers end in VPMN of thalamus.
d. A convoluted mass of gray matter.
a. Carries unconscious proprioception from upper limbs & neck
b. Affect level of arousal & consciousness.
c. It gives anterior external arcuate fibers.

questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards auditory pathway, for each description in left column, choose its appropriate part from right column:
questions.explanation: This matching tests cranial nerve nuclei: hypoglossal nucleus ( GSE) - tongue muscles; nucleus ambiguus (SVE) - pharynx/larynx; dorsal motor nucleus of X (GVE) - thoracic/abdominal viscera.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles

pairs.premise: 57) Some of its fibers end in inferior colliculus.
60) Originates from bipolar nerve cells in spiral ganglion.

questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the medial longitudinal bundle, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus runs in the brainstem and receives input from the vestibular nuclei, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the superior colliculus. It coordinates head and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei
options: It extends from thalamus to spinal cord.
In spinal cord, it is formed of ascending & descending tracts.
Its ascending fibers project to motor nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV & V.
Its descending fibers include tectospinal fibers.
Its ascending fibers are connected with interstitial nucleus of Cajal.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column?
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius is the visceral afferent column. It receives taste (SVA) from anterior 2/3 tongue via chorda tympani (CN VII) and posterior 1/3 tongue via CN IX, and general visceral afferent (GVA) from thoracic and abdominal viscera via CN X.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor muscles supplied by CN V, not nucleus ambiguus
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Special visceral afferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: Special visceral afferent nuclei include the nucleus solitarius, which receives taste sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue (via chorda tympani, CN VII) and posterior 1/3 (via CN IX).
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) column includes:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the only pontine cranial nerve attached at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle, supplying the second pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) muscles.
questions.keyConcept: CN V attached at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Nucleus ambiguuus supplies all the following muscles EXCPT:
questions.explanation: Nucleus ambiguus supplies: pharyngeal constrictors, tensor palati, levator palati, laryngeal muscles. STYLO PHARYNGEUS is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not nucleus ambiguus - hence the correct exception.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V is 1st neuron for mastication proprioception
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For each nucleus in left column, choose the appropriate structure supplied by it in right column:
questions.explanation: Different cranial nerve nuclei supply specific structures. The facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression. Nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles. Dorsal motor nucleus of X supplies thoracic/abdominal viscera. Hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei have specific structural targets
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of glossopharyngeal N. & structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: Nuclei of the glossopharyngeal nerve: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to stylopharyngeus muscle (elevates pharynx); (2) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from posterior one-third of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensation from middle ear, pharynx, and posterior tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (stylopharyngeus), inferior salivary (parotid), nucleus solitarius (taste), spinal V (sensation)
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL NERVE: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) — motor to stylopharyngeus muscle (elevates pharynx); (2) INFERIOR SALIVATORY NUCLEUS (GVE) — parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) — taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) — general sensation from middle ear, pharynx, posterior tongue.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of GSA column & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: GSA COLUMN NUCLEI: (1) TRIGEMINAL NUCLEI (principal and spinal) in pons/medulla → general sensation from face, scalp, teeth, meninges; (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI (dorsal and ventral) at pontomedullary junction → hearing; (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI (superior, medial, lateral, inferior) → balance and spatial orientation.
questions.keyConcept: CN V1 innervates dura above tentorium
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GSA COLUMN: (1) TRIGEMINAL NUCLEI (principal and spinal) in pons/medulla → general sensation from face, scalp, teeth, meninges; (2) COCHLEAR NUCLEI (dorsal and ventral) at pontomedullary junction → hearing; (3) VESTIBULAR NUCLEI (superior, medial, lateral, inferior) → balance and spatial orientation. These nuclei receive afferents from head and neck receptors.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards trigeminal ganglion, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal ganglion is INCORRECTLY described as lying at the apex of petrous temporal bone. It actually lies in Meckel's cave on the ANTERIOR surface of the petrous temporal bone, not at its apex.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion lies in Meckel's cave on the anterior surface of petrous temporal bone, not at the apex.
options: Anterolaterally, it gives attachment to divisions of trigeminal nerve.
It lies at apex of petreous temporal bone.
Central processes of its cells form sensory root of trigeminal nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from:
questions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion receives its parasympathetic preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus via the nervus intermedius, greater petrosal nerve, and facial nerve. These fibers continue in the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII), which joins the lingual nerve and synapses in the submandibular ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then innervate the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. The lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX) supplies the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from the chorda tympani nerve (CN VII).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate boundaries of Infratemporal fossa.
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa is a pyramidal space deep to the mandibular ramus and zygomatic arch. It communicates extensively with adjacent anatomical spaces and is bounded by several bony and soft tissue structures.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: anterior = posterior maxilla; medial = lateral pterygoid plate; lateral = ramus of mandible; roof = infratemporal surface of greater wing of sphenoid; posterior = carotid sheath.
questions.modelAnswer: ANTERIOR: posterior surface of maxilla. POSTERIOR: anterior border of carotid sheath and styloid process. SUPERIOR: infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of greater wing of sphenoid. INFERIOR: medial pterygoid muscle attached to angle of mandible. LATERAL: ramus of mandible. MEDIAL: lateral pterygoid plate and medial pterygoid muscle.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate contents of Infratemporal fossa.
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa contains numerous important structures including muscles, nerves, vessels, and glands that are essential for mastication, mandibular movement, and facial sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Contents of infratemporal fossa: muscles of mastication, mandibular nerve, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus, chorda tympani, otic ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: Contents of the infratemporal fossa include: muscles of mastication (medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid, and inferior head of temporalis); mandibular nerve (CN V3) and its branches; maxillary artery and its branches; pterygoid venous plexus; chorda tympani nerve; otic ganglion; sphenomandibular ligament; and the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of mandibular nerve.
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (CN V3) is the largest division of the trigeminal nerve. It carries both sensory and motor fibers and divides into several branches that supply the teeth, tongue, skin, and muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve branches: auriculotemporal, buccal, lingual, inferior alveolar, and motor branches to muscles of mastication.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the mandibular nerve include: sensory branches—auriculotemporal nerve (to temple and temporomandibular joint), buccal nerve (to cheek skin and buccal mucosa), lingual nerve (to anterior two-thirds of tongue for general sensation), inferior alveolar nerve (to lower teeth, lower lip, and chin); motor branches—masseteric nerve, deep temporal nerves, nerve to lateral pterygoid, nerve to medial pterygoid, and mylohyoid nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe distribution of lingual nerve.
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, then passes anterior to the hyoglossus muscle into the floor of the mouth. It receives the chorda tympani (carrying taste and parasympathetic fibers) and provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and lingual gingiva.
questions.keyConcept: Lingual nerve (CN V3) provides general sensation to anterior two-thirds of tongue and receives chorda tympani.
questions.modelAnswer: The lingual nerve is a sensory branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, then passes anterior to the hyoglossus muscle into the floor of the mouth. In the infratemporal fossa, it is joined by the chorda tympani (VA VII) which carries taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion. The lingual nerve provides general sensation (pain, temperature, touch) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and lingual gingiva of the mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of maxillary nerve.
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (CN V2) is the second division of the trigeminal nerve. It leaves the trigeminal ganglion through the foramen rotundum and gives branches in the pterygopalatine fossa, infraorbital canal, and face. It carries general somatic sensation from the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, upper teeth, palate, and nasal cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve (CN V2) branches include zygomatic, pterygopalatine, posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, and palatine nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) include: in the cranial cavity—middle meningeal nerve (recurrent branch); in the pterygopalatine fossa—zygomatic nerve, greater and lesser palatine nerves, nasopalatine nerve, posterior superior alveolar nerve, and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion; in the infraorbital canal—anterior and middle superior alveolar nerves; terminal branches on the face—infraorbital nerve dividing into inferior palpebral, external nasal, and superior labial branches.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of auriculotemporal nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3) that arises by two roots encircling the middle meningeal artery. It supplies sensory innervation to the temple, temporomandibular joint, external auditory meatus, and tympanic membrane. It also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3) supplies temple, TMJ, external ear, and carries parasympathetic fibers to parotid gland.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the auriculotemporal nerve include: (1) Articular branches—to the temporomandibular joint. (2) Parotid branches—carrying postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. (3) Anterior auricular branches—to the skin of the auricle. (4) Branches to the external auditory meatus—supplying skin and tympanic membrane. (5) Superficial temporal branches—terminal branches supplying the skin of the temple and scalp.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe boundaries of pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa is a small pyramidal space between the pterygopalatine fissure posteriorly, the orbit anteriorly, the nasal cavity medially, and the infratemporal fossa laterally. It contains the maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion, and terminal branches of the maxillary artery.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa communicates with orbit, nasal cavity, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and pharynx.
questions.modelAnswer: Boundaries of the pterygopalatine fossa: anterior—maxilla (posterior surface); posterior—pterygoid process and greater wing of sphenoid (with foramen rotundum superiorly, pterygoid canal inferiorly); medial—perpendicular plate of palatine bone with sphenopalatine foramen; lateral—pterygomaxillary fissure opening into infratemporal fossa; superior—orbital process of palatine bone with inferior orbital fissure; inferior—pyramidal process of palatine bone with greater and lesser palatine foramina. It communicates with the orbit, nasal cavity, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and pharynx.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of maxillary artery.
questions.explanation: The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery that supplies deep structures of the face, jaws, nasal cavity, and cranial dura. It is divided into three parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary artery has three parts: mandibular (1st), pterygoid (2nd), and pterygopalatine (3rd).
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of the maxillary artery: First (mandibular) part—deep auricular, anterior tympanic, middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, and inferior alveolar arteries. Second (pterygoid) part—masseteric, pterygoid, buccal, and deep temporal arteries. Third (pterygopalatine) part—posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater palatine, lesser palatine, nasopalatine, sphenopalatine, and artery of pterygoid canal.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which one of the following is a paired bone?
questions.explanation: The parietal bone is a PAIRED bone—there are two parietal bones, one on each side of the skull forming the lateral walls and roof of the cranial cavity. The frontal, occipital, and sphenoid bones are unpaired (single midline bones). The ethmoid is also unpaired, forming the nasal cavity and part of the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal bone is PAIRED (two parietal bones); forms lateral cranial wall. Frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid are unpaired.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 25 year old woman suffers from a traumatic scalp avulsion due to a revolving machinery at her workplace. All the following are considered boundaries for the scalp EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The scalp is bounded by: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (laterally), and supraorbital arch/ridge (anterior). The EXTERNAL OCCIPITAL PROTUBERANCE is a landmark on the skull but the scalp's posterior boundary is the superior nuchal line, not the protuberance itself. The zygomatic arch is the lateral boundary; zygomatic bone is part of the face, not a boundary of the scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp boundaries: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (lateral), supraorbital arch (anterior). External occipital protuberance is a skull landmark, not scalp boundary.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior branch of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein unites with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.选项A正确. The answer is A. The external jugular drains the face and scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein + posterior auricular vein = external jugular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All are contents of infratemporal fossa Except:
questions.explanation: Infratemporal fossa contents: lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion.选项E正确. The answer is E. The pterygoid muscles and vessels are key contents.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa: pterygoid muscles, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion - NOT the orbit.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The otic ganglion:
questions.explanation: Otic ganglion: parasympathetic ganglion near foramen ovale, receives fibers from lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX), sends postganglionic to parotid gland.选项E正确. The answer is E. It is suspended from V3.
questions.keyConcept: Otic ganglion: parasympathetic to parotid - receives CN IX via lesser petrosal, suspended from V3.
options: Lies deep to the mandibular nerve.
Is functionally connected to the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Is closely related to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.
Its sympathetic root is derived from the plexus around internal carotid artery.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: One of the relays nuclel of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus. The trapezoid body also passes through this area.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive (binaural hearing) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Basis pontis contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Basis pontis contains corticospinal fibers, corticonuclear fibers, transverse pontine fibers, and pontine nuclei. Pontine reticulospinal fibers are in the TEGMENTUM, not basis pontis.
questions.keyConcept: Basis pontis: corticospinal, corticonuclear, transverse pontine fibers. Tegmentum: reticulospinal, sensory nuclei.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus carries somatosensory information (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), not auditory information. Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the lateral lemniscus formed of?
questions.explanation: The lateral lemniscus is formed from ALL THREE acoustic stria (dorsal, intermediate, and ventral) plus fibers from the superior olivary nucleus and trapezoid body nuclei. It carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral lemniscus: from all 3 acoustic stria + superior olive + trapezoid nuclei → inferior colliculus.
options: Fibers from the nuclei of the trapezoid body
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the boundaries of temporal fossa?
questions.explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly by the superior temporal line and inferiorly by the zygomatic arch. It contains the temporalis muscle and is continuous with the infratemporal fossa deep to the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Temporal fossa: superior temporal line to zygomatic arch. Temporalis muscle is the key content.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior temporal line of the skull. Inferiorly: zygomatic arch. The temporal fossa is the space between these boundaries, containing the temporalis muscle, temporal fascia, and deep temporal arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the boundaries of infratemporal fossa?
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa is bounded laterally by the ramus of mandible, medially by the lateral pterygoid plate, anteriorly by the posterior surface of maxilla, posteriorly by the styloid process, and superiorly by the greater wing of sphenoid.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa boundaries: lateral = mandibular ramus, medial = pterygoid plate, anterior = maxilla, posterior = styloid, superior = sphenoid.
questions.modelAnswer: Laterally: ramus of mandible. Medially: lateral pterygoid plate. Anteriorly: posterior surface of maxilla. Posteriorly: styloid process. Superiorly: greater wing of sphenoid. The fossa contains muscles of mastication, vessels, and nerves.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the communications of infratemporal fossa?
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates with: temporal fossa (via gap deep to zygomatic arch), middle cranial fossa (foramen ovale and spinosum), orbit (inferior orbital fissure), and pterygopalatine fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure).
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa: communicates with temporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, orbit, pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.modelAnswer: With temporal fossa through the gap deep to zygomatic arch, with middle cranial fossa through foramen ovale and foramen spinosum, with the orbit through inferior orbital fissure, and with pterygopalatine fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the medial relations of lateral pterygoid.
questions.explanation: The medial relations of the lateral pterygoid include: deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palati, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament. These structures are medial to the lateral pterygoid muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Medial pterygoid relations (medial): deep medial pterygoid head, tensor palati, MMA, V3 trunk, otic ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: Deep head of medial pterygoid, tensor palatini, middle meningeal artery, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve trunk, otic ganglion, and sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the boundaries of pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa boundaries are: anterior = posterior surface of maxilla, posterior = pterygoid process (lateral and medial pterygoid plates), medial = palatine bone, lateral = opens into infratemporal fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: anterior = maxilla, posterior = pterygoid process, medial = palatine bone, lateral = opens to infratemporal fossa.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: posterior surface of maxilla. Posteriorly: pterygoid process (lateral and medial pterygoid plates). Medially: palatine bone. Laterally: opens into infratemporal fossa through pterygomaxillary fissure.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the contents of pterygopalatine fossa
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa contains: the third part of the maxillary artery (giving off all terminal branches), the maxillary nerve (V2) with its branches, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (parasympathetic ganglion).
questions.keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa: 3rd part maxillary artery, V2, pterygopalatine ganglion.
questions.modelAnswer: Third part of maxillary artery (terminal portion with all its branches), maxillary nerve (V2) giving off ganglionic branches, and pterygopalatine ganglion (parasympathetic ganglion receiving V2 input).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the site, sympathetic root, parasympathetic root, and distribution of otic ganglion.
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion is located below the foramen ovale. Its sympathetic root is from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery (from superficial petrosal nerve - from ICA plexus). Parasympathetic root is from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX, tympanic plexus, and lesser petrosal nerve. It distributes to the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Otic ganglion: below foramen ovale; sympathetic = around MMA; parasympathetic = lesser petrosal nerve (from IX); distribution = parotid.
questions.modelAnswer: Site: below foramen ovale on medial surface of V3. Sympathetic root: from plexus around middle meningeal artery (derived from external carotid artery sympathetic plexus). Parasympathetic root: from inferior salivatory nucleus via tympanic branch of CN IX → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion. Distribution: postganglionic fibers to parotid gland.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Compare between otic ganglion, submandibular ganglion, sphenopalatine ganglion (according to its sympathetic root)
questions.explanation: The sympathetic roots of the three parasympathetic ganglia differ: otic ganglion has sympathetic from middle meningeal artery plexus; submandibular ganglion has sympathetic from facial artery plexus; sphenopalatine ganglion has sympathetic from deep petrosal nerve (from ICA plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic roots: otic = MMA plexus; submandibular = facial artery plexus; sphenopalatine = deep petrosal (ICA).
questions.modelAnswer: Otic ganglion: sympathetic root around middle meningeal artery. Submandibular ganglion: sympathetic root around facial artery. Sphenopalatine ganglion: sympathetic root from deep petrosal nerve (around internal carotid artery).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Compare between the cervical sympathetic ganglion(site)
questions.explanation: The three cervical sympathetic ganglia are located at specific vertebral levels: superior cervical ganglion at C2-C3, middle cervical ganglion at C6-C7, and inferior cervical ganglion at C7 (often fused with T1 to form the stellate ganglion).
questions.keyConcept: Cervical sympathetic ganglia: superior = C2-3, middle = C6-7, inferior = C7 (stellate with T1).
questions.modelAnswer: Superior cervical ganglion: at level of C2-C3 vertebrae. Middle cervical ganglion: at level of C6-C7 vertebrae. Inferior cervical ganglion: at level of C7 vertebra (often fused with first thoracic ganglion to form stellate ganglion).
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which structure contains the first order neurons for facial pain and temperature?
questions.explanation: The trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion) contains first-order neurons for facial pain and temperature sensation. Central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion is the sensory ganglion for facial pain and temperature via cranial nerve V.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which area of the brain, when damaged, causes contralateral hemiplegia?
questions.explanation: The internal capsule contains descending corticospinal fibers that, when damaged, cause contralateral hemiplegia. Fibers are already crossed at the medullary pyramids, so internal capsule lesions affect the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule damage causes contralateral motor deficits due to already-crossed corticospinal fibers.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient has difficulty voluntarily moving both eyes to the right side. This deficit is most likely due to a lesion in which area?
questions.explanation: Horizontal gaze palsy indicates lesion in the abducens nucleus (CN VI) or PPRF (paramedian pontine reticular formation). The patient cannot voluntarily move eyes to the right, suggesting left PPRF/nucleus lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal gaze control localizes to the pons (PPRF/CN VI nucleus) for voluntary eye movements.
questions.chapterTitle: IV. Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity & Temporal Region
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The medial geniculate body is connected to the brachium of which structure?
