questions.text: Explain the significance of gamma motor neurons in the maintenance of muscle tone.
questions.explanation: Gamma (γ) motor neurons are crucial for maintaining muscle tone through their regulation of muscle spindle sensitivity. While alpha motor neurons control extrafusal muscle fibers (force production), γ motor neurons control intrafusal fiber tension within spindles. γ activation: 1) Contracts intrafusal fibers, 2) Increases spindle sensitivity to stretch, 3) Increases Ia afferent discharge, 4) Facilitates alpha motor neurons via stretch reflex, 5) Increases muscle tone. γ tone is influenced by descending pathways (reticulospinal, vestibulospinal facilitate; corticospinal modulates). In UMN lesions, γ bias increases causing spasticity (velocity-dependent hyperreflexia). In cerebellar lesions, γ dysregulation contributes to atonia. γ system allows central commands to preload spindles, adjusting reflex sensitivity for planned movements.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons maintain muscle tone by regulating muscle spindle sensitivity, influencing stretch reflex responsiveness.

questions.text: Explain the basic mechanism which maintain the upright posture.
questions.explanation: Postural maintenance is a complex process involving multiple sensory and motor systems. The upright posture is maintained through: 1) Sensory input - visual (eyes provide spatial orientation), vestibular (detects head position and movement), proprioceptive (muscle spindles, joint receptors detect body position); 2) Central processing - brainstem (vestibular nuclei, reticular formation), cerebellum (coordinates and fine-tunes responses), basal ganglia (sets postural tone); 3) Motor output - descending tracts adjust muscle tone, coordinated muscle activation maintains center of gravity over base of support. Key reflexes: 1) Righting reflexes - correct abnormal head and body positions; 2) Equilibrium reactions - maintain balance when base of support is challenged; 3) Stepping movements - automatic adjustments when standing on moving platform. The postural control system adapts to changing conditions through feedforward (anticipatory) and feedback (corrective) mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Posture is maintained by integrating visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive inputs through brainstem and cerebellar processing.

questions.text: List the areas of the brain believed to be involved in the production of speech and their function, describe the different types of aphasias produced by damage
questions.explanation: Speech production involves Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, dominant hemisphere) - responsible for speech planning and formulation; Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) - responsible for language comprehension; motor cortex (face area) - executes speech movements; cerebellum - coordinates speech rhythm; basal ganglia - modulates motor output. Functions: Broca's area generates grammatically complex speech; Wernicke's area processes language meaning; connections between them (arcuate fasciculus) allow repetition. Aphasias: 1) Broca's aphasia (expressive/motor) - non-fluent, effortful speech, good comprehension, poor repetition; 2) Wernicke's aphasia (receptive/sensory) - fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension, poor repetition; 3) Global aphasia - both expression and comprehension impaired; 4) Conduction aphasia - fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition (arcuate fasciculus lesion); 5) Transcortical aphasias - repetition preserved.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's and Wernicke's areas, connected by arcuate fasciculus, are the core language network, producing different aphasia patterns when damaged.

questions.explanation: Pyramidal tracts (corticospinal and corticobulbar) originate from motor cortex (areas 4, 6, 3, 1, 2) and descend through internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, pons, and medulla. Non-pyramidal tracts (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal) originate in brainstem, descend in spinal cord, and control: 1) Posture and tone; 2) Proximal limb movements; 3) Equilibrium; 4) Automatic movements. They facilitate flexors (rubrospinal) or extensors (vestibulospinal). Non-pyramidal lesions cause: 1) Difficulty with posture and walking; 2) Impaired righting reflexes; 3) Slowness of movement. questions.text: Give a short account on mechanism of action of α-methyl dopa.
questions.explanation: α‑Methyl dopa (methyldopa) is a centrally acting antihypertensive that is metabolized to α‑methyl norepinephrine, which acts as a false neurotransmitter at central α2‑adrenergic receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa acts as a false neurotransmitter at central α2‑receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow from the brainstem.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism of action of α‑methyl dopa: (1) α‑Methyl dopa enters the brain and is converted to α‑methyl norepinephrine (α‑MeNE) by dopamine β‑hydroxylase in the same pathway as endogenous norepinephrine synthesis. (2) α‑MeNE is a false neurotransmitter — it is stored in and released from synaptic vesicles instead of norepinephrine, but has lower potency at α‑adrenergic receptors. (3) In the brainstem (rostral ventrolateral medulla), α‑MeNE activates central presynaptic α2‑adrenergic autoreceptors more potently than norepinephrine, leading to profound reduction in sympathetic nervous system outflow. (4) Decreased sympathetic tone → reduced peripheral vascular resistance, heart rate, and blood pressure. (5) Also thought to reduce plasma renin activity and form false neurotransmitters peripherally. Note: Despite its central mechanism, it does not cross the BBB well, which limits its site of action to areas with an imperfect BBB.

questions.text: The floor of digastric triangle ; formed by:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and superiorly by the inferior border of the mandible. Its floor is formed by the mylohyoid muscle anteriorly and by the hyoglossus and geniohyoid muscles more posteriorly and medially, separating the submandibular region from the oral cavity floor.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of digastric triangle = mylohyoid and hyoglossus (and geniohyoid).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection in the neck just in front of prevertebral fascia may spread downwards till the limit of:
questions.explanation: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles and extends laterally to form the axillary sheath enclosing the brachial plexus and subclavian artery. Infections posterior to the prevertebral fascia remain localized because the fascia is tough. However, infections anterior to the prevertebral fascia can spread downward into the posterior mediastinum and laterally into the axilla through the axillary sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Infection anterior to prevertebral fascia can spread to posterior mediastinum and axilla.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: External jugular vein drains into:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is formed by the union of the posterior auricular and posterior branch of the retromandibular veins behind the angle of the mandible. It descends in the superficial fascia, crosses the sternocleidomastoid, and terminates by draining into the subclavian vein near the clavicle.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein drains into subclavian vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding digastric triangle, all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and superiorly by the lower border of the mandible. It contains the submandibular gland and submandibular lymph nodes. The hyoid bone is NOT the superior boundary; the mandible is.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle is bounded superiorly by mandible, NOT hyoid bone.
options: It is bounded anteriorly by anterior belly of digastric.
It is bounded posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric & stylohyoid.
It is bounded superiorly by hyoid bone.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which one of the following is used as a venous manometer?
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein that drains from the posterior auricular and retromandibular veins, crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and empties into the subclavian vein near the clavicle. Because it is superficial, thin-walled, and readily visible under the skin, it is commonly used clinically as a venous manometer to estimate central venous pressure, particularly in patients with heart failure or volume overload.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein is used as a clinical venous manometer.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards anterior jugular vein, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The anterior jugular vein begins below the chin from the confluence of the submental veins, descends superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle near the midline, and drains into the external jugular vein jugular arch near the sternal end of the clavicle before emptying into the subclavian vein. The incorrect statement is that it drains INTO the external jugular vein; rather, the jugular arch connects the two anterior jugular veins and then drains into the subclavian vein or external jugular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior jugular vein drains via jugular arch to subclavian vein (not directly into external jugular vein).
options: It descends on the side of median plane of neck.
Right & left veins are united above suprasternal notch.
It drains into external jugular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is attached to all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia attaches superiorly to the mandible, mastoid process, ligamentum nuchae, and superior nuchal line. Inferiorly, it attaches to the acromion, clavicle, and manubrium. It covers the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. It is NOT directly attached to the hyoid bone as a specific named attachment point; rather, the pretracheal fascia attaches to the hyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Investing layer does NOT attach to hyoid bone; pretracheal fascia does.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe formation of external jugular vein & enumerate its tributaries.
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein formed near the angle of the mandible by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein. It descends superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein near the clavicle. Its tributaries include the posterior external jugular vein, transverse cervical vein, suprascapular vein, and the anterior jugular vein (via a communicating branch).
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein = posterior auricular + posterior retromandibular; tributaries include posterior external jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and anterior jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: The external jugular vein is formed near the angle of the mandible by the union of the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It descends superficially over the sternocleidomastoid muscle, pierces the deep fascia at the midclavicular point, and drains into the subclavian vein. Its tributaries include: (1) posterior external jugular vein, (2) transverse cervical vein, (3) suprascapular vein, and (4) anterior jugular vein (communicating branch).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate branches of inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSG).
questions.explanation: The inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSG) is usually fused with the first thoracic ganglion to form the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion at the neck of the first rib. Its branches include: (1) gray rami communicantes to C7-C8 and T1; (2) a vascular plexus around the vertebral artery (vertebral plexus); (3) plexuses around the subclavian and axillary arteries; (4) cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus; and (5) tracheal, esophageal, and bronchial branches.
questions.keyConcept: ICSG branches: gray rami C7-C8-T1, vertebral plexus, subclavian plexus, cardiac branches, and tracheal/bronchial branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Branches of ICSG (often fused with T1 to form stellate ganglion): (1) gray rami to C7, C8, and T1; (2) vertebral artery plexus; (3) subclavian and axillary artery plexuses; (4) cardiac branches to deep cardiac plexus; (5) tracheal, esophageal, and bronchial branches.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve of the branchial arch that gives the upper part of the body of the hyoid bone is:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII, 2nd arch nerve) innervates muscles derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch, including the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and the posterior belly of digastric. The upper part of the body of the hyoid bone is formed from the 2nd arch cartilage (Reichert's cartilage).
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve (2nd arch) innervates 2nd arch derivatives; upper hyoid body is a 2nd arch derivative.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve that supplies muscles derived from 2nd branchial arch is:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. It innervates all muscles derived from the 2nd arch, including the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. It also carries taste and parasympathetic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the 2nd arch; innervates muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: During the 4th week of development, branchial apparatus develops in:
questions.explanation: During the 4th week of embryonic development, the branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus forms in the head and neck region. This includes the branchial arches, pouches, clefts, and membranes, which give rise to most head and neck structures. The branchial apparatus development is initiated at the end of the 3rd week and peaks during the 4th week.
questions.keyConcept: Branchial apparatus develops in the head and neck region during the 4th week of embryonic development.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following muscles arise from second pharyngeal arch, Except:
questions.explanation: The temporalis muscle is derived from the first pharyngeal arch and is innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3). All the other muscles listed (buccinator, posterior belly of digastric, platysma, and orbicularis oculi) are derived from the second pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis muscle is the only 1st arch muscle listed; all others (buccinator, digastric posterior belly, platysma, orbicularis oculi) are 2nd arch.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding the branchial cyst?
questions.explanation: A branchial cyst is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His (the second pharyngeal cleft), located near the angle of the mandible and along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It is lined by ectoderm (stratified squamous epithelium). The statement that it is related to the posterior border of sternomastoid is INCORRECT—the cyst lies along the ANTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid, not posterior.
questions.keyConcept: Branchial cyst = remnant of cervical sinus; lined by ectoderm; lies along ANTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid (not posterior).
options: Covers all clefts except the first.
Is usually close to the angle of mandible.
It is related to the posterior border of sternomastoid muscle.
It is the remnant of cervical sinus.
It is lined by ectoderm (stratified squamous epithelium).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches.
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal pouches give rise to important head and neck structures. The first pouch gives eustachian tube, middle ear, and mastoid air cells. The second pouch gives palatine tonsil. The third pouch gives thymus and inferior parathyroids. The fourth pouch gives superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial body. The fifth pouch gives parafollicular C cells.
questions.keyConcept: 1st pouch= Eustachian tube/middle ear; 2nd= tonsil; 3rd= thymus/inferior parathyroids; 4th= superior parathyroids; 5th= parafollicular C cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Derivatives of pharyngeal pouches: (1) 1st pouch: tubotympanic recess forming eustachian tube, middle ear cavity, and mastoid air cells. (2) 2nd pouch: palatine tonsil and tonsillar fossa. (3) 3rd pouch: ventral wing gives thymus; dorsal wing gives inferior parathyroid glands. (4) 4th pouch: ventral wing gives ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells); dorsal wing gives superior parathyroid glands. (5) 5th pouch: rudimentary, contributes to parafollicular C cells.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe the derivatives & nerve supply of 1st pharyngeal arch.
questions.explanation: The first pharyngeal arch is also called the mandibular arch. Its nerve is CN V3 (mandibular division of trigeminal). Skeletal derivatives include mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, malleus, incus. Muscular derivatives include muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.
questions.keyConcept: 1st arch: nerve CN V3; skeletal = mandible, maxilla, malleus, incus; muscles = mastication muscles, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani/palati.
questions.modelAnswer: First pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bone, squamous temporal bone, malleus, incus (from Meckel's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini. (4) Associated structures: Meckel's cartilage (first arch cartilage), sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe the derivatives & nerve supply of 2nd pharyngeal arch.
questions.explanation: The second pharyngeal arch is also called Reichert's cartilage. Its nerve is CN VII (facial nerve). Skeletal derivatives include stapes, styloid process, lesser horn and upper body of hyoid. Muscular derivatives include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric.
questions.keyConcept: 2nd arch: nerve CN VII; skeletal = stapes, styloid process, lesser horn/upper hyoid; muscles = facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric.
questions.modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch derivatives and nerve supply: (1) Nerve: Facial nerve (CN VII). (2) Skeletal derivatives: Stapes, styloid process of temporal bone, lesser horn of hyoid, upper part of body of hyoid (from Reichert's cartilage). (3) Muscular derivatives: Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric. (4) Associated structures: Stylohyoid ligament. These muscles form the superficial muscle group of the face and some ear structures.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 22-year-old-female consulted a plastic surgeon about the presence of multiple holes along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle.
questions.explanation: Multiple holes (fistulae) along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicate a branchial fistula, typically from the second pharyngeal cleft/cervical sinus remnant. The external auditory meatus develops from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the thymus develops from the ventral wing of the third pharyngeal pouch.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple fistulae along sternocleidomastoid = branchial fistula (2nd cleft/cervical sinus remnant). External meatus = 1st cleft; thymus = ventral 3rd pouch.

questions.text: A 22-year-old-female developed cystic swelling undercover the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle.
questions.explanation: A cystic swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicates a branchial sinus (internal or external), which is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His. The superior parathyroid develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The cervical sinus is a depression between the second arch and the third, fourth, and sixth arches.
questions.keyConcept: Cystic swelling along sternocleidomastoid = branchial sinus (cervical sinus remnant); superior parathyroids from dorsal 4th pouch.

subQuestions.text: TYPE: essay Name the congenital anomaly.
subQuestions.explanation: A cystic swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicates a branchial sinus (internal or external), which is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His. The superior parathyroid develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The cervical sinus is a depression between the second arch and the third, fourth, and sixth arches.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Cystic swelling along sternocleidomastoid = branchial sinus (cervical sinus remnant); superior parathyroids from dorsal 4th pouch.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Branchial sinus.

subQuestions.explanation: A cystic swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicates a branchial sinus (internal or external), which is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His. The superior parathyroid develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The cervical sinus is a depression between the second arch and the third, fourth, and sixth arches.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Cystic swelling along sternocleidomastoid = branchial sinus (cervical sinus remnant); superior parathyroids from dorsal 4th pouch.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: It is due to the failure of the obliteration of the cervical sinus.

subQuestions.explanation: A cystic swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid indicates a branchial sinus (internal or external), which is a remnant of the cervical sinus of His. The superior parathyroid develops from the dorsal part of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The cervical sinus is a depression between the second arch and the third, fourth, and sixth arches.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Cystic swelling along sternocleidomastoid = branchial sinus (cervical sinus remnant); superior parathyroids from dorsal 4th pouch.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Dorsal part of 4th pharyngeal pouch.

questions.text: The mastoid process is a part of the:
questions.explanation: The mastoid process is a prominence on the inferior aspect of the temporal bone, posterior to the external auditory meatus. It contains air cells that communicate with the middle ear cavity. It develops after birth (visible on imaging by age 2) in response to traction from the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The squamous and petrous parts of temporal bone are also parts of the temporal bone.
questions.keyConcept: Mastoid process is part of the TEMPORAL bone; contains mastoid air cells communicating with middle ear.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection of scalp area behind the ear affects which group of LNs
questions.explanation: Infection of scalp area behind the ear affects occipital lymph nodes. The scalp behind auricle drains to occipital and posterior auricular nodes.选项E正确. The answer is E. These nodes drain posterior scalp and neck.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior auricle/scalp drains to occipital and posterior auricular lymph nodes.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A muscle attached to the coronoid process of mandible:
questions.explanation: Muscle attached to coronoid process of mandible: temporalis (and lateral pterygoid attaches to condylar neck and articular disc).选项D正确. The answer is D. Temporalis inserts on coronoid process and anterior mandibular ramus.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis muscle inserts on coronoid process of mandible - elevation and retraction of mandible.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the CERVICAL spinal cord, not the whole length. It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination. It does not extend into the lumbosacral cord.
questions.keyConcept: MLF: brainstem to cervical cord; connects vestibular nuclei to control head/neck movements.
options: receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck
extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Muscle of facial expression are developed from which pharyngeal arch: ___
questions.explanation: Muscles of facial expression are derived from the second pharyngeal arch (stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, stapedius, and all muscles of facial expression). The second arch is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.keyConcept: Second pharyngeal arch: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric. Nerve: CN VII (facial).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the muscles that are supplied by motor nucleus of trigeminal.
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal supplies the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids) and four non-mastication muscles: tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric.
questions.keyConcept: Motor V: 4 mastication muscles + tensor tympani, tensor palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.
questions.modelAnswer: The four muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid) plus tensor tympani (in middle ear), tensor veli palatini (palate), mylohyoid (floor of mouth), and anterior belly of digastric (suprahyoid).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of inferior alveolar nerve.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives off: mylohyoid nerve (to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric before entering mandibular foramen), mental nerve (exits mental foramen to chin and lower lip), and incisive nerve (continues in mandible to anterior teeth).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior alveolar branches: mylohyoid nerve, mental nerve, incisive nerve. These provide sensory and motor innervation.
questions.modelAnswer: Mylohyoid nerve (motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric - branches off before entering mandibular foramen), mental nerve (sensory to chin and lower lip), and incisive nerve (sensory to anterior teeth and premolars).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the tributaries of external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein receives: anterior jugular vein (from anterior neck), transverse cervical vein (from shoulder region), suprascapular vein (from scapular region), and posterior external jugular vein (from posterior scalp and neck).
questions.keyConcept: External jugular tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior jugular vein (from anterior neck), transverse cervical vein, suprascapular vein, and posterior external jugular vein. It drains into the subclavian vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the boundaries of digastric triangle.
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries: anteriorly = anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly = posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, superiorly = inferior border of mandible to mastoid. The roof is skin, superficial fascia, and deep fascia. The floor is mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior = anterior digastric, posterior = posterior digastric + stylohyoid, superior = mandible, floor = mylohyoid + hyoglossus.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: anterior belly of digastric. Posteriorly: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid. Superiorly: inferior border of mandible and a line from angle of mandible to mastoid process. Roof: skin, superficial fascia, investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Floor: mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention 5 contents of digastric triangle.
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle contains: submandibular gland (major content), submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (on the gland), facial artery (grooving the gland), and facial vein (superficial to the gland).
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle: submandibular gland, submandibular LN, submandibular ganglion, facial artery, facial vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Submandibular gland (the main content), submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion, facial artery (pierces the gland), and facial vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the contents of the muscular triangle.
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid muscles (strap muscles): sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid. These muscles attach the hyoid bone to the larynx, sternum, and scapula.
questions.keyConcept: Muscular triangle: contains infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid).
questions.modelAnswer: Infrahyoid muscles including sternohyoid (from sternum to hyoid), sternothyroid (from sternum to thyroid cartilage), thyrohyoid (from thyroid cartilage to hyoid), and omohyoid (from scapula to hyoid).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lymph from central part of upper lip drop, directly to:
questions.explanation: Lymph from the central part of the upper lip (philtrum area) drains directly to the submental lymph nodes, located beneath the chin between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles. This is part of the facial lymph drainage system.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains directly to submental lymph nodes
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding digastric triangle. All are true Except:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded by the inferior border of the mandible superiorly (not the hyoid bone), the anterior belly of digastric anteriorly, and the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid posteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle bounded superiorly by mandible, not hyoid bone - FALSE statement
options: It is bounded anteriorly by anterior belly of digastric.
It is bounded posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid.
It is bounded superiorly by hyoid bone.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nucleus is located in the special visceral efferent (SVE) column?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is located in the SVE (special visceral efferent) column and innervates muscles derived from pharyngeal arches: stylopharyngeus (IX), pharyngeal muscles (X), sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus is the SVE column nucleus for pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which ligament prevents the mandible from posterior dislocation?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle has upper and lower heads; the articular disc and capsule of the TMJ are attached to the condylar neck. The temporomandibular ligament prevents posterior dislocation of the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Temporomandibular ligament (lateral) prevents excessive posterior mandibular displacement.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which artery is located below the posterior belly of the digastric muscle?
questions.explanation: The occipital artery is located below the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. It runs with the greater occipital nerve and supplies the posterior scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital artery courses deep to the posterior digastric belly, supplying posterior scalp.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Tributaries of external jugular vein:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein receives tributaries including the anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular veins, draining superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: EJV tributaries: anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, posterior external jugular.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Boundaries of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle boundaries are: anterior belly of digastric, posterior belly of digastric with stylohyoid, and the inferior border of mandible to mastoid; the floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle: anterior/posterior bellies of digastric, mandible to mastoid; floor mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: anterior belly of digastric; Posterior: posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid; Superior: inferior border of mandible to mastoid; Roof: skin, superficial, deep fascia; Floor: mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 5 contents of digastric triangle:
questions.explanation: Five contents of the digastric triangle are the submandibular gland, submandibular lymph nodes, submandibular ganglion (parasympathetic), facial artery, and facial vein.
questions.keyConcept: Digastric triangle contents: submandibular gland, LN, ganglion, facial artery and vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Submandibular gland, submandibular LN, submandibular ganglion, facial artery, facial vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Contents of muscular triangle:
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid, which stabilize the larynx and hyoid during swallowing and speech.
questions.keyConcept: Muscular triangle contains infrahyoid strap muscles.
questions.modelAnswer: Contents of the muscular triangle: Infrahyoid (strap) muscles - sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and omohyoid. These muscles attach the hyoid bone to the larynx, sternum, and scapula.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The only tributary of the subclavian vein is:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is the only named tributary of the subclavian vein, carrying blood from the superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein: only named tributary of subclavian vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The viscera of the neck are surrounded by ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath around the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland, fusing laterally with the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical viscera.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A nerve running along the posterior border of sternomastoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve runs along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle, arising from C2 ventral ramus to supply the scalp behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve: posterior border of SCM.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fracture of neck of mandible can lead to injury of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve runs on the lateral surface of the mandibular neck, so it can be injured in fractures; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves are also at risk, but auriculotemporal is not typically affected.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular neck fracture: masseteric, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves at risk.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A branch from the 2nd part of subclavian artery is:
questions.explanation: The second part of subclavian artery gives rise to the internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk (supplying thyroid, neck, and chest wall structures).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery part 2: internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match the muscle in column A with its main action in column B.
questions.explanation: Matching pairs: Masseter elevates mandible, Temporalis retracts mandible, Medial pterygoid elevates and protrudes, Lateral pterygoid protrudes and opens, Digastric opens mouth, Buccinator compresses cheeks.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle actions: masseter elevate, temporalis retract, pterygoids protrude, digastric open, buccinator compress.

pairs.target: B) Lateral flexion of the skull.

questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the:
questions.explanation: The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) descends into the neck to supply the platysma muscle. The temporal, zygomatic, and buccal branches supply facial muscles above the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve innervates the platysma
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe branches of facial nerve in neck & its terminal branches.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve gives the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Its five terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical
questions.modelAnswer: The facial nerve gives off the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Within and beyond the parotid, it divides into five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The common motor nucleus of IX, X and XI cranial nerves is:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It gives rise to special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) fibers that supply pharyngeal arch muscles (stylopharyngeus via IX, pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles via X, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius via XI).
questions.keyConcept: SVE column - pharyngeal arch muscles
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of facial nerve & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: Nuclei of the facial nerve: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) - motor to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal gland (via greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion), submandibular and sublingual glands (via chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion); (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA) - taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS OF V - proprioception from facial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve nuclei: motor (facial expression muscles), superior salivary (lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands), solitarius (taste)
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of facial nerve and their supplied structures: (1) Facial motor nucleus (SVE) - supplies muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric; (2) Superior salivary nucleus (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal gland (via greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion), submandibular and sublingual glands (via chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion); (3) Nucleus solitarius (SVA) - taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani; (4) Mesencephalic nucleus of V - proprioception from facial muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate derivatives of the pharyngeal arch supplied by the facial nerve.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch. All muscles, cartilages, and bones derived from the second arch are supplied by CN VII. These include muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and the styloid process of the hyoid bone.
questions.keyConcept: CN VII (facial nerve) supplies: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and styloid process.
questions.modelAnswer: Derivatives of the second pharyngeal arch supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII): (1) Muscles—muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. (2) Bones—styloid process of hyoid bone and lesser horn of hyoid (via Reichert's cartilage). (3) Ligaments—stylohyoid ligament. All these structures are innervated by CN VII regardless of their final anatomical position.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the
questions.explanation: The branch of facial nerve that supplies the platysma is the cervical branch (also called mandibular branch in some texts).选项E正确. The answer is E. Platysma is a neck muscle of facial expression.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical branch of facial nerve supplies platysma - the only muscle in the neck from facial nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of anterior horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains motor nuclei organized somatotopically: Medial motor nuclei (medial column) supply muscles of neck and trunk; Lateral motor nuclei (lateral column) supply limb muscles, divided into anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius), posterior lateral (forearm flexors), and postural (limb extensors). The phrenic nucleus at C3,4,5 supplies the diaphragm. These are lower motor neuron cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn motor nuclei: medial, lateral (with subdivisions), and phrenic nucleus
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of anterior horn: (1) Medial motor nuclei - in medial column, supply muscles of neck and trunk; (2) Lateral motor nuclei - in lateral column, supply limb muscles; (a) Anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius); (b) Posterior lateral (flexors of forearm); (c) Postural (extensors of limb); (3) Phrenic nucleus (C3,4,5) - supplies diaphragm.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For the Genu of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The genu (knee) of the internal capsule is the bend between the anterior and posterior limbs, located at the level of the interventricular foramen. It contains corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers that control voluntary movement of the contralateral face, tongue, and throat, as well as some corticospinal fibers for the neck.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of internal capsule contains corticonuclear fibers for contralateral face/tongue/pharynx movement.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The interstitiospinal tract (from interstitial nucleus of Cajal) is primarily responsible for the head righting reflex, which maintains head position in space. The tectospinal tract is for neck reflexes in response to visual stimuli. Vestibulospinal maintains posture. Reticulospinal for autonomic functions.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitiospinal tract: from interstitial nucleus of Cajal, head righting reflex, descends in MLF.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention 2 extrapyramidal tracts.
questions.explanation: The two major extrapyramidal tracts (motor pathways outside the corticospinal tract) are the tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus, controls neck muscles) and the rubrospinal tract (from red nucleus, controls limb flexor muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: tectospinal (neck control), rubrospinal (flexor muscles). Both modulate movement.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Tectospinal tract - originates from superior colliculus, crosses in dorsal tegmental decussation, descends to cervical spinal cord to control neck and upper trunk muscles in response to visual stimuli. 2) Rubrospinal tract - originates from red nucleus, crosses in ventral tegmental decussation, descends to control flexor muscles of the upper limb.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate communications of Infratemporal fossa.
questions.explanation: The infratemporal fossa communicates with multiple anatomical spaces in the head and neck, allowing the spread of pathology such as infections and tumors between these compartments.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa communicates with orbit, middle cranial fossa, pterygopalatine fossa, and oral cavity.
questions.modelAnswer: Communications of the infratemporal fossa: (1) Orbit—through inferior orbital fissure; (2) Middle cranial fossa—through foramen ovale, foramen spinosum, and foramen lacerum; (3) Pterygopalatine fossa—through pterygomaxillary fissure; (4) Oral cavity—between maxilla and medial pterygoid muscle; (5) Temporal fossa—deep to zygomatic arch; (6) Submandibular region—along medial pterygoid muscle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is a tributary of subclavian vein?
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein that descends in the neck superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein proximal to its junction with the internal jugular vein. It serves as a major venous drainage pathway from the scalp and face and is clinically important as an easily accessible vein.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein drains into subclavian vein.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSE) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (often fused with the first thoracic ganglion to form the stellate ganglion) is located at the level of C7 near the neck of the first rib. It gives communicating branches to C7 and C8, vascular plexus around the vertebral artery, cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus, and branches to the subclavian artery. It does NOT give pharyngeal branches, which originate from the superior cervical ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pharyngeal branches come from superior cervical ganglion, NOT inferior cervical ganglion.
options: A cardiac branch to deep cardiac plexus.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the muscles derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch.
questions.explanation: The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini. The nerve of the first arch is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
questions.keyConcept: 1st arch muscles: muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor palati; nerve = CN V3.
questions.modelAnswer: Muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (innervated by CN V3): muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Complete: Tecto spinal tract forms the dorsal tegmental decussation which the rubro spinal tract forms the ___ tegmental decussation
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract forms the dorsal (posterior) tegmental decussation at the inferior colliculus level. The rubrospinal tract forms the ventral (anterior) tegmental decussation at a slightly higher level. These two decussations separate the neck and limb motor control pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal: dorsal tegmental decussation. Rubrospinal: ventral tegmental decussation. Both control different body regions.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nerves represents a motor component arising from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve?
questions.explanation: The postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion traveling along the internal carotid artery represent the motor component arising from the postganglionic sympathetic chain.
questions.keyConcept: Postganglionic sympathetics from superior cervical ganglion travel on internal carotid artery for cranial vasomotor control.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Muscles supplied by motor nucleus of trigeminal:
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve supplies the four muscles of mastication plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric.
questions.keyConcept: Motor V supplies mastication muscles, tensor tympani/palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.
questions.modelAnswer: 4 muscles of mastication, Tensor palate, Tensor tympani, Anterior belly of digastric, Mylohyoid.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nerves that supply scalp & face is not derived of Trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) derives from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. All other listed nerves are branches of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) is NOT a branch of the trigeminal nerve
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Injury of motor root of trigeminal nerve would cause paralysis of:
questions.explanation: Injury of motor root of trigeminal nerve (portio minor) would cause paralysis of: muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini.选项B正确. The answer is B. These are all innervated by CN V3 motor root.
questions.keyConcept: Motor root of CN V: mastication muscles, mylohyoid, digastric, tensor tympani/veli palatini - all affected.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplying scalp and face Is not derived from trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is derived from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. It supplies the skin over the parotid gland and mastoid area. The auriculotemporal, zygomaticotemporal, supraorbital, and supratrochlear are all trigeminal branches.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve from C2-C3 cervical plexus, not trigeminal (V)
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve is the motor branch of the posterior division of the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid nerve is the motor branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It innervates the mylohyoid muscle and anterior belly of the digastric muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Mylohyoid nerve from V3 posterior division supplies mylohyoid and anterior digastric muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2) that supplies the skin of the scalp posterior to the ear and the upper part of the lateral surface of the auricle. The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the posterior scalp near the midline. The posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII) supplies behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior and lateral to the ear (posterolateral scalp).
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Corticonuclear fibers pass through ……… of internal capsule to reach the brain stem.
questions.explanation: Corticonuclear fibers (corticobulbar tract) pass through the genu (bend) of the internal capsule to reach brainstem cranial nerve nuclei for voluntary control of face and neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Corticonuclear fibers pass through genu of internal capsule.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Tectospinal tract origin is......
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract originates from the contralateral superior colliculus and descends to the cervical spinal cord, mediating reflex adjustments of head and neck position in response to visual stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract originates from superior colliculus for head-neck reflexes to visual inputs.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Complete: Tectospinal
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus, decussates, and descends to control reflex head/neck movements toward visual stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract
questions.modelAnswer: Origin: superior colliculus; Function: reflex head and neck movements toward visual stimuli.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sensory supply of the skin over the angle of the mandible is by:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3), a branch of the cervical plexus, supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The infraorbital and mental nerves supply the upper and lower lips.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection of scalp area behind the ear affects ......... group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: The occipital group of lymph nodes lies at the apex of the posterior triangle and drains the posterior scalp region behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp behind the ear drains to occipital lymph nodes
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sensory supply of the skin over the angle of the mandible is carried by:
questions.explanation: The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), which arises from the cervical plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Angle of mandible = C2–C3 via great auricular nerve
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The floor of digastric triangle of the neck is formed by which muscle:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle (submandibular triangle) is bounded by the anterior belly of digastric anteriorly, the posterior belly of digastric posteriorly, and the inferior border of the mandible superiorly. Its floor is formed primarily by the mylohyoid muscle anteriorly and the hyoglossus muscle posteriorly. The mylohyoid separates the submandibular gland from the sublingual gland region.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of digastric triangle = mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The artery present in anterior part of digastric triangle of neck is:
questions.explanation: The digastric triangle contains the facial artery and vein as they course over the submandibular gland. In the anterior part of the triangle, the facial artery is a prominent content as it crosses the mandible to supply the face. The external carotid artery is deep to the posterior belly, while the internal carotid artery ascends outside the triangle within the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery is present in the anterior part of the digastric triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The posterior part of the floor of carotid triangle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded posteriorly by the sternocleidomastoid, superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and inferiorly by the superior belly of omohyoid. Its floor is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering the pharyngeal constrictors; specifically, the posterior part of the floor consists of the middle and inferior constrictors of the pharynx.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior floor of carotid triangle = middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The floor of anterior part of carotid triangle is formed of:
questions.explanation: The anterior part of the carotid triangle is bounded inferiorly by the superior belly of omohyoid medially and the anterior belly of digastric superiorly. The floor of the anterior part is formed by the mylohyoid muscle anteriorly and the hyoglossus muscle posteriorly, both of which lie deep to the contents of the submandibular region.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior floor of carotid triangle = mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle forms floor of anterior lower part of carotid triangle?
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is subdivided by the digastric and omohyoid muscles. The anterior lower part is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid posteriorly and the superior belly of omohyoid superiorly. The mylohyoid muscle forms its floor in the anterior lower part, separating the contents from the oral cavity structures.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of anterior lower carotid triangle = mylohyoid muscle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following arteries is a content of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck contains the subclavian artery (third part), trunks of the brachial plexus, spinal accessory nerve, transverse cervical artery, suprascapular artery, and external jugular vein. The transverse cervical artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk that crosses the floor of the posterior triangle to supply the trapezius muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse cervical artery is a content of the posterior triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The ansa cervicalis is found in:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a loop formed by the union of the descending hypoglossal nerve (C1) and descending cervical nerve (C2-C3). It lies superficial to the carotid sheath in the lower part of the carotid triangle. It runs on the anterior surface of the common carotid artery and supplies all infrahyoid muscles except the thyrohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis is found in the carotid triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which infrahyoid muscle is not supplied by the ansa cervicalis?
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid (both bellies), and thyrohyoid (via a branch from C1 to hypoglossal). However, the thyrohyoid is officially supplied by a branch from C1 that runs with the hypoglossal nerve and then descends as the nerve to thyrohyoid, bypassing the ansa cervicalis proper. Wait, among the options, thyrohyoid IS supplied by ansa fibers (C1) but NOT by the ansa loop itself. So E is the best answer.
questions.keyConcept: Thyrohyoid is supplied by nerve to thyrohyoid from C1 via hypoglossal, not by the ansa proper.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia invests all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia surrounds the neck like a collar, enclosing the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, submandibular gland, and parotid gland. The thyroid gland, however, is enclosed by the pretracheal fascia, not the investing fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Thyroid gland is enclosed by pretracheal fascia, not investing fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding sternocleidomastoid all are true Except:
questions.explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle arises from the manubrium sterni (anterior surface, not back) and the medial third of the clavicle. The anterior jugular vein crosses superficial (not deep) to the SCM in the superficial fascia. The external jugular vein is superficial to it, the lesser occipital nerve runs along its posterior border, and it is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior jugular vein crosses superficial, NOT deep, to sternocleidomastoid.
options: It arises from the back of the manubrium.
Anterior jugular vein crosses deep to it.
It is related superficially to the external jugular vein.
Lesser occipital nerve runs along its posterior border.
It is supplied by spinal part of accessory nerve.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of following muscles subdivides the posterior triangle of neck:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck is subdivided by the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle into the occipital triangle (above, larger) and the supraclavicular triangle (below, smaller). This muscle creates a visible muscular landmark during dissection and surgery and contains the accessory nerve superiorly.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior belly of omohyoid subdivides posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular triangles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following structures form floor of post. triangle of neck Except:
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by prevertebral muscles covered by prevertebral fascia: from above downward, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius, and scalenus posterior. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia forms the roof (superficial boundary), not the floor, of the posterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Investing fascia forms ROOF (not floor) of posterior triangle.
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sternocleidomastoid, omohyoid and trapezius bound which of the following triangles?
questions.explanation: The occipital triangle is the upper subdivision of the posterior triangle, bounded by the sternocleidomastoid anteriorly, the trapezius posteriorly, and the inferior belly of the omohyoid inferiorly. It contains the accessory nerve and trunks of the brachial plexus exiting between the scalene muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital triangle is bounded by SCM, trapezius, and inferior belly of omohyoid.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following lie in the posterior triangle of the neck Except:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle contains the spinal accessory nerve (superficial to floor), external jugular vein (superficial), trunks of brachial plexus (between scalene muscles), transverse cervical vessels, and suprascapular vessels. The first part of the subclavian artery, however, lies medial to the anterior scalene muscle in the root of the neck, not within the posterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: First part of subclavian artery is in root of neck, NOT posterior triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The anterior triangle of the neck includes all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The anterior triangle of the neck is bounded by the mandible superiorly, the sternocleidomastoid posterolaterally, and the midline anteriorly. It is subdivided into the submental triangle, digastric (submandibular) triangle, carotid triangle, and muscular triangle. The occipital triangle is part of the posterior triangle, not the anterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital triangle is part of posterior triangle, NOT anterior triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: One of the following arteries is not a content of the carotid triangle:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle contains the common carotid artery, its bifurcation, the internal carotid artery, and the external carotid artery with its branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial, ascending pharyngeal, occipital). The superficial temporal artery, however, is a terminal branch of the external carotid that ascends within the parotid gland behind the temporomandibular joint, outside the carotid triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery is NOT in carotid triangle; it is in parotid region.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following muscle bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly:
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded posteriorly by the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Anteriorly it is bounded by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric, and inferiorly by the superior belly of omohyoid. The sternocleidomastoid forms the posterior muscular boundary.
questions.keyConcept: Sternocleidomastoid bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following are contents of the digastric triangle Except:
questions.explanation: The digastric (submandibular) triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, hypoglossal nerve, lingual nerve, nerve to mylohyoid, and submandibular lymph nodes. The submental lymph nodes, however, are located in the submental triangle below the chin, not in the digastric triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Submental lymph nodes are in submental triangle, NOT digastric triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cutaneous nerve supply over the anterior triangle of the neck is largely from:
questions.explanation: The skin over the anterior triangle of the neck is supplied mainly by the transverse cutaneous nerve (transverse cervical nerve), a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3). It emerges from behind the sternocleidomastoid and runs horizontally across the anterior triangle to supply the skin over this region.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse cutaneous nerve (cervical plexus C2-C3) supplies skin of anterior triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following muscles are in the muscular triangle Except:
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid, and thyrohyoid. The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue that lies deep to the digastric triangle and floor of the mouth, not within the muscular triangle of the neck.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle, NOT an infrahyoid strap muscle in muscular triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient developed painful spasm of the neck muscles; this is most likely due to irritation of:
questions.explanation: Torticollis (wry neck) is characterized by painful spasm and contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, causing twisting of the neck. Since the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, irritation or injury to this nerve can trigger severe painful spasm of these muscles. The other options listed are purely cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus, which would cause sensory loss rather than muscle spasm.
questions.keyConcept: Painful neck muscle spasm (torticollis) is due to spinal accessory nerve irritation.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Ansa cervicalis is formed by fibers from:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a nerve loop formed by the union of the descending hypoglossal nerve (C1 fibers from the cervical plexus descending with the hypoglossal nerve) and the descending cervical nerve (C2-C3 fibers). It lies superficial to the carotid sheath and innervates the infrahyoid (strap) muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid, and thyrohyoid (the latter via a separate branch from C1, not through the ansa itself).
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis is formed by C1, C2, C3 fibers.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match the nerve in the left column with its related statement in the right column:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus gives cutaneous branches to the skin of the head, neck, and shoulder region. The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies skin over parotid gland and mastoid. The maxillary nerve (CN V2) carries general sensation from upper teeth. The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) carries taste from posterior one-third of tongue. The facial nerve (CN VII) controls lacrimal gland secretion. The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular = parotid skin; CN IX = taste posterior tongue; CN VII = lacrimal secretion; CN XI = SCM and trapezius.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following muscles receive motor fibers from the cervical nerves except:
questions.explanation: All infrahyoid and tongue-hyoid muscles in the list receive motor supply either from the cervical plexus (via ansa cervicalis or hypoglossal C1 fibers) or from cranial nerves. The mylohyoid is the exception, receiving its motor supply from the mandibular nerve (CN V3) via the nerve to mylohyoid, not from cervical spinal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Mylohyoid is supplied by mandibular nerve (CN V3), not cervical nerves.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Painful spasm of the neck muscles is most likely due to irritation of which nerve?
questions.explanation: Painful spasm of neck muscles, known as torticollis or wry neck, is most commonly caused by irritation of the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Irritation triggers involuntary painful contraction of these muscles, twisting the neck to one side. The other nerves listed are purely sensory cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Neck muscle spasm (torticollis) is due to spinal accessory nerve irritation.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following are cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus Except:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus (C1-C4) gives four main cutaneous branches: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2-C3), transverse cervical (C2-C3), and supraclavicular (C3-C4). The dorsal scapular nerve, however, arises from the ROOTS of the brachial plexus (C5) and primarily supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae; it is NOT a branch of the cervical plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal scapular nerve is from brachial plexus (C5), NOT cervical plexus.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The following are branches of the cervical plexus Except:
questions.explanation: The cervical plexus gives branches to the skin (cutaneous branches) and muscles. The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (formed by C5-C6), NOT from the cervical plexus. It supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. All other listed nerves (phrenic, great auricular, supraclavicular, lesser occipital) are cervical plexus branches.
questions.keyConcept: Suprascapular nerve arises from brachial plexus upper trunk (C5-C6), NOT cervical plexus.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The ansa cervicalis:
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis is a nerve loop composed of fibers from the first three cervical nerves (C1-C3) via descending hypoglossal and descending cervical roots. It lies superficial to the carotid sheath, often crossing the internal jugular vein. It supplies most infrahyoid muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid (but not thyrohyoid, which receives a separate C1 branch via the hypoglossal nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis = C1-C3 loop; lies on carotid sheath/IJV; supplies most infrahyoid muscles.
options: Is a nerve loop on the internal jugular vein.
Is formed of fibers from the upper three cervical nerves.
Supplies most of the infrahyoid muscles.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards investing layer of deep cervical fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia lies deep to the platysma, splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, forms the roof of the posterior triangle, and surrounds the submandibular and parotid glands. The sphenomandibular ligament, however, is an accessory ligament of the temporomandibular joint derived from Meckel's cartilage ( cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch), NOT from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament is from Meckel's cartilage, NOT from investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
options: It forms roof of posterior triangle of neck.
It is thickened to form Sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the boundaries of the posterior triangle of neck, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle of the neck is bounded anteriorly by the POSTERIOR border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (not the anterior border), posteriorly by the anterior border of the trapezius, inferiorly by the clavicle (base), superiorly by the meeting of SCM and trapezius (apex), with a roof formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and a floor formed by the prevertebral fascia overlying prevertebral and scalene muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle is bounded anteriorly by POSTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid, NOT anterior border.
options: Roof - investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following are contents of posterior triangle of neck EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle contains the spinal ACCESSORY nerve (not cranial part), trunks of the brachial plexus, transverse cervical artery and vein, suprascapular vessels, external jugular vein, and occipital artery. The cranial part of the accessory nerve joins the vagus nerve within the jugular foramen and exits the skull along with CN X; it does NOT enter or cross the posterior triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial part of accessory nerve joins vagus; spinal part crosses posterior triangle.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards contents of posterior triangle, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The transverse cervical artery (also known as the cervicodorsal trunk) usually arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. However, anatomical variations occur where the transverse cervical artery may arise directly from the subclavian artery as a deep branch (dorsal scapular artery). The suprascapular artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, not the costocervical trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse cervical artery may arise directly from subclavian artery as a variant.
options: Anterior jugular vein ends in subclavian vein.
Subclavian artery lies infront of Scalenus anterior.
Subclavian artery may give deep branch of transverse cervical artery.
Suprascapular artery is a branch of costocervical trunk.
Lymph nodes in lower part of triangle drain posterior 1/3 of scalp.
questions.chapterTitle: V. Anatomy of the Neck
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards submental triangle, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The submental triangle is bounded on each side by the ANTERIOR bellies of the digastric muscles (not posterior bellies), with the base formed by the hyoid bone and the apex at the symphysis menti of the mandible. It contains the submental lymph nodes and the facial artery. Since the boundary should be anterior bellies, stating posterior bellies is incorrect.
