questions.explanation: The sacral canal contains the filum terminale, cauda equina, cerebrospinal fluid, and the dural/arachnoid tube extending to S2. The ligamentum denticulatum anchors the spinal cord to the dura and does not extend into the sacral canal.
questions.keyConcept: Ligamentum denticulatum is absent in the sacral canal
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The spinal dura extends from the level of the foramen magnum to the level of which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Below this, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal dura extends from foramen magnum to S2
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the spinal cord; choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater does NOT continue below L1 as the filum terminale. The filum terminale is a pial structure extending from the conus medullaris to the coccyx, pierced by the dura and arachnoid at S2. The dura itself ends at S2.
questions.keyConcept: Filum terminale is pial, not dural; dura ends at S2
options: In adults, it ends at lower border of L1.
It is anchored to the dura mater by denticulate ligaments.
Its covering dura mater below the level of L1 forms filum terminale.
Lumbar puncture may be done between L3 and L4.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe the site of exit of spinal nerves from vertebral column.
questions.explanation: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves (C1-C7) exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebra. From T1-L1, nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebra. Below L1, the cauda equina (L2-S5 nerves) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective sacral foramina. This somatotopic arrangement is essential for interpreting segmental neurological deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerve exit above/below vertebrae and cauda equina arrangement
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves exit above their corresponding vertebra (C1-C7 exit above C1-C7). From T1-L1, nerves exit below their corresponding vertebra. The cauda equina (L2-S5) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective foramina.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion of frontal cortex in the dominant hemisphere results in all but one of the following:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) is caused by lesions of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe lesions cause expressive aphasia, contralateral paralysis, and behavioral changes.
questions.keyConcept: Receptive aphasia is temporal, not frontal lobe lesion
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding motor speech center, all statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia is caused by Wernicke's area lesion, not Broca's area. Broca's area is the motor speech center; its lesion causes expressive/motor aphasia, not receptive aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's lesion causes motor, not receptive aphasia
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Its lesion leads to receptive aphasia.
Lies in area of rami of lateral sulcus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Astereognosis & receptive aphasia characterize lesions in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and receptive aphasia (inability to understand language) are both features of dominant parietal lobe lesions, particularly involving the angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Dominant parietal lobe lesions cause astereognosis
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lawyer suffered a bad fall that resulted in head trauma. His motor, sensory, and language skills were intact after the incident, and he had no visual problems. In the following weeks, he began to lose interest in his work and did not seem to care much about his family. The trauma most likely affected the:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex controls personality, social behavior, and executive functions. A lawyer losing interest in work and not caring about family indicates damage to the prefrontal area, consistent with frontal lobe trauma.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal lesion causes personality/behavior changes
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection in the mastoid air cells may spread to which sinus?
questions.explanation: The sphenoparietal sinus is a tributary of the cavernous sinus, running along the lesser wing of sphenoid. It drains the dura of the frontal and parietal lobes.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenoparietal sinus tributary of cavernous sinus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sinus that runs along the junction between the flax cerebri and the tentorium cerebelli is the:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses in its upper and lower borders respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri between cerebral hemispheres with sagittal sinuses
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to the crista galli anteriorly and the tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri is dura between hemispheres
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Occlusion of this artery in dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia:
questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the posterior temporal lobe including Wernicke's area (sensory speech area). Occlusion of the PCA in the dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia), characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension. Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior cerebral artery supplies Wernicke's area; PCA occlusion in dominant hemisphere causes sensory aphasia.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: For the Retrolentiform part of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule is located posterior to the lentiform nucleus. It contains the optic radiations (visual fibers from the lateral geniculate body to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe) and parietotemporopontine fibers. Damage causes visual field defects such as homonymous hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform part contains optic radiations (visual fibers from lateral geniculate body to visual cortex).

pairs.target: Contains optic radiations (visual fibers from lateral geniculate body to visual cortex) and parietotemporopontine fibers

questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding the motor speech center, all the statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes. All other statements about motor speech center are true.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area supplied by MCA; damage causes expressive aphasia; connected to Wernicke's area.
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus
Its lesion leads to expressive aphasia
Is supplied by anterior cerebral artery
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does lesion of Areas 5 & 7 cause?
questions.explanation: Areas 5 and 7 are somatosensory association areas. Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and inability to judge size, shape, and texture of objects despite intact primary sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 5 & 7: somatosensory association cortex; lesion → astereognosis (tactile agnosia).
questions.modelAnswer: Astereognosis - inability to identify objects by touch despite intact primary sensation. The patient cannot recognize the size, shape, or texture of objects placed in their hand.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the site of inferior parietal lobule?
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule consists of the supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus) and the angular gyrus (around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule: supramarginal gyrus + angular gyrus. Part of Wernicke's area for language.
questions.modelAnswer: Supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of lateral sulcus) and angular gyrus (around the posterior end of superior temporal sulcus).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the 3 speech centers?
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech, inferior frontal gyrus), Wernicke's area (sensory speech, posterior superior temporal gyrus), and the supplementary motor area (medial frontal gyrus).
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (expressive), Wernicke's (receptive), supplementary motor area (planning).
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Broca's area - pars triangularis and opercularis of inferior frontal gyrus (expressive speech). 2) Wernicke's area - posterior superior temporal gyrus (receptive speech). 3) Supplementary motor area - medial frontal gyrus (speech planning and initiation).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does lesion of Areas 44 and 45 cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area) causes expressive (motor) aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension. The patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate words properly.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 44-45 (Broca's) lesion: expressive aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech, good comprehension.
questions.modelAnswer: Expressive (motor) aphasia - the patient has difficulty producing speech, speaks in short, effortful phrases, telegraphic speech. Comprehension is preserved. Patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate properly.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does the limbic lobe consist of?
questions.explanation: The limbic lobe consists of a C-shaped ring of cortical tissue including the subcallosal area, cingulate gyrus, isthmus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus, forming the emotional processing center of the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic lobe components and structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Subcallosal area (paraolfactory gyrus)
Cingulate gyrus
Isthmus
Parahippocampal gyrus
Uncus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate the long association fibers.
questions.explanation: The five major long association fibers are: superior longitudinal fasciculus (connecting frontal to parietal/occipital/temporal), inferior longitudinal fasciculus (temporal to occipital), fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus (frontal to temporal), and cingulum (cingulate to entorhinal cortex).
questions.keyConcept: Long association fibers and their connectivity
questions.modelAnswer: Superior longitudinal bundle, inferior longitudinal bundle, fronto occipital bundle, uncinate bundle, cingulum
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match the named cerebral vessels in left column with their corresponding anatomical sites in right column.
questions.explanation: The matching pairs are: Posterior cerebral winds round crus cerebri; Circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis) is in interpeduncular fossa; Basilar lies in median pontine groove; Anterior cerebral runs above corpus callosum; Middle cerebral lies in lateral sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral vessel anatomical relationships

pairs.target: b. Median groove on ventral surface of pons
e. above trunk of corpus callosum

questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arterial supply of upper 1/2 of internal capsule is derived from:
questions.explanation: Upper half of internal capsule is supplied by central branches of anterior cerebral artery; lower half receives branches from anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule upper half supply
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A patient develops behavioral changes and wears inappropriate clothing after an accident affecting frontal bone. Which cortical area is affected?
questions.explanation: The orbitofrontal cortex (ventromedial prefrontal cortex) is associated with personality, social behavior, and impulse control. Damage causes disinhibition, inappropriate social conduct, and lack of insight.
questions.keyConcept: Orbitofrontal lesions cause personality changes and social disinhibition due to impaired impulse control.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 28-year-old man sustains a head injury. After recovery, his family reports marked personality change. Which area is affected?
questions.explanation: Damage to the frontal lobe can cause personality changes, poor judgment, and inappropriate social behavior (pseudopendulous swinging describes cerebellar ataxia, not frontal lobe damage).
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe damage causes executive dysfunction and behavioral changes rather than primary motor deficits.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A young athlete sustains a head injury and later develops a severe headache followed by sudden death. Rupture of an aneurysm in which structure is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic headache with meningeal signs suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage. CT may be negative early; lumbar puncture would show xanthochromia (yellowtinged CSF from hemoglobin breakdown).
questions.keyConcept: Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache; CT may be initially negative requiring LP.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which blood vessel arises as a branch from the third part of the maxillary artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary artery (third part) and enters the middle cranial fossa through the foramen spinosum to supply the meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery from maxillary artery supplies the cranial meninges via foramen spinosum.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Site of inferior parietal lobule:
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule (areas 40, 39) is located below the intraparietal sulcus, behind the lateral sulcus, comprising supramarginal and angular gyri.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule
questions.modelAnswer: Below intraparietal sulcus, consisting of angular and supramarginal gyri.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of inferior parietal lobule causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule causes Gerstmann syndrome (left lesion): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: 3 speech centers:
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech), Wernicke's area (comprehension), and the arcuate fasciculus connecting them.
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers
questions.modelAnswer: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, arcuate fasciculus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Site of primary motor area:
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (M1) is located in the precentral gyrus (area 4) of the frontal lobe, anterior to the central sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor area
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus (area 4) of frontal lobe.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fracture of anterior cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically tear the cribriform plate, causing CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia; blood tracks into orbital contents producing subconjunctival hemorrhage and orbital ecchymosis.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, subconjunctival and orbital hemorrhage.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF rhinorrhea, orbital hemorrhage and subconjunctival hemorrhage.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Fracture of middle cranial fossa:
questions.explanation: Middle cranial fossa fractures frequently involve the petrous temporal bone, causing CSF otorrhea, Battle sign (mastoid bruising), and commonly affecting CN VII and VIII with facial paralysis and hearing loss.
questions.keyConcept: Middle fossa fracture: CSF otorrhea, Battle sign, CN 7 and 8 involvement.
questions.modelAnswer: Bleeding and CSF otorrhea, CN 7 & 8 involvement.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the condition of unilateral inattention (neglect)?
questions.explanation: Unilateral neglect syndrome involves ignoring stimuli from the contralateral side, often manifesting as failure to dress or groom that side, typically caused by right parietal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Neglect: ignoring contralateral stimuli, often with dressing/grooming deficits on that side.
options: Loss of all sensation on one side of the body
Ignoring stimuli from the opposite side, often with failure to dress or shave that side
Loss of proprioception with preserved touch
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cauda equina is composed of:
questions.explanation: The cauda equina (horse's tail) consists of the dorsal and ventral roots of the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves traveling within the subarachnoid space below L1-2.
questions.keyConcept: Cauda equina: dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral, coccygeal nerves.
options: The lower part of the spinal cord
Dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerves
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Retrolentiform part of internal capsule DOESN'T transmit:
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of internal capsule contains visual radiation, occipito-pontine, and parieto-pontine fibers, but the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform: visual/occipito-parieto-pontine fibers; auditory goes sublentiform.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the speech areas:
questions.explanation: Speech areas are typically asymmetric; Broca's and Wernicke's areas are usually dominant in one hemisphere (left in right-handers), not equally present in both.
questions.keyConcept: Speech areas are not present equally in both hemispheres.
options: Motor area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Sensory area lies in parietal and temporal lobes.
Sensory area is concerned with understanding visual and auditory information.
Both areas are present in both cerebral hemispheres.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match the cortical area in column A with the result of lesion in column B.
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area lesion: word comprehension loss; primary auditory: decreased hearing; secondary auditory: sound understanding; frontal eye field: voluntary gaze loss; primary visual: hemianopia with macular sparing.
questions.keyConcept: Lesion effects: Wernicke (comprehension), 1ary auditory (hearing), 2ary auditory (sound meaning), eye field (gaze), 1ary visual (hemianopia).

pairs.target: Inability to understand written or spoken words.
Loss of voluntary conjugate eye movement.

questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The dural fold which is attached to the skull vault is:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves is not related to cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: The inferior sagittal sinus runs along the lower free margin of the falx cerebri and drains into the straight sinus. It receives blood from the medial aspects of the cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior sagittal sinus in lower falx cerebri
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the branches of glossopharyngeal nerve.
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) gives off: tympanic branch (to middle ear and meninges), carotid branch (to carotid body and sinus), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus), tonsillar branches (to tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue).
questions.keyConcept: CN IX branches: tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular (stylopharyngeus), tonsillar, lingual.
questions.modelAnswer: Tympanic branch (to middle ear and mastoid air cells), carotid branch (to carotid sinus and body), pharyngeal branches (to pharyngeal mucosa), muscular branch (to stylopharyngeus muscle), tonsillar branches (to palatine tonsil), and lingual branches (to posterior 1/3 of tongue for taste and general sensation).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A lesion in the Broca’s area of the cerebral hemisphere leads to:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It coordinates the motor aspects of speech production. Lesions here cause motor aphasia with hesitant, non-fluent speech but preserved comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area lesion causes motor aphasia
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Broca’s area.
questions.explanation: Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus controls motor speech production. Lesions in the dominant hemisphere cause motor aphasia (difficulty producing speech with preserved comprehension).
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area causes motor aphasia when lesioned
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Frontal lobe in dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, not in the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe contains areas 4, 6, 8, and supplementary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area is in temporal lobe, not frontal
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is the motor speech center present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). It is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and coordinates speech production, not sensory aspects.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area present in dominant hemisphere only
options: It is located in middle frontal gyrus.
It is present in the dominant hemisphere.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Parietal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following Except:
questions.explanation: Facial recognition is processed in the inferior temporal lobe (fusiform gyrus), not the parietal lobe. The parietal lobe is concerned with stereognosis, proprioception, and spatial processing.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal, not parietal lobe
options: Comprehension of received auditory & visual information.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cortical areas in temporal lobe include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral eye movements is the occipital eye field (area 18), not the temporal lobe. The temporal lobe contains auditory areas and parts of Wernicke's area and facial recognition area.
questions.keyConcept: Involuntary eye movement control is occipital, not temporal
options: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral movements of eye.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Regarding Broca’s area, select the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (not middle) and is a motor speech center (not sensory). It is present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) and is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not anterior cerebral artery.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area: motor speech center in inferior frontal gyrus of dominant hemisphere, supplied by MCA.
options: It is a sensory speech center
It is located in middle frontal gyrus
It is present in the dominant hemisphere
It is supplied by anterior cerebral artery
None of the above is correct
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Frontal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following functions Except:
questions.explanation: Understanding received auditory information (receptive language) is a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe handles speech production, skilled movements, eye movement initiation, and behavior control.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe functions: speech production (Broca), skilled movements, conjugate eye movements, behavior control.
options: Initiation of conjugate lateral eye movements
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Frontal lobe in the non-dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus), not in the frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere. The non-dominant hemisphere contains the same motor areas as the dominant but lacks speech areas.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere frontal lobe contains motor areas (4,6,8) but NOT Wernicke's area (temporal lobe).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Broca’s area is located in......
questions.explanation: Broca's area (expressive speech center) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (usually left), Brodmann areas 44 and 45.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus controls motor speech production.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A 52‑year‑old man has had progressive headaches and concentration difficulties for two months. His behaviour becomes odd, and he then suffers a generalised seizure. MRI shows a large, necrotic mass in the left cerebral hemisphere that crosses the corpus callosum into the right hemisphere. Which neoplasm is most likely?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme typically crosses the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma), shows necrosis and ring enhancement, and has poor prognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma features
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Site of Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area (speech apraxia) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of the dominant hemisphere, usually the left.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area location
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of dominant hemisphere.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lesion of Broca’s area:
questions.explanation: Lesion of Broca's area causes expressive (motor) aphasia: non-fluent speech with good comprehension but impaired repetition.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Expressive aphasia: non-fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the prefrontal cortex?
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex mediates executive functions including planning, decision-making, personality expression, and social behavior, distinguishing humans from other primates.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal cortex: executive functions and personality.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The genu of the corpus callosum is supplied mainly by the:
questions.explanation: The ACA supplies the genu of the corpus callosum.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of corpus callosum supplied by anterior cerebral artery.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The supplementary motor area is located in the:
questions.explanation: The SMA lies on the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the leg area.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area located in medial aspect of frontal lobe (medial area 6).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Broca's motor speech area lies in the:
questions.explanation: Broca's area = pars opercularis/triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Brocas motor speech area in inferior frontal gyrus (dominant hemisphere).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The spinal dura mater ends at the vertebral level of:
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale to form the coccygeal ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal dura mater ends at S2
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Arachnoid mater of spinal cord ends at the level of which vertebra:
questions.explanation: The spinal arachnoid mater extends to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal arachnoid mater ends at S2
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the
questions.explanation: Denticulate ligaments are pial extensions that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater laterally; the coccygeal ligament (filum terminale externum) attaches the cord terminus to the coccyx.
questions.keyConcept: Denticulate ligaments spinal cord anchoring
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Protrusion of meninges and brain tissue through a defect in the skull is:
questions.explanation: Meningoencephalocele involves protrusion of both meninges and brain tissue through a skull defect; meningocele involves only meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Meningoencephalocele: meninges and brain tissue protrude through skull defect.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the blood supply of internal capsule.
questions.explanation: The internal capsule blood supply varies by region: the upper anterior and posterior limbs receive MCA branches; the lower anterior limb and genu receive ACA branches; the lower posterior limb receives the anterior choroidal artery; and the retrolentiform/sublentiform parts receive the anterior choroidal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule vascular supply zones
questions.modelAnswer:
Upper half of anterior limb and upper half of posterior limb: MCA
Lower ½ of anterior limb and genu: ACA
Lower ½ of posterior limb: Post communicating and anterior choroidal artery
Retrolentiform and Sublentiform: Anterior choroidal artery
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery supply:
questions.explanation: ACA supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory for lower limb), medial aspect of frontal/parietal lobes; auditory cortex is supplied by MCA, not ACA.
questions.keyConcept: ACA supply territories
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Lateral boundaries:
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle consist of the superior cerebellar peduncle superiorly, the inferior cerebellar peduncle and gracile/cuneate tracts inferiorly, and the lateral recess extending toward the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral boundaries: SCP above, ICP and dorsal columns below, lateral recess.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: SCP; Inferiorly: ICP + gracile and cuneate tracts; Lateral recess.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle are: superiorly = the superior cerebellar peduncle; inferiorly = the inferior cerebellar peduncle plus the gracile and cuneate tracts; laterally = the lateral recess (extending toward the cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle lateral boundaries: superior = SCP, inferior = ICP + gracile/cuneate tracts, lateral recess.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior cerebellar peduncle. Inferiorly: inferior cerebellar peduncle and the gracile and cuneate tracts. The lateral boundary also includes the lateral recess, which extends toward the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Concerning the fourth ventricle; choose the most correct answer:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof
options: Its floor is formed by the closed medulla and pons.
Its roof is formed by the superior and inferior medullary vela.
Its choroids plexus is present in the floor of the ventricle.
It has a communication with the lateral ventricle.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe roof of 4th ventricle.
questions.explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle has two layers: (1) SUPERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - connects the superior cerebellar peduncles, contains lingula and central lobule of cerebellum; (2) INFERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - stretches between the two inferior cerebellar peduncles; (3) The fastigium marks the apex of the roof. The roof is completed by the cerebellar vermis and its white matter. Choroid plexus protrudes through the lateral apertures.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela, fastigium (apex), cerebellar vermis
questions.modelAnswer: STRUCTURES IN TEGMENTUM PONTIS: (1) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: Abducent, facial, vestibulocochlear; (2) TRACT: Medial longitudinal fasciculus; (3) LEMNISCI: Medial lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus; (4) NUCLEI: Superior olivary, cochlear, vestibular, nuclei of reticular formation; (5) PYRAMID does NOT continue here (interrupted by transverse fibers).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following structures lies between limbs of inferior fovea?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is a bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve wrapping around it. It lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus between limbs of inferior fovea
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers that loop around it (the facial nerve genu). This creates a prominence in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus overlies abducent nucleus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cranial dura is supplied by all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The cranial dura mater receives sensory innervation from the maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), as well as from upper cervical spinal nerves (C1-C3) via the hypoglossal, vagus, and glossopharyngeal nerves (for the posterior cranial fossa). The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) does NOT supply the cranial dura; its sensory fibers are distributed to the pharynx, middle ear, carotid sinus, and posterior tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) does NOT innervate the cranial dura.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is considered as a multiple venous sinus?
questions.explanation: The basilar plexus of sinuses is an irregular, intercommunicating venous plexus located on the dorsum sellae and basi-occiput, posterior to the cavernous sinuses. It connects the two inferior petrosal sinuses and communicates with the vertebral venous plexus and internal vertebral venous plexus, forming an important alternative venous drainage pathway from the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar plexus of sinuses is a multiple/intercommunicating venous plexus posterior to cavernous sinuses.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe pterygoid plexus of veins.
questions.explanation: The pterygoid plexus of veins is a network of veins located around the lateral and medial pterygoid muscles in the infratemporal fossa. It receives tributaries from the deep facial vein, middle meningeal veins, sphenopalatine veins, and branches corresponding to the maxillary artery. It drains via the maxillary vein into the retromandibular vein.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus connects maxillary veins to cavernous sinus via emissary veins.
questions.modelAnswer: The pterygoid plexus of veins is located in the infratemporal fossa around the pterygoid muscles. It receives tributaries corresponding to the branches of the maxillary artery (deep temporal, pterygoid, masseteric, buccal, middle meningeal, inferior alveolar veins), the sphenopalatine vein, and veins from the nasal cavity and palate. It communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins through the foramen lacerum, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum. It drains posteriorly into the maxillary vein, which continues as the retromandibular vein.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Foramen spinosum gives passage to:
questions.explanation: Foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and transmits the middle meningeal artery (and its associated vein) into the cranial cavity. The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery and is the main arterial supply to the meninges. Foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve; foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery (branch of maxillary artery) into the cranial cavity.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Greater wing of sphenoid shows:
questions.explanation: The greater wing of the sphenoid bone shows the foramen rotundum (transmitting maxillary nerve from middle cranial fossa to pterygopalatine fossa), as well as the superior orbital fissure, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum. The hypoglossal canal, mastoid foramen, sigmoid sinus, and carotid canal are features of the occipital and temporal bones, not the greater wing of sphenoid.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen rotundum is in the greater wing of sphenoid; transmits maxillary nerve (CN V2) to pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which structure receives the drainage of the inferior petrosal sinus as it exits the cranial cavity?
questions.explanation: The inferior petrosal sinus drains into the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen. It receives blood from the cavernous sinus and drains the inferior part of the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior petrosal sinus drains directly into the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Borders of open medulla:
questions.explanation: The open medulla's borders are defined by the medullary striae marking the base (floor of fourth ventricle), the apex continuous with the central canal, and the hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones forming the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Open medulla borders: striae at base, central canal at apex, trigones as floor.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary striae; Apex: continuous with central canal; Floor: hypoglossal, vagal, and vestibular trigones.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Paired sinuses:
questions.explanation: The paired dural sinuses include sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse sinuses, occurring on both sides of the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
questions.modelAnswer: Sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of trigeminal nerve & structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) runs in the superior wall (roof) of the cavernous sinus, along with the oculomotor and abducent nerves. The ophthalmic nerve (V1) runs in the lateral wall.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV in superior wall of cavernous sinus
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF TRIGEMINAL NERVE: (1) MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) in pons → muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric; (2) PRINCIPAL SENSORY NUCLEUS (GSA) in pons → discriminative/light touch from face; (3) SPINAL NUCLEUS (GSA) in medulla → pain and temperature from face; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS in midbrain → proprioception from mastication muscles, teeth, TMJ.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle. The facial motor nucleus is more lateral, and the hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nucleus: floor of 4th ventricle, lower pons, near midline; supplies lateral rectus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which structure receives its sensory innervation from the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The dura mater receives sensory innervation from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The anterior cranial fossa is innervated by V1, the middle cranial fossa by V2 and V3.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater sensory innervation is provided by all three trigeminal divisions via meningeal branches.
options: Skin over the angle of the mandible
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle overlies the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: In dorsal surface of medulla oblongata, choose CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea
options: Gracile tubercle is the most medial structure of open medulla.
Base of open medulla is formed by medullary stria.
Vestibular trigone lies between limbs of inferior fovea.
Hypoglossal trigone forms most medial trigone of superior fovea.
Apex of open medulla is continuous with cerebral aqueduct.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - connects medulla to cerebellum; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - visible at the pontomedullary junction; (3) FLOOR OF FOURTH VENTRICLE: divided into MEDULLARY TRIGONE (containing hypoglossal trigone over hypoglossal nucleus and vagal trigone over dorsal motor nucleus of X) and PONTINE TRIGONE. The gracile and cuneate tubercles (over dorsal column nuclei) are visible above the trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal medulla: inferior/middle cerebellar peduncles, hypoglossal and vagal trigones in fourth ventricle floor
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI IN MEDULLA: (SOMATIC EFFERENT) Hypoglossal nucleus; (VISCERAL EFFERENT) Dorsal motor nucleus of X, inferior salivary nucleus; (VISCERAL AFFERENT) Nucleus solitarius; (TRIGEMINAL) Spinal nucleus of V; (AUDITORY) Cochlear nuclei; (VESTIBULAR) Vestibular nuclei; (OTHER) Olivary nuclei, cuneate/gracile nuclei, accessory cuneate nucleus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of pons.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the pons forms the upper part of the floor of the fourth ventricle: (1) FACIAL COLLICULUS - elevation over abducens nucleus and facial nerve fibers internally; (2) TRIGEMINAL TUBERCLE - over the principal sensory nucleus of CN V; (3) MEDIAL EMINENCE - longitudinal elevation; (4) SUPERIOR and INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES form the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle at this level.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal pons: facial colliculus, trigeminal tubercle, forms upper fourth ventricle floor with peduncles as lateral borders
questions.modelAnswer: INFERIOR OLIVARY COMPLEX: (COMPONENTS) Main olivary nucleus (folded gray matter), medial accessory olivary nucleus, dorsal accessory olivary nucleus; (CONNECTIONS) Receives input from red nucleus, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex; (OUTPUT) Olivocerebellar fibers cross and enter cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle; (FUNCTION) Involved in motor learning and coordination.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Describe the arterial supply of medulla oblongata.
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale gives passage to emissary veins connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus of veins. This provides a route for infection spread from face to meninges.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen ovale has emissary veins of cavernous sinus
questions.modelAnswer: ARTERIAL SUPPLY OF MEDULLA: (1) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY → supplies medial medulla (pyramids, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus) - thrombosis causes medial medullary syndrome; (2) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → supply lateral surfaces; (3) POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) → supplies lateral medulla (olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular/cochlear nuclei) - thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome; (4) Direct medullary branches from vertebral arteries.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducens nucleus (CN VI) and internal genu of facial nerve - located on the floor of the 4th ventricle in the pons.选项E正确. The answer is E. It's a bulge caused by these nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: overlies abducens nucleus and facial nerve genu - floor of fourth ventricle in pons.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What forms the floor of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle has two parts: pontine part (upper) showing medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; and medullary part (lower) showing hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle floor: pontine = eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area; medullary = hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones.
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part: medial eminence, facial colliculus (CN VI nucleus with CN VII fibers), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei). Medullary part: hypoglossal trigone (over hypoglossal nucleus), vagal trigone (over dorsal vagal nucleus), and vestibular trigone (vestibular nuclei).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Floor of fourth ventricle:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle floor has two parts: the pontine part contains the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; the medullary part contains the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of fourth ventricle: pontine (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area) and medullary (three trigones).
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine part (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area); Medullary part (hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, vestibular trigone).

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A tumor in the floor of the fourth ventricle (facial colliculus region) most directly damages which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus in the floor of the 4th ventricle overlies the abducent (CN VI) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: facial nerve wraps around abducens nucleus in floor of fourth ventricle.

questions.text: The cisterna magna of subarachnoid space is a name given to the:
questions.explanation: The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern located between the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.
questions.keyConcept: Cisterna magna location
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of GVE column & the structures supplied by each nucleus.
questions.explanation: The inferior petrosal sinus connects the cavernous sinus to the internal jugular vein. It passes through the jugular foramen along with the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior petrosal connects cavernous sinus to IJV
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GVE COLUMN: (1) EDINGER-WESTPHAL NUCLEUS (III) in midbrain → ciliary ganglion → ciliary muscle and sphincter pupillae; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (VII) → pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia → lacrimal, nasal, palatal glands, submandibular, sublingual glands; (3) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (IX) → otic ganglion → parotid gland; (4) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X → cardiac, pulmonary, GI parasympathetic.

questions.text: A patient with an abscess in the upper lip was advised not to squeeze it for fear of spread of pus to a venous sinus inside skull.
questions.explanation: The facial vein lacks valves and communicates with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins. Squeezing an abscess in the upper lip (danger triangle) can force infected thrombi into the cavernous sinus, causing thrombosis.
questions.keyConcept: Upper lip abscess → risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis via valveless facial vein

subQuestions.text: What is the name of sinus at risk?
subQuestions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via valveless ophthalmic veins, making it the sinus at risk.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Facial vein → cavernous sinus via ophthalmic veins
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Cavernous sinus.

subQuestions.text: Describe 2 alternate pathways for passage of infection to the sinus.
subQuestions.explanation: The facial vein has two main connections to the cavernous sinus: directly via the superior ophthalmic vein and indirectly via the deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Facial vein connects to cavernous sinus via superior ophthalmic vein and pterygoid plexus
subQuestions.modelAnswer: First pathway: via the angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus. Second pathway: via the deep facial vein → pterygoid plexus → emissary veins → cavernous sinus.

subQuestions.text: What other areas have similar risk?
subQuestions.explanation: These areas drain into the facial vein and its tributaries, which communicate with the cavernous sinus without valves.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Danger triangle includes medial eye, nose, and upper lip
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The upper lip, nose, and medial angle of the eye (danger triangle of the face) have similar risk because the facial vein is valveless and communicates with the cavernous sinus.

questions.text: A 12-years old boy fell from a bicycle & wounded his scalp. At the hospital, the doctor sutured the wound to limit its gaping & to stop the bleeding. Later, the boy returned to the hospital with black eye. The doctor prescribed an antibiotic to avoid dangerous complications.
questions.explanation: Scalp bleeding requires suturing because dense connective tissue prevents vasoconstriction. Gaping indicates aponeurosis involvement. Black eye results from blood tracking through loose areolar tissue to the eyelids. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a dangerous complication.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp wound complications: profuse bleeding, black eye, cavernous sinus thrombosis

subQuestions.text: Why scalp bleeding cannot be stopped except by suturing?
subQuestions.explanation: Dense fibrous septa in the subcutaneous tissue hold vessels open, preventing natural vasoconstriction.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Scalp dense fibrous tissue prevents vasoconstriction → requires suturing
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the fibrous tissue in the connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in this layer.

subQuestions.text: Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of which layer of scalp?
subQuestions.explanation: The epicranial aponeurosis is inelastic; when cut, the frontalis and occipitalis muscles retract, causing the wound to gape.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Aponeurosis cut → wound gapes due to muscle retraction
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis muscle.

subQuestions.text: Explain the development of black eye.
subQuestions.explanation: Blood in the subaponeurotic layer tracks anteriorly beneath the frontalis to the eyelids due to gravity.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Subaponeurotic hematoma tracks to eyelids → black eye
subQuestions.modelAnswer: If the wound causes subaponeurotic hematoma, the blood gravitates to the eyelids deep to the frontal bellies of the occipito-frontalis muscle which are attached to the skin of eyebrows, and so hematoma extends deep to it and reaches eyelids causing black eye.

subQuestions.text: What dangerous complication did the doctor expect?
subQuestions.explanation: Infected blood from the scalp can spread via emissary veins to the cavernous sinus, causing thrombosis.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Scalp infection can spread via emissary veins → cavernous sinus thrombosis
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.text: Give an idea about lumbar puncture.
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF or inject medications. The safe site is between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below the L4 spinous process). The patient is positioned on the side or sitting forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, and arachnoid mater to reach the subarachnoid space containing CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture site (L3-L4/L4-L5), layers traversed, and subarachnoid CSF space
questions.modelAnswer: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF for diagnosis or inject medication/anesthesia. Site: between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below L4 spine). The patient lies on side or sits forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater to reach subarachnoid space (containing CSF).

questions.text: A 25 year old patient had an operation under spinal anesthesia. During recovery, he could not feel the back of his lower limb with difficulty in climbing the stairs by the right foot.
questions.explanation: This case describes normal anatomy during lumbar puncture: The correct lumbar puncture site is just above or below the L4 spinous process (L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace). The spinal cord normally ends at the lower border of L1 vertebra in adults. The meninges terminate at: Dura and arachnoid end at S2; Pia mater continues as filum terminale to the coccyx. These are safe landmarks because the cauda equina floats freely in the subarachnoid space below L1.

questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The nerve that runs in the floor of the cavernous sinus is:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve and oculomotor nerve are not related to the cavernous sinus. The optic nerve is in the optic canal; the oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal (V1, V2), and abducent nerves traverse the cavernous sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve not related to cavernous sinus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sinus that runs along the lesser wing of sphenoid is:
questions.explanation: The straight sinus (not cavernous) is enclosed within the tentorium cerebelli at its attachment to the falx cerebri. The cavernous sinus is in the middle cranial fossa, lateral to the sella turcica.
questions.keyConcept: Straight sinus enclosed in tentorium cerebelli
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The inferior petrosal sinus connects the cavernous sinus to the:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the greater wing of the sphenoid, not through the cavernous sinus. It passes through the foraman spinosum to supply the dura.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery not in cavernous sinus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following foramina gives passage to emissary veins of the cavernous sinuses?
questions.explanation: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery causes extradural hemorrhage. This arterial bleeding creates a biconvex/lens-shaped collection that can cause rapid deterioration due to arterial pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery causes extradural hematoma
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The most superior nerve that runs in lateral wall of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: Extradural hematoma occurs due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery, which passes through the foramen spinosum in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. This creates the classic 'lens-shaped' hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen spinosum transmits middle meningeal artery
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The sinus that is enclosed within the tentorium cerebelli is:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus lies between the outer (endosteal) and inner (meningeal) layers of dura, but NOT between the layers of the falx cerebri. The falx contains the sagittal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus not between falx cerebri layers
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Cavernous sinus is related laterally to:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery is NOT a tributary of the cavernous sinus. It is a branch of the maxillary artery that supplies the dura. The cavernous sinus receives the sphenoparietal sinus, superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, and middle cerebral vein.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery not tributary of cavernous sinus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards the cavernous sinus, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein is not a direct communication of the cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus communicates with the pterygoid plexus (via foramen ovale), superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, and ultimately the internal jugular via the inferior petrosal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus communicates via petrosal sinuses, not directly to IJV
options: Internal carotid artery runs in its floor.
Abducent nerve is embedded in its lateral wall.
It receives the ophthalmic veins anteriorly.
It is connected with pterygoid plexus of veins.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: A tributary of cavernous sinus is:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery supplies the dura of the cranial vault, particularly the lateral parts. It does not supply the dura of the cranial base, which is supplied by other arteries like the occipital and vertebral arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery supplies dura of vault
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The venous sinus enclosed within the lower concave margin of the falx cerebri is:
questions.explanation: The inferior sagittal sinus runs along the lower free margin of the falx cerebri before draining into the straight sinus. The superior sagittal sinus runs along the upper attached border.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior sagittal sinus in lower falx margin
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following venous sinuses lie between outer (endosteal) & inner (meningeal) layers of dura EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is located between the meningeal and endosteal layers of dura in the middle cranial fossa. It is NOT between the layers of the falx cerebri, which contains the sagittal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus between meningeal layers in middle fossa
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following are tributaries of cavernous sinus EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery is NOT a tributary of the cavernous sinus. It is a branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid system) that supplies the dura through the foramen spinosum. Cavernous sinus tributaries include sphenoparietal sinus and ophthalmic veins.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal not tributary of cavernous sinus
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The cavernous sinus communicates with all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus does not communicate directly with the internal jugular vein. It drains indirectly via the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, which connect to the transverse/sigmoid sinuses and ultimately the jugular bulb.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains via petrosal sinuses, not directly to IJV
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following structures is embedded in the lateral wall of cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) runs within the cavernous sinus, not in its lateral wall. The lateral wall contains the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic (V1), and maxillary (V2) nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CN VI inside cavernous sinus, not in lateral wall
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Middle meningeal artery supplies dura of:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery supplies the dura mater of the cranial vault (convexities), not the cranial base. The base of the skull dura is supplied by branches from the vertebral, ascending pharyngeal, and other arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal supplies vault dura, not base
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: All the following are paired sinuses Except:
questions.explanation: Most dural venous sinuses are paired, including the cavernous sinuses, transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses, superior petrosal sinuses, inferior petrosal sinuses, and occipital sinuses. The straight sinus, however, is an unpaired midline structure formed by the union of the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein (vein of Galen) at the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.
questions.keyConcept: Straight sinus is unpaired; most other dural venous sinuses are paired.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: As regards relations of cavernous sinus, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is located in the middle cranial fossa on either side of the sella turcica, not in the posterior cranial fossa. Statement A is incorrect. It lies between the superior orbital fissure anteriorly and the apex of the petrous temporal bone posteriorly, rests on the body and greater wing of the sphenoid bone, receives blood from facial and ophthalmic veins, and transmits pulsations from the internal carotid artery to promote venous outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus is in the middle cranial fossa, NOT the posterior cranial fossa.
options: It lies in posterior cranial fossa.
The endosteal dura forms its roof.
It lies between inferior orbital fissure & apex of petreous temporal bone.
It lies on either side of greater wing of sphenoid.
Expansile pulsation of external carotid artery helps the passing of the blood outside the sinus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which one of the following structures is not embedded in lateral wall of cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), ophthalmic nerve (V1), and maxillary nerve (V2), arranged from superior to inferior. The abducent nerve (CN VI) is the exception—it runs through the body of the cavernous sinus, lateral to the internal carotid artery, not in the lateral wall.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nerve (CN VI) runs through the body of cavernous sinus, not its lateral wall.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Enumerate structures embedded in lateral wall of cavernous sinus & the structures running within its cavity.
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus contains important cranial nerves and vascular structures in its lateral wall and cavity. Understanding these relationships is crucial for diagnosing cavernous sinus pathologies such as thrombosis, carotid-cavernous fistula, and tumors.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall: CN III, IV, V1, V2. Body: ICA and CN VI.
questions.modelAnswer: Structures embedded in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), ophthalmic nerve (V1), and maxillary nerve (V2). Structures running within the cavity of the cavernous sinus: internal carotid artery with its sympathetic plexus (medial side), and the abducent nerve (CN VI) lateral to the internal carotid artery.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Foramen ovale gives passage to:
questions.explanation: Foramen ovale is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), accessory meningeal artery, and emissary veins connecting the cavernous sinus to the pterygoid venous plexus. Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery. The internal carotid artery passes through the carotid canal, not foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Foramen ovale transmits mandibular nerve (CN V3), accessory meningeal artery; foramen spinosum transmits middle meningeal artery.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Which one of the following is a part of the posterior cranial fossa?
questions.explanation: The transverse sulcus (for the transverse sinus) runs across the occipital bone and forms part of the posterior cranial fossa floor. The body of the sphenoid and crista galli are in the middle and anterior cranial fossae respectively. The cribriform plate is in the anterior cranial fossa. The lesser wing of sphenoid forms the posterior limit of the anterior cranial fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse sulcus is in posterior cranial fossa (occipital bone); marks the junction with middle cranial fossa.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Infection from dangerous area of face may be transmitted to the following venous sinus:
questions.explanation: Infection from dangerous area of face (upper lip, nose, orbit) may spread via facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus.选项E正确. The answer is E. This is why facial infections can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.keyConcept: Facial vein connects to cavernous sinus via angular and superior ophthalmic veins - spread route for infection.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: The falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri: a dura mater fold between cerebral hemispheres, attached to crista galli anteriorly and tentorium posteriorly, contains superior sagittal sinus.选项B正确. The answer is B. It prevents hemisphere displacement.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dura fold between hemispheres, contains superior sagittal sinus - prevents midline shift.
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does lesion of inferior parietal lobule cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule (dominant hemisphere) causes receptive (sensory) aphasia - difficulty understanding language. In the non-dominant hemisphere, it causes contralateral hemisensory neglect.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule lesion: dominant hemisphere → receptive aphasia (Wernicke's area connections).
questions.modelAnswer: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) - fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. Patient speaks fluently but cannot understand or produce meaningful language.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What are the borders of the open medulla?
questions.explanation: The open medulla has the following borders: base = the medullary stria ( fibers crossing to cerebellum), apex = continuous with the cerebral aqueduct above and central canal below, floor = hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular area.
questions.keyConcept: Open medulla borders: base = stria; apex = aqueduct/canal; floor = hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones.
questions.modelAnswer: Base: medullary stria (transverse fibers crossing to cerebellum). Apex: continuous superiorly with cerebral aqueduct and inferiorly with central canal. Floor: hypoglossal trigone (overlies hypoglossal nucleus), vagal trigone (overlies dorsal vagal nucleus), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What does fracture of anterior cranial fossa cause?
questions.explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically cause CSF rhinorrhea (cerebrospinal fluid leaking through nose), orbital hemorrhage, and subconjunctival ecchymosis (blood tracking into the orbit and around eyes).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cranial fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, orbital hemorrhage, subconjunctival hemorrhage.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea (CSF leak from nose due to meningeal tear), hemorrhage into the orbital cavity causing orbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), and subconjunctival hemorrhage. May also cause anosmia if olfactory nerves are damaged.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the 4 single sinuses.
questions.explanation: The four single (unpaired) dural venous sinuses are: superior sagittal sinus (in falx cerebri superiorly), inferior sagittal sinus (in falx cerebri inferiorly), straight sinus (confluence of falx and tentorium), and occipital sinus (in falx cerebelli).
questions.keyConcept: Single sinuses: superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, occipital.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior sagittal sinus (in upper border of falx cerebri), inferior sagittal sinus (in lower border of falx cerebri), straight sinus (junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli), and occipital sinus (in falx cerebelli).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: List the 6 paired sinuses.
questions.explanation: The six paired dural venous sinuses are: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse. These drain blood from the brain to the internal jugular vein via the sigmoid sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
questions.modelAnswer: Sphenoparietal sinus (along lesser wing of sphenoid), cavernous sinus (lateral to sella turcica), superior petrosal sinus (along petrous ridge), inferior petrosal sinus (below petrous ridge), sigmoid sinus (continuation to jugular bulb), and transverse sinus (in tentorium cerebelli).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention the structures present inside the cavernous sinus.
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus) and several cranial nerves: oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), maxillary division (V2), and abducent (VI).
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus contents: ICA, CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI. Important clinical relevance for cavernous sinus syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), maxillary nerve (CN V2), abducent nerve (CN VI), and the internal carotid artery (with its surrounding sympathetic plexus). These structures run in the lateral wall (nerves) and center (ICA) of the sinus.
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: Mention 4 tributaries of the cavernous sinus
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus receives blood from: superior ophthalmic vein (from orbit), inferior ophthalmic vein, central vein of retina, and superficial middle cerebral vein. These tributaries drain the orbit and cerebral surface.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus tributaries: superior/inferior ophthalmic veins, central retinal vein, superficial middle cerebral vein.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior ophthalmic vein (draining the orbit and face), inferior ophthalmic vein, central vein of retina, and superficial middle cerebral vein (draining the cerebral cortex).
questions.chapterTitle: VII. Cerebrum, Meninges & Higher Brain
questions.subject: anatomy

questions.text: What is the drainage of the cavernous sinus
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus drains posteriorly via the superior petrosal sinus (to transverse-sigmoid sinus junction) and inferiorly via the inferior petrosal sinus (directly to internal jugular bulb).
